p: A note from Ilaria

Hi, I’m Ilaria. I wrote these guides to share what I’ve learned about RVC while developing Ilaria RVC, training voice models and working with other tools. The explanations and recommendations reflect my experience and what I understand at the time of writing. I can misunderstand a setting, miss an exception or describe a step that changes in a later release.

The same instructions can give different results on another computer. For example, a button might move after an update, a feature may depend on your GPU or driver, and settings that work for one voice might sound worse on another. When you see a suggested value, treat it as a starting point. Try it on a short clip and compare the result before using it on a whole project. Before replacing files or updating a working installation, keep a copy you can come back to.

If something doesn’t match what you see, check the app name, version and exact error first. Then compare with the release notes or the instructions for your build. If you spot a mistake, let me know which page and step you followed, which version you used and what happened. That gives me enough information to test the issue and improve the guide.
For any problems, suggestions or updates, contact me on Discord.

l: A few fun facts about the site and Ilaria
p: Born from real troubleshooting: Ilaria (TheStingerX / thestingerx on Discord) wrote and expanded these docs directly while building Ilaria RVC, training models (such as Itaila), and testing real setups on Windows, Kaggle, Google Colab, and Lightning AI.

From 1.1 Beta to 2.4.7: Ilaria RVC started as a themed Windows WebUI and evolved to support NVIDIA RTX 50 series (Blackwell) on CUDA 12.8, native BF16 training, Kokoro v1.0 TTS, Safetensors ↔ PTH conversion, and built-in model/pretrain catalogs.

More than one app: Over time, Ilaria Docs grew into a full voice-conversion hub covering 11 RVC apps and forks (Ilaria RVC, Applio, Mainline, Okada, TGR, Deiteris, Vonovox, RedPanda, RVC Blue, RVC-GUI, and RVC Model Merger) plus Non-RVC tools like YuneVoix, Causal Voice Changer, UVR5, and MVSep.
Synchronized in 6 languages: Every single guide on this site is maintained 1:1 across English, Italian, Spanish, French, German, and Portuguese.

Retrieval-based voice conversion (RVC) takes a vocal recording and synthesizes a version with the character of a trained voice.
Download Ilaria RVC 2.4.7 for Windows (ZIP)

Retrieval-based voice conversion (RVC) takes a vocal recording and synthesizes a version with the character of a trained voice. The recording supplies the performance, including the words, rhythm and much of the pitch contour. The model determines how that performance is rendered. For a spoken line, record the pronunciation and delivery you want to hear in the result. A pitch adjustment changes the register without translating or rewriting the line.
A pitch predictor estimates the fundamental frequency, or F0, in voiced sections. Pitch-guided models can use this contour during synthesis.
An embedder represents the sound of each short section of the input. Common RVC workflows use ContentVec or a HuBERT-based feature extractor.
Clipped peaks, room echo and other voices can contaminate later stages.
Compare retrieval on and off if the result sounds muffled or the source timbre is too prominent.
Decode the source

Generic HuBERT checkpoints are not recommended as the default encoder for voice conversion. Their speech prediction training does not explicitly remove speaker identity, so the features can carry source timbre into the output. For RVC, use the encoder expected by the model, such as ContentVec when the voice was trained with it.
Listen for metallic textures, missing consonants and changes in level.
Reads the audio and prepares it for analysis.

Stage
Synthesize the output
The model turns the conditioned features into a waveform at its supported synthesis rate.
Unclear words can follow the input into the output, even with a good model.
Unexpected note jumps or unstable sustained notes can point to pitch tracking.
What it does
What to listen for
When a compatible index is available, the converter can blend nearby features from the model's training data with the source features.
Pitch shift offsets the detected contour by semitones. Start at zero and change it if the performance is outside the target voice's comfortable register.
Pitch predictor changes how the contour is measured. Compare predictors on a passage that contains the problem, such as a sustained note or the transition from talking to a breath.

Index rate changes the balance between source and retrieved features. Zero disables the retrieval contribution in standard RVC workflows. A high setting can emphasize characteristics of the training data, including unwanted artifacts.

Sample rate describes how many audio samples represent a second. The source file rate, the model's synthesis rate and the exported file rate can differ. Resampling a file changes its representation without making an incompatible checkpoint loadable.
For app-specific conversion controls, see Voice conversion.

Confirm the model family and architecture. Use a runtime that explicitly supports the model. Classic RVC v1 and v2 use different feature dimensions, commonly 256 and 768 respectively in RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC). Some forks also support architectures that require their own runtime.

Check the embedder. The runtime should supply the feature representation the model was trained to expect. A model trained with a custom embedder can need that embedder at inference time. A similar file extension or a matching sample rate alone provides little evidence of support.

Use the inference export. A ready-to-use .pth and a training checkpoint can have the same extension. Select the file identified by the publisher as the inference model. A ZIP is a container for the files and is only directly importable where the app supports ZIP import.

Pair retrieval data with its checkpoint. An .index built for another voice or embedder can fail or degrade the result. Keep the model and its index together and check that the app selected the expected pair. If you only have a compatible model, use the no-retrieval workflow supported by your client.
Test a short file. Try a clean clip with default settings. A model that loads can still sound wrong if the runtime uses the wrong feature extractor or the input is far outside the voice's range.

Obtain model files from the original publisher or another source you trust. Loading a PyTorch checkpoint can involve deserializing Python objects. Keep the protections in your loader enabled and request a supported export if it refuses a file. PyTorch loading reference

l: Judge the result with a repeatable test
p: Keep a dry reference clip and use that same clip for every comparison. Include a quiet phrase, a sentence with sharp consonants and a sustained vowel. Keep playback levels similar so that loudness alone does not make one output seem better.
Render a baseline using the app's defaults.
Check word clarity first. If both the dry and converted clips are hard to understand, re-record the source.
For pitch wobble, compare two supported pitch predictors before changing retrieval.
For a timbre or texture problem, compare with retrieval disabled, then adjust the index rate if the matching index helps.
Save the working settings with the model name, release and input. When a later update changes the sound, those notes give you a starting point.

In RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) training, trained_*.index is the FAISS index after it has learned how to organise features, before the feature vectors are added. added_*.index is the populated version. l: Choose a model for the job
p: Listen to demos that resemble your intended input. For speech, listen for consonants, quieter words and natural pauses. For singing, check sustained notes and the high and low ends of your range. If you plan to use it live, test speaking freely and changing volume. Check the documented engine and model version, known language limitations and terms of use. A model that sounds good in one language may sound uneven in another, even when the training dataset includes both.
Download from a source you trust and read the included notes. Model files can be unsafe when loaded by software that deserializes arbitrary objects.
Keep each voice and version in its own folder, with the exported .pth, its optional .index and any notes. Filenames alone are insufficient to match an index to a model.

In Ilaria RVC, open Other → Import Local Models. Choose the inference .pth or a supported ZIP, then add the matching .index if you have it. Other apps may ask you to refresh the model list after import.
Record about ten seconds of one voice in a quiet room, without music, heavy reverb or clipping.
Select the intended model, leave index retrieval off and start at zero pitch shift. Save the converted WAV as a reference.
If the register sounds strained, compare small pitch changes in semitones using the same input. Pitch shift changes the register, so judge it separately from voice identity.

Once pitch is set, try a small increase in retrieval with the matching index. Listen for clearer voice character, then check whether breaths or consonants become rough. Keep the setting that sounds best, including zero.
Symptom
What to check
The app cannot load the model
Confirm the engine, version and file type. Extract the ZIP if the importer rejects it, then select the exported inference weights.
The result still sounds like the source
Compare with another known-good model using the same clip. Persistent source timbre can come from the model or its training embedder, including HuBERT variants. More retrieval may not resolve it.
Breaths or consonants sound metallic
Compare with retrieval off. If the problem persists across clean inputs and settings, it may be in the model and require retraining.
Only the live output stutters
Try the same model with a file. If file conversion works, check the microphone, audio routing and buffer in the live app.

l: Keep a model ready to reuse
p: Save the working app version, model version, selected pitch and retrieval settings with a short reference clip. Test again after changing apps or updating the model. If you train your own voices, keep the export for inference and the files needed to resume training in separate folders.

A pitch extractor (also called an F0 extraction method) is the algorithm or neural network that tracks the fundamental frequency (pitch, melody, and intonation) of the input voice over time.
While an embedder reads what words and phonemes are being spoken or sung, the pitch extractor measures how high or low the voice goes at every fraction of a second.

Compatibility: Unlike embedders, pitch extractors do not lock you into one choice. Even if a model was trained using rmvpe for dataset preprocessing, you can use any available pitch extractor during inference and live voice changing without breaking compatibility.
Single & Batch Inference (CUDA): rmvpe (default), swift, beatrice, fcpe, parselmouth, harvest, crepe. (On DirectML builds: pm, harvest, rmvpe, fcpe.)

Other RVC forks: Tools like Applio or Deiteris may also expose hybrid[...] or ONNX pitch variants.

No universal "best" or "fastest": Results vary by voice, hardware, and backend. Start with rmvpe and compare fcpe, swift, beatrice, or crepe on the same audio if you hear octave jumps or timing issues.

l: rmvpe vs rmvpe_gpu: what is the difference?
p: In Ilaria RVC and RVC Mainline, rmvpe_gpu is a Training feature extraction option (allowing multi-GPU worker assignment via gpus_rmvpe), whereas Single & Batch Inference expose rmvpe directly (running on your configured inference device). If rmvpe_gpu triggers CUDA out of memory during dataset feature extraction on a low-VRAM card, switch to rmvpe or fcpe.

l: Choosing the right method for your task
p: Preparing / Training a new model: Use rmvpe_gpu (if you have an NVIDIA GPU with 6+ GB VRAM) or rmvpe. Clean dataset F0 tracking prevents pitch glitches in the trained voice.
Converting songs or voiceovers offline: Start with rmvpe or rmvpe_gpu. Only test crepe-full or hybrid if a specific high singing note has an octave jump.
Live microphone / Discord: Start with fcpe for lowest delay, or rmvpe if your GPU handles your chunk size smoothly without crackling.

An embedder (also called a content encoder) is the neural network that reads your input audio and converts what is being said or sung into numerical content features before the RVC voice model reconstructs it in the target speaker's timbre.

An embedder (also called a content encoder) is the neural network that reads your input audio and converts what is being said or sung into numerical content features before the RVC voice model reconstructs it in the target speaker's timbre.

l: What an embedder does and how it works
p: In an RVC pipeline, the audio is split into separate streams of information:
Content (what you say): extracted frame by frame by the embedder (phonemes, pronunciation, articulation, and timing).
Pitch / F0 (the melody): extracted separately by a pitch tracker (such as RMVPE or FCPE).
Speaker timbre (who is speaking): supplied by the trained RVC .pth voice model (and optionally reinforced by a matching .index file).
Because the RVC generator is trained to expect features from one specific embedder, two rules always apply:

Training and inference must match: if a voice model was trained with contentvec, you must convert audio with contentvec. Using a different embedder during inference (or live conversion) causes distorted pronunciation, metallic artifacts, or a completely broken voice.

Speaker-identity leakage: generic speech-recognition encoders (such as standard HuBERT models) were not trained to strip out the original speaker's identity. Using them can cause your own voice timbre to bleed into the converted output.
Alternative Fairseq/HuBERT-based speaker-invariant encoder.

l: When you actually need to touch the embedder setting
p: Leave it on Auto or contentvec for almost every voice model and training run.

Only change it if you downloaded a pre-trained voice whose author explicitly states it was trained with a specific embedder (for example spin-v2 or japanese-hubert-base). Even then, only change it for inference on that specific model, not as your default for new training.
Do not switch embedders mid-training: changing the embedder requires re-extracting features (3_feature768) in a separate experiment.

A pretrained base model (also called a pretrain) is a pair of starting checkpoint files: a Generator (G_.pth) and a Discriminator (D_.pth), already trained on hundreds of hours of multi-speaker audio.

A pretrained base model (also called a pretrain) is a pair of starting checkpoint files: a Generator (G_*.pth) and a Discriminator (D_*.pth), already trained on hundreds of hours of multi-speaker audio. When you train a new RVC voice, training does not start from scratch; instead, it fine-tunes this pretrained pair on your target speaker's dataset.

l: What pretrained models do and why they exist
p: Starting from a pretrained pair allows RVC to learn a new voice in minutes or hours instead of weeks:
The Generator (G) already knows how to turn content features and pitch into natural speech or singing.
The Discriminator (D) already knows how to judge whether generated audio sounds realistic or artificial.
Your training run adapts those existing weights to your target voice.
Every pretrained pair is locked to specific architectural parameters that must match your training setup exactly:
Sample rate (32 kHz, 40 kHz, 44.1 kHz, or 48 kHz)
Vocoder architecture (HiFi-GAN, RefineGAN, or MRF HiFi-GAN)
RVC version & pitch guidance (almost all community pretrains are RVC v2 with F0 pitch guidance)
Expected embedder (usually contentvec, though some variants require spin-v2)
If any of these settings do not match the pretrained pair, training will either crash immediately or produce heavily distorted audio.

Beginner-friendly guide to RVC precision modes (FP16, FP32, and BF16): what they mean, GPU compatibility, training vs inference, and how to avoid NaN or HalfTensor errors.
When training or converting voices in RVC, you will often see a setting called Precision (with options like FP32, FP16, and BF16).

If you are new to AI audio, those names sound technical, but the idea behind them is actually very simple. This guide explains what each mode means, which one matches your graphics card, and how to avoid the most common precision errors.
An AI voice model is made of millions of decimal numbers (called weights). Every time RVC trains or converts your voice, your GPU has to multiply millions of those decimal numbers per second.
Precision simply controls how detailed each number is (how many bits of memory each number uses):
FP32 (Full Precision, 32-bit): Keeps full decimal detail and a huge number range. It is the safest and most compatible mode, but it uses more VRAM and runs slower.

FP16 (Half Precision, 16-bit): Uses half the memory of FP32 and runs much faster on modern NVIDIA GPUs. Because the numbers have a smaller range, very large or tiny spikes during training can occasionally overflow (NaN loss).

BF16 (Brain Float 16, 16-bit): Uses the same small memory as FP16, but keeps the huge safe number range of FP32 (by trading away a tiny bit of decimal fine-tuning). In short: BF16 gives you FP16 speed and low VRAM with almost FP32 stability.

Simple rule of thumb: Think of FP32 as a heavy-duty calculator that never overflows, FP16 as a fast sports car that needs smooth roads (clean audio), and BF16 as a modern sports car with off-road suspension (fast, light on VRAM, and very hard to crash).

l: 3. Which Precision should YOU choose? (By GPU)
p: Choosing the right precision depends almost entirely on what graphics card you have:

l: NVIDIA RTX 30 / 40 / 50 series (and A100 / L4 / H100)
p: Best choice: BF16 (if your RVC app supports it, such as Ilaria RVC or Applio). You get fast training, low VRAM usage, and far fewer NaN crashes than FP16.
Fallback: FP16 works great too if BF16 is not listed in your app.

l: NVIDIA RTX 20 series, GTX 16 series, or Cloud T4 (Colab / Kaggle)
p: Best choice: FP16. These cards do not support hardware BF16, so FP16 gives you the biggest speed and VRAM boost.
When to switch: If you hit NaN loss during training, clean any clipped audio in your dataset or switch to FP32.

l: NVIDIA GTX 10 series (1060, 1070, 1080 Ti) or older
p: Best choice: FP32 only. GTX 10-series (Pascal) does not have Tensor Cores for fast FP16, and forcing FP16 often triggers HalfTensor errors or actually runs slower than FP32.
Best choice: FP32 only. DirectML and CPU backends usually crash on FP16 or BF16 with expected scalar type Half but found Float.

l: 4. Training Precision vs Export / Inference Precision
p: Beginners often confuse training precision with model export precision:
Modern RVC trainers use Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) when you pick FP16 or BF16. This runs the heavy GPU math in 16-bit for speed while keeping key master values safe in 32-bit.
Changing precision during training does not make the finished voice sound robotic or low-quality; a cleanly trained BF16, FP16, and FP32 model sound practically identical.

l: During Inference, Model Export & Voice Blender
p: Inference FP16 (or saving an .pth in fp16): Cuts the .pth file size roughly in half (around 45-55 MB instead of 95-110 MB) and runs faster on NVIDIA CUDA GPUs with zero audible quality loss.
Inference FP32 (or saving an .pth in fp32): Produces a larger .pth file, but works on every setup (including older GTX 10 cards, DirectML, and CPU).
You can freely use an FP16-exported .pth in an app running FP32 inference (the app automatically casts it when loading), or convert between FP16 and FP32 when using Voice Blender.

Complete guide to RVC .pth voice model files: exported voice models vs raw G and D checkpoints, FP16 vs FP32 sizes, compatibility rules, and common errors.

When you download, train, or share an RVC voice, the .pth file is the single most important file. While an .index file is optional, the .pth file is mandatory: without it, RVC cannot convert a voice at all.

This guide explains what is inside a .pth file, the critical difference between an exported voice .pth and raw training checkpoints (G_*.pth / D_*.pth), why file sizes vary, and how to fix common .pth errors.
A .pth file is a PyTorch checkpoint storing the trained neural network (the Generator) that knows how to synthesize your target speaker's voice timbre.
Inside a properly exported RVC inference .pth, two things are saved:
Model weights (weight): Millions of numbers learned during training that shape the target voice's tone, resonance, and vocal character.
Voice configuration (config and metadata): Settings recorded when the voice was exported, including:
Sample rate: 32 kHz, 40 kHz, or 48 kHz (44.1 kHz on select RefineGAN variants).
RVC architecture: v1 (256-d) or v2 (768-d).
Pitch guidance (f0): Enabled (1) or disabled (0).
Vocoder: HiFi-GAN, MRF HiFi-GAN, or RefineGAN.
Embedder: For example contentvec, spin-v2, or klm-vocal-contentvec.

l: 2. Exported voice .pth vs Raw checkpoints (G_*.pth / D_*.pth)
p: One of the most common beginner mistakes is grabbing the wrong .pth file from logs/:
File type
Typical location
Typical size
What it is for
Exported voice .pth (e.g. MyVoice.pth)
models/ (Ilaria RVC 2.4.0+) or weights/
45 - 110 MB (fp16 vs fp32)
Inference & sharing. Contains only the lightweight Generator weights + voice config.
Raw Generator (G_*.pth) & Discriminator (D_*.pth)
logs/experiment_name/
200+ MB each
Training resume & pretrains only. Contains full optimizer/training state. Never copy these into models/ for inference!

If you put a raw G_*.pth file into models/ and try to convert audio with it, RVC will crash with Missing key(s) in state_dict or report missing voice configuration. Always use your app's Export tool (or test checkpoints saved directly to models//weights/ during training).

l: 3. File size (FP16 vs FP32) & formats (.pth vs .safetensors / .onnx)
p: Why is one .pth ~50 MB and another ~105 MB? The difference is usually the model's export precision (see Precision). FP16 stores weights using 16 bits instead of 32, reducing file size by approximately 50% compared to FP32 for the same architecture. Both formats generally deliver virtually identical audio quality, and on supported NVIDIA GPUs FP16 inference can also improve performance. Importantly, export precision is independent of inference precision: most RVC applications can load an FP16 model and automatically convert its weights to FP32 when running on older NVIDIA GPUs, DirectML, or CPU, so an FP32-exported model is not required for compatibility with those devices as long as the inference app supports automatic precision conversion.

.pth vs .safetensors: .pth uses Python's pickle format (which is why PyTorch 2.6+ enforces weights_only=True security checks), whereas .safetensors stores weights without executable code. In Ilaria RVC 2.4.5+, you can convert safely between .pth and .safetensors in Safetensors ↔ PTH Converter.
.pth vs .onnx: Standard RVC training and inference use .pth. Some real-time voice changers (such as w-okada or Deiteris DirectML) can also convert/run .onnx exports for AMD/Intel GPUs.

l: 4. Compatibility rules (Why a .pth might fail or sound wrong)
p: Matching Embedder: If a .pth was trained with contentvec (the standard default), convert with contentvec (or leave Embedder on Auto). Mixing embedders causes garbled pronunciation or source-voice bleed.
Supported Vocoder: Make sure your RVC app supports the vocoder baked into the .pth. Models trained with MRF HiFi-GAN or RefineGAN require an up-to-date app (such as Ilaria RVC 2.3.0+ or Applio).

PyTorch 2.6+ UnpicklingError: Older .pth files can trigger Weights only load failed (fairseq.data.dictionary.Dictionary) on older builds. Updating to Ilaria RVC 2.4.0+ or latest Applio handles this safely.

l: 5. Where to put .pth files & how to inspect them
p: Where to place them: In Ilaria RVC 2.4.0+, extract any .zip first and place your .pth file (plus its matching added_*.index) into the root models/ folder (other apps may use assets/weights/ or weights/). Click Refresh in Inference.
Inspecting unknown .pth files: In Ilaria RVC, open Other → Model information, select the .pth, and click Read model information to view its sample rate, RVC version, vocoder, embedder, and precision.
Sharing a voice cleanly: Use Other → Export model ZIP to bundle your .pth and matching added_*.index with zero training logs or private recordings.
Check file size: a valid .pth is 40 - 110+ MB, not a few KB. Delete and re-download cleanly.

Complete guide to RVC .index files (Feature Retrieval): added vs trained index files, how to tune Index Rate, and how to rebuild a missing index.
When you download or train an RVC voice model, you will usually see two files: a .pth file and an .index file. While the .pth file is mandatory, the .index file is often misunderstood.

This guide explains what an .index file actually does, the critical difference between added_*.index and trained_*.index, how to tune Index Rate, when to turn it down or off, and what to do if an .index file is missing.
An RVC voice conversion happens in two main parts:
The .pth file (the Generator): A neural network that learned how to turn speech features into the target speaker's voice.

The .index file (the Feature Database): A FAISS vector index storing the actual acoustic feature vectors extracted by the embedder (such as contentvec) from every clip of the speaker's training dataset.

During conversion, Feature Retrieval compares each tiny slice of your input audio against the .index database, finds the closest matching frames from the original speaker's recordings, and blends them with your input features before passing them to the .pth generator.
In simple words:
The .pth is the engine (required).
The .index is a reference library of the speaker's real vocal habits (optional): subtle breathiness, vowel color, rasp, nasal tone, and inflection nuances that a .pth alone might smooth over.
Compatibility: An .pth model works completely fine without an .index file (Index Rate = 0). If a model you downloaded did not come with an .index, you can still use it normally.
When RVC builds a feature index inside logs/experiment_name/, it typically saves two .index files:
File name
What it contains
Should you use it?
added_*.index
The full FAISS index with all dataset feature vectors added inside (for example added_IVF256_Flat_nprobe_1_MyVoice_v2.index).
YES. Always use this one for inference and sharing.
trained_*.index
Only the intermediate cluster structure trained before the dataset vectors were populated.
NO. Do not select or distribute this file; it gives poor or empty retrieval.
If you share or export a model (for example using Export model ZIP in Ilaria RVC), always pair the .pth with added_*.index, never trained_*.index.

l: 3. How to tune Index Rate (0 to 1.0)
p: 100% original input features (0% FAISS retrieval); .pth still runs normally.
Effect on features
Index Rate
Light-to-moderate blend toward the index's acoustic feature vectors.
Maximum retrieval weight; heavily replaces original features with index matches.
Starting range to test for clean, same-language singing when the index matches.
Starting range to test for speech or cross-language conversion.
Stronger pull toward the index's feature vectors.
Suggested starting point for testing
Test cautiously only on very clean matched datasets; higher risk of slurred consonants.

The Index Rate (or Index Ratio) slider controls how strongly retrieved FAISS feature vectors (retrieved_features) are blended with your input's extracted features (original_features) before the .pth generator runs (features = retrieved_features * index_rate + original_features * (1 - index_rate)). The .pth generator is always used regardless of Index Rate:
Useful diagnostic baseline without FAISS feature retrieval, lowest CPU load, and merged models.

l: 4. When you should lower or disable Index Rate
p: Raising Index Rate toward 1.0 does not automatically make a voice better. Lower it to 0.2 - 0.4 (or 0) whenever you notice:

Noisy or reverberant training datasets: An .index stores extracted feature vectors, not raw audio recordings (it does not inject raw audio waves directly), but a noisy or reverberant dataset distorts those feature vectors, which can degrade conversion quality at high Index Rates.
Garbled words or a strange accent: If you speak one language into a model trained on a different language, a high Index Rate tries to force foreign vowel/consonant habits onto your speech.
Blended / Merged voices: Merging two .pth models in Voice Blender does not create a new .index. Always test blended models at Index Rate = 0 first.
Live Voice Changer stutters: Searching a large FAISS index on every live audio chunk adds CPU work. Turning Index Rate down or to 0 reduces latency and CPU spikes.

l: 5. Compatibility rules (Why you cannot mix .index files)
p: An .index file is strictly tied to the exact model and embedder architecture it was built from:

Same dimension / RVC version: A v1 model uses 256-dimensional features (3_feature256), while a v2 model uses 768-dimensional features (3_feature768). Mixing v1 and v2 causes a dimension mismatch error.
Same embedder: An index built with contentvec will not match a model expecting a different encoder representation.
Same speaker: Putting Voice A's .index on Voice B's .pth does not create a clean Voice Blend; it feeds the wrong acoustic features into Voice B's decoder and usually sounds muffled or broken.

l: 6. How to regenerate a missing .index file
Case A: You only have a downloaded .pth file
p: You cannot recreate a real .index from a .pth file alone. The .index is built from the extracted feature vectors (.npy files) of the original training audio, which are not stored inside an exported .pth. Simply set Index Rate = 0 and use the .pth by itself.

l: Case B: You trained the model and still have logs/<experiment_name>/
p: If your experiment folder still contains the extracted feature folder (3_feature256 or 3_feature768), you can rebuild the index in seconds without re-training:
Open the Train tab in Ilaria RVC (or Applio / RVC Mainline).
Enter the exact same Experiment Name, RVC Version (v1/v2), Sample Rate, and Embedder used during training.
Click Train Feature Index only (do not run Dataset Preprocessing or Train Model again).
Once finished, check logs/experiment_name/ for the new added_*.index file.

l: Case C: Building the index crashes with RAM / Pagefile errors
p: Large datasets (thousands of audio slices) require significant system RAM during FAISS clustering. If indexing crashes with WinError 1455 or freezes Windows, close other apps, increase your Windows Virtual Memory (Pagefile) (see Troubleshooting), or trim redundant clips from the dataset.
Complete guide to RVC .onnx model files: why they are usually used for real-time voice changing on AMD and Intel GPUs via DirectML, and how they compare to .pth.
Alongside .pth and .index files, you will occasionally run into .onnx files when using RVC voice changers.
In the RVC ecosystem, .onnx models are usually used for real-time voice changing on AMD and Intel GPUs (through DirectML / ONNX Runtime on Windows), as well as certain cross-platform live clients.

ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is an open, framework-independent format for running trained neural networks. Instead of relying on PyTorch and NVIDIA's CUDA runtime, an .onnx file runs through ONNX Runtime, which works across different graphics cards and operating systems.
For RVC users, this matters most in live / real-time voice changers (such as Deiteris w-okada Fork, w-okada VCClient, or RVC Mainline DirectML):
AMD Radeon and Intel Arc / integrated GPUs cannot run NVIDIA CUDA.
Running an exported .onnx model through ONNX Runtime + DirectML lets AMD and Intel GPUs accelerate real-time voice conversion on Windows smoothly.

l: 3. How to get an .onnx model from a .pth
p: Most RVC voices on the internet are shared as .pth files rather than .onnx. If you need an .onnx version:
Automatic conversion in live clients: Some real-time apps (such as w-okada and Deiteris) can accept a .pth directly or convert it to .onnx for DirectML.
Manual ONNX export: Apps like Ilaria RVC, Applio, and RVC Mainline include an Export ONNX option that converts an exported inference .pth into an .onnx file for external real-time clients.

Keep your original .pth: Never delete the original .pth and added_*.index after exporting to .onnx, since .onnx cannot be merged, converted to .safetensors, or used in standard PyTorch training/tools.
Use FP32 on DirectML if you hit glitches: DirectML on AMD/Intel GPUs often fails or glitches with FP16; switch precision to FP32 if audio breaks up.

Test Windows HAGS only if needed: Hardware-Accelerated GPU Scheduling (HAGS) is not harmful by default, but on some setups with heavy background GPU load you can test toggling it off in Windows Graphics Settings (restart, compare before/after, and restore if unchanged).
Match 48000 Hz everywhere: Set your microphone, headphones, and VB-CABLE endpoints to 48000 Hz in Windows Sound Control Panel (mmsys.cpl) to prevent PortAudioError or pitch drift.

For a first run, load your RVC v2 voice and listen to a short microphone test before routing audio into another app. Then lower the block size gradually while speaking normally. Restore the previous setting if you hear dropouts or chopped syllables. Test again alongside the game or streaming app you plan to use, because both share the same GPU. Vonovox audio configuration

VCClient handles live voice conversion with a client and server. You can run them together on one machine or put the server on a second machine to move the conversion workload away from your main computer. Select a release that supports the RVC model you want to load. The maintained downloads live on Hugging Face, and the project's English README explains Windows standard, Windows CUDA, Apple Silicon, and Linux options. VCClient English README · Official VCClient downloads

Check the model format as well as the accelerator. For example, the project's older Windows v1 instructions limit AMD and Intel GPU acceleration to ONNX models. The tg-develop/voice-changer project is a community fork in the w-okada family via the deiteris fork. Compare audio stability with your usual apps running before relying on the setup for a recording or stream.

Applio supports RVC voice-model management, file conversion, training, and realtime. Its Desktop and Python/Gradio editions have different setup flows. The desktop docs identify NVIDIA CUDA, supported AMD configurations, and Apple MPS and explain how to check the engine status after installation. Use the Applio conversion steps for your edition.

Retrieval-based-Voice-Conversion-WebUI is the upstream RVC project. Its WebUI handles training and file inference. The project's realtime GUI has its own launcher. The main branch documents separate CUDA dependencies for newer and older NVIDIA cards, plus a CPU dependency set for AMD and Intel systems. On Windows, DirectML may be available for supported operations. Follow the RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) conversion steps for the Windows package.

Redpanda-vc is an Applio fork whose realtime interface supports RVC, Beatrice, and Rectified Flow. It offers multiple model families, so select the RVC workflow for an RVC voice. l: Compare apps with the same voice
p: Choose the package for your operating system, GPU, and model format. Check whether the app supports your model's RVC generation and feature encoder.
Start with the same short recording or repeat the same few sentences into your microphone. Load the same inference model and its matching index in both apps if supported.
Use the same pitch shift and turn off optional voice effects for the first comparison. Judge clear words, stable pitch, and natural pauses before adjusting the sound.
For live use, run the game, call, or streaming app you normally use and record the routed output for at least a minute. Listen for gaps, hard cuts, and delayed audio before reducing the buffer.

HAGS (Hardware-Accelerated GPU Scheduling) lets the GPU manage its own memory queue, which works well for most games/apps but can occasionally cause VRAM/latency contention on some AI + gaming setups.

HAGS is not inherently harmful and does not need to be turned off on every PC. If you hit unexplained live stuttering, test turning it OFF in Windows Settings → System → Display → Graphics → Advanced Graphics Settings, restart your PC, and compare before/after. If there is no clear improvement, turn HAGS back ON and restart.

Lower Batch Size step by step (from 8 down to 4, 2, or 1). Turn OFF "Cache dataset in GPU/VRAM", and close any live voice changer before training.

Practical guide to downloaded model safety (.pth vs .safetensors), voice consent, licensing, cloud notebook security, and protecting credentials.

l: Voice AI Safety, Privacy & Model Licensing
p: Practical guidance, not legal advice: This page summarizes technical safety practices and common licensing rules for RVC models, datasets, and cloud notebooks. Always read the specific license attached to any model, pretrained weight, or dataset you use.

Why .pth files require trust: Standard PyTorch .pth files use Python pickle serialization. Loading an untrusted .pth file on older or unpatched loaders can execute arbitrary code. Modern apps like Ilaria RVC 2.4.0+ and Applio include safer loading protections (weights_only), but you should still only download .pth files from trusted authors and official repositories (such as Hugging Face or GitHub Releases).

Why .safetensors is safer: .safetensors stores only raw tensor weights and metadata, so it cannot execute code when loaded. When sharing or archiving models, converting .pth to .safetensors with Safetensors Converter is a good practice.

Verify downloads before loading: Check file sizes (a real RVC inference .pth is typically ~40–110 MB, not a few KB HTML redirect), verify SHA-256 hashes or digital signatures when provided, and never load raw G_*.pth / D_*.pth training checkpoints from unknown sources.

Consent & third-party recordings: Only train models on your own voice, authorized voice actors, or datasets whose license explicitly permits voice modeling. Avoid training on private calls, confidential meetings, or copyrighted/commercial recordings without permission.

Commercial vs. non-commercial use: Even when RVC software itself is open-source (e.g. MIT), individual pretrained weights and voice models carry their own licenses (some allow commercial use, such as Sakura in RVC Blue, while others are strictly non-commercial / CC-BY-NC or research-only). Always check the model card and Pretrained models notes before publishing or monetizing output.

Sharing models responsibly: When publishing a voice model, include the exact RVC version (v2), sample rate (32k/40k/48k), embedder (contentvec, spin-v2, etc.), matching added_*.index, and clear usage/attribution terms.

Keep Kaggle, Colab, and Lightning AI sessions private: Launch cells in notebooks (such as Ilaria-RVC-Kaggle.ipynb) print live tunnel URLs and WebUI / FileBrowser passwords. Never share screenshots, terminal logs, or public notebook versions containing active passwords or URLs.

Protect API tokens & drives: Never paste Ngrok authtokens, Horizon IDs, or Hugging Face write tokens into public notebooks. Use platform secrets when available, and stop cloud tunnels (STOP = True) when finished.

Data privacy on cloud VMs: Cloud providers run on remote shared infrastructure. For confidential or sensitive voice recordings, clean and convert audio locally instead of uploading it to public web tools or third-party cloud VMs.
Cross-cutting guide to GPU utilization, VRAM, thermal/power throttling, CUDA vs CPU bottlenecks, and gaming conflicts in RVC apps.

Voice conversion and RVC training rely heavily on GPU compute, memory bandwidth, and steady scheduling. Use this guide to diagnose why an app runs slowly, runs out of memory, or stutters during live conversion.

l: 1. Key GPU metrics that actually matter
p: GPU Utilization & Compute: During training, high GPU utilization (often 80–99%) is normal and desirable. During live voice conversion, GPU load comes in short bursts per audio chunk; if the GPU is already at 95–100% from a 3D game, live audio chunks wait in line and crackle.
VRAM (Video Memory): Training Batch Size, model sample rate, and GPU dataset caching determine VRAM usage. If VRAM fills up, Windows spills into slower system RAM or throws CUDA out of memory.
Temperature & Thermal Throttling: When a GPU exceeds its thermal threshold, it automatically lowers clock speeds to protect the hardware, causing sudden epoch slowdowns or live GPU Delay spikes.
Power Limits & Clock Fluctuations: Laptops on battery or tight power budgets cap GPU wattage and clocks. Plug in AC power and check OEM performance profiles before troubleshooting.

Gaming + Live Voice Changer: Cap in-game FPS (so GPU load stays below ~80–85%), lower heavy ray-tracing/resolution settings, or raise Block Size one step.

Windows HAGS: Hardware-Accelerated GPU Scheduling is not harmful by default, but if you see unexplained VRAM contention or live stuttering, test toggling it off in Windows Graphics Settings, restart, and compare before/after.
CPU bottlenecks: Slow dataset preprocessing, too few Workers, or heavy CPU-side audio resampling can stall the GPU. Keep sample rates aligned at 48000 Hz in Windows Sound settings.
Drivers & cooling: Use a clean NVIDIA Studio or Game Ready driver and keep laptop/desktop vents dust-free.

On supported NVIDIA GPUs, locking graphics clocks with nvidia-smi is an optional advanced test that may reduce clock-ramping jitter in live voice changers like Vonovox. See Vonovox Advanced Performance Optimization for the full, reversible procedure and BAT helpers.
VRAM & Training Estimator
How to measure RVC training speed, inference real-time factor, GPU Delay, end-to-end latency, VRAM, and thermal throttling with repeatable A/B tests.
Never rely on guesswork or single-number claims when tuning RVC training or live conversion. Measure your own hardware with repeatable A/B tests where you change one variable at a time.
Steps per second & Epoch duration: How fast each training update and full dataset pass completes (visible in the training log / TensorBoard).
VRAM usage: Peak GPU memory used (nvidia-smi or Task Manager) at your chosen Batch Size, Precision (FP32/FP16/BF16), and GPU Caching setting.
GPU power draw & temperature: Watch for thermal or power throttling (nvidia-smi -i 0 -q -d PERFORMANCE) during multi-minute runs.
Inference time & Real-Time Factor (RTF): For file conversion, how long it takes to convert a clip divided by the clip's duration (RTF 1.0 means faster than real time).

GPU Delay vs. End-to-End Latency: GPU Delay measures only GPU inference time per chunk. Total end-to-end latency includes mic capture, Block Size, crossfade/context, virtual cable buffering, and Discord/OBS/game audio buffers.
Audio dropouts / crackles
Average GPU Delay & peak spike (Live)
Baseline (Test A)
Change one setting (Test B): Adjust only one parameter (e.g. Batch Size, BF16 vs FP32, Block Size, or rmvpe vs fcpe) while keeping everything else (including background GPU load) identical.
Compare objectively:
Epoch duration / Steps per sec (Training)
Establish a baseline (Test A): Reset optional tweaks (such as clock locks) to defaults, load one fixed voice model, one fixed test clip or spoken script, and identical audio/training settings.
Keep only proven gains: If Test B shows no measurable improvement, or introduces heat, instability, or worse audio, revert to Test A.
Metric
Peak VRAM & GPU temperature
Stabilize and measure: Run the test long enough to catch thermal warm-up (e.g. 10–15 minutes for live voice changers, or several full epochs for training).

l: Why You Should Not Manually Upgrade PyTorch
p: Ilaria RVC bundles a tested, pinned combination of PyTorch (2.10.0), CUDA (12.8 or 12.6), torchaudio, torchvision, faiss, and audio dependencies. Do not manually run pip install --upgrade torch or replace CUDA wheels inside the portable runtime:
Upgrading PyTorch alone can break binary compatibility with torchaudio, fairseq, onnxruntime, or compiled C++/CUDA extensions.
Newer PyTorch/CUDA releases can drop support for older GPU architectures (such as Maxwell, Pascal, or Volta) or introduce UnpicklingError / tensor API changes.
If a newer runtime is needed, wait for an official Ilaria RVC release or updater package instead of modifying the bundled environment manually.

l: The model is missing or the audio sounds wrong
p: Symptom
First check
A voice is missing from Voice Model
Check the import log, then click Refresh. Select an inference .pth export. A G or D training checkpoint belongs to the experiment.
A file fails to decode
Play it outside the app. Export a short PCM WAV to a writable local folder and test that copy.
Conversion fails only with the index
Set Index Ratio to zero and try without an index. If that works, check that the optional .index matches the model and its embedder.
The voice still sounds like the source
Confirm the selected model and its expected embedder. Generic HuBERT encoders can retain source timbre. Test the same phrase with retrieval off before comparing settings.
Breaths or consonants are metallic
Test several clean clips with effects off. If the same model keeps distorting those sounds, inspect breath and consonant examples in the training data, correct them and retrain.
A long file fails but a short one works
Check VRAM and try Split Audio or shorter segments. Listen across each join before exporting.
Start with Pitch 0, a short dry WAV and one known-good model. Change one setting per test. See Inference controls for the effects and export options.

Check which stage failed. In Process Data, confirm the dataset path points to readable recordings and the output drive has space. In Feature Extraction, check that preprocessing completed and the chosen pitch and embedder assets are available.

If Train Pth runs out of VRAM, unload the inference model, close competing GPU jobs, reduce Batch Size and disable GPU dataset caching if enabled. Check Training Log for the effective settings before retrying.

If Train Index fails, check that the extracted features belong to the selected experiment. An index is optional for conversion. You can test a working inference export at Index Ratio 0 while diagnosing the index.

To interrupt training, click Stop and save and wait for confirmation. To resume, use the same experiment name and compatible settings. Keep the G/D checkpoints and experiment state together. An inference export alone cannot resume training.
If you changed the sample rate, vocoder or embedder, create a separate experiment and prepare features for that configuration. Keep the original run available for comparison.

If the browser link stops working, check whether the Kaggle session is still running. After reopening the services, use the new links and the current credentials shown for each service. WebUI and FileBrowser have separate logins. Export and download your results before resetting the session. Follow the Kaggle guide for the backup steps.

Copy the app version, exact GPU and first error. Include the button you pressed and a short sequence that reproduces the problem. For training, include the failed stage, sample rate, embedder and whether you resumed a run. For conversion, mention whether the same clip worked with another model or with retrieval off. If available, use Training Dashboard → Diagnostic report. Review the report before sharing and remove private paths, passwords and session links.
An inference export can be used for conversion.

Release

RMVPE High Register adds pitch modes, detection limits and an F0 comparison plot for high singing notes. ElevenLabs joins the TTS engines. Enter your ElevenLabs API key and select a voice. Portuguese HuBERT Base is an optional inference embedder. In RVC v2 Training you can upload and save a custom HuBERT embedder. The app selects it and carries its configuration into the exported model.

l: Tune training only after a short test
p: Setting
What to do for the first run
Training Precision
The notebook starts with FP16 when all visible GPUs are T4. Try FP32 for a comparison if needed. When resuming, match the existing checkpoint's configuration.
Batch Size

The UI value is per GPU for a fresh run with this notebook. One T4 at batch 8 and two T4s at batch 4 both give a global batch of 8 when those are the devices used by the run. Check the effective values in Training Log. Start smaller if memory is tight.
Workers and prefetch

Leave them at 2 each for the first run. The notebook suggests 4 workers and prefetch 8 when comparing with the older loader configuration. Change one factor at a time and compare the timing in train.log.
Fused AdamW
Leave it off at first. Test it in a new run if you want to compare performance. Keep the original batch configuration when resuming.
Two GPUs do not pool their VRAM into a single larger device. If a run runs out of memory, reduce the per-GPU batch and verify the effective settings in the log before retrying.

After conversion or after Stop and save confirms the checkpoint, set EXPORT = True and run Export results. Leave TRAINING_MODEL blank for regular model and audio exports, or enter the exact model name to include its resumable experiment files. Open FileBrowser or use the link displayed by the export cell and download Ilaria-RVC-results.zip. The archive is written in /kaggle/working/ilaria-shared. Confirm you can open it locally before closing the session.

When finished, set STOP = True and run Stop or restart. This shuts down the WebUI, FileBrowser and their tunnels. To reopen them in the same session, rerun section 4. To refresh the app code, save your work, stop the services, and rerun steps 1–4.

l: Prepare your dataset and plan a training run
Clean the audio with MVSEP only where needed
p: Keep an untouched copy of your recordings. If they already contain a single clean, dry voice, skip separation. Use material you have permission to upload to MVSEP and to train on. For confidential recordings, clean them locally.

Isolate the voice. Upload a short example and choose a vocal separation option. Download the vocal stem in WAV when available. Replay it against the original and listen through headphones for music, other voices, clipped syllables, and watery or metallic artifacts.

Remove backing vocals only if present. For songs with harmonies or a chorus underneath the target, use a lead-versus-backing separation option on the vocal stem. Keep the lead output. If the singers still overlap or the lead has holes, use a clean section or a different take.

Reduce reverb only where audible. If the voice has a wide stereo reverb tail, first test a stereo de-reverb option on a copy. For remaining room reflections, compare a room de-reverb pass. You can skip either stage. Listen for truncated consonants and breaths at each pass.

Remove echo only if it repeats the voice. An audible delayed repeat calls for a separate short test. Keep the original or replace that take if removal strips out words. Avoid stacking passes on otherwise clean audio.

Prepare the final clips. Trim unusable noise and long empty sections in an editor such as Audacity, while keeping useful breaths and natural phrasing. Export clean WAVs. Put the approved files together in a ZIP and keep a few clean clips outside it for evaluation.

Test the full cleanup chain on a few seconds before treating the entire dataset. A model can learn artifacts that are left in its training audio. Check several clips from different sessions before uploading.

l: Clean a dataset locally with Ultimate Vocal Remover (UVR)
p: UVR separates an audio file into tracks called stems. Use it when the target voice is mixed with music, sound effects or other vocals. If you already have a clean voice recording, keep the original. UVR processes audio on your computer after the required models are downloaded. Cloud runs the later RVC training job separately.

l: Install UVR and prepare a test clip
p: Download the installer or package for your operating system from UVR releases. Launch the desktop app after installing it.
Make a 15–30 second copy of an example that contains a clear line and a section where the music overlaps it. Keep the original safe.
Click Select Input and choose that test clip. Use Select Output to choose a new writable folder, such as uvr-test. Choose WAV for the output format.

Select a Process Method and a model that separates vocals from instrumental, for example a vocals model under MDX-Net. If the list is empty, open the settings Download Center, select the corresponding model family and download a suitable model. Return to the main window and select it.

Enable GPU Conversion only if your installed build recognizes a supported device. If that option causes an error, turn it off and test on the CPU. CPU processing can be slower, so start with a short clip.

Click Start Processing. When it finishes, find the vocals stem in the output folder. Some models also write an instrumental stem. Play the original and the vocals stem at similar volume. Check consonants, breaths, held notes, and sections where the accompaniment is loud. If you still hear instruments or the voice sounds watery or metallic, compare another model on the same test clip before processing the full dataset.
If you've selected the wrong stem, check the filenames or listen to each output. Keep the one that contains your target lead voice.

l: Clean the remaining problems one at a time
p: What remains
What to try in UVR
Backing vocals or harmonies
Feed the isolated vocal stem into a model intended for lead and backing separation, if your installation offers one. Keep the lead output and verify that the target vocal is complete.
Reverb tails between phrases
Try a model intended for de-reverb if available. Compare before and after on the same passage. Keep the original stem if de-reverb damages consonants or held notes.
Audible delayed repeats
Test an echo-removal model if available. If it removes words or distorts breaths, use another take or exclude the affected section.
Room hum, clipped peaks or other voices
Check the original. If treatment keeps damaging the voice, replace or exclude the clip. Separation cannot reconstruct peaks lost to clipping.

Process the full set only after a short comparison sounds right. Use Audacity or another editor to trim unusable material. Keep natural pauses and breaths, export the approved clips as WAV, and pack only those clips into the dataset ZIP. Keep the instrumental and rejected stems out of the ZIP. Next, upload it in Training on Ilaria RVC and confirm Path to Dataset points to the imported recordings.

What to do in this Ilaria RVC notebook

l: Listen before deciding which checkpoint to keep
p: Use a short set of held-out clips. Include a plain sentence, one with sharp consonants, and a pause. For singing, also test a held note and a transition between registers. Start with pitch at zero, retrieval disabled, and optional effects off. Keep the model whose results are clearest across the set. If all versions have the same metallic breaths or muffled words, revisit the dataset instead of extending the run blindly.

Keep the inference export and its matching index if you used one. To continue a run later, save the complete experiment with the notebook export cell and keep your original dataset separately. Open the downloaded ZIP and check its contents before ending the Kaggle session.

p: In Training, choose a new Model Name. Import your audio or ZIP through the dataset upload controls. Wait for import completion and confirm Path to Dataset points to the imported recordings.

Run the Dataset Checker and listen to any suspect recordings. Confirm your RVC V2 architecture, sample rate, embedder and pitch settings match your selected G/D pretrains if you use them. Start with a batch size that fits the allocated GPU.
Run Process Data, then Feature Extraction. Read the status of each before continuing. If you change the dataset or encoder, prepare fresh files for that experiment before training.
Run Train Pth with a modest first target and save periodic checkpoints. Keep a short test clip out of the training data. Compare exported checkpoints on that same clip before starting a longer run.
Build the feature index if you need retrieval, then try the inference export at Index Ratio 0 first. For a detailed explanation of each setting, see Training controls and workflow.
If you want to stop mid-run, use Stop and save inside Ilaria RVC and wait until the log confirms the save. Download the results while the Cloud session is still active.

The notebook's optional Export results cell makes one archive in /kaggle/working/ilaria-shared/Ilaria-RVC-results.zip. A live session is temporary. Verify that you have the backup on your own computer before stopping or resetting the session.

For inference files only: set EXPORT = True and leave TRAINING_MODEL = . The archive includes .pth and .index files in models, plus files written to InferOutput. Use the player's download button for any conversion that did not write a file there.

To keep a resumable training experiment: wait for Stop and save or for training to finish saving. Set EXPORT = True and enter the exact experiment name in TRAINING_MODEL. Enter the name only, without a folder path. The export includes its logs/name tree alongside the regular outputs.

Run that code cell. Open the displayed link or download Ilaria-RVC-results.zip through Kaggle Output. Open the ZIP locally and confirm it contains what you need. Keep your original dataset separately. The export cell does not package datasets.

To stop only the app, set STOP = True in Stop or restart and run that optional cell after saving. Run step 4 again to reopen it in the same session. Stopping or resetting the whole Kaggle session is a separate action.

l: Google Colab limits, compute units, and policies
p: Before starting a long run, understand how Google Colab manages resources:

Free tier vs. Paid plans (Compute Units): Colab's free tier offers GPUs when available, but runtime length, idle timeouts, and GPU type (such as T4) are dynamic and never guaranteed. Paid tiers (Colab Pro, Pro+, and Pay As You Go) use compute units consumed dynamically based on the GPU/TPU you select; when your compute unit balance runs out, the account reverts to free-tier limits.

Disallowed activities & WebUI restrictions: Google's Disallowed Activities policy prohibits hosting files, serving public web applications unrelated to interactive computing, running remote proxies, bypassing safety/access limits, using multiple accounts to evade quotas, or creating deepfakes. While interactive Gradio notebooks are not blanket-banned in every scenario, running persistent public WebUI tunnels on the free tier frequently triggers runtime disconnections or policy warnings.

Disconnections, saving, and privacy: Colab can disconnect idle or long-running sessions and wipe local VM storage. Export your results (EXPORT = True) or sync important checkpoints to Google Drive regularly, and never upload confidential audio or credentials to public/shared notebooks.
Alternatives: If Colab disconnects or lacks GPU availability, use Kaggle (free weekly GPU quota after phone verification) or Lightning AI Studio.

Set EXPORT = True and run the export cell. Enable INCLUDE_CHECKPOINTS if you need to resume training. Save the ZIP locally before stopping the session, then run the stop cell with STOP = True.
If the first cell cannot see the GPU, check your accelerator and rerun it. If the interface does not open, read the launch cell output, confirm the server is ready and reopen the view.

For inference, verify your exported WAV and model files. For training, enable INCLUDE_CHECKPOINTS to include the experiment logs, then verify the archive before closing the session. Keep the original dataset separately.

If installation fails, read the first error and rerun the failed cell after fixing it. If the app opens but your model is missing, check the import log and refresh the list. For out-of-memory errors, start with a shorter clip or lower the training batch size. If the Web UI closes, reopen it from the same launch cell or port while the session is still active.

l: Prepare your dataset and plan a training run
Clean the audio with MVSEP only where needed
p: Keep an untouched copy of your recordings. If they already contain a single clean, dry voice, skip separation. Use material you have permission to upload to MVSEP and to train on. For confidential recordings, clean them locally.

Isolate the voice. Upload a short example and choose a vocal separation option. Download the vocal stem in WAV when available. Replay it against the original and listen through headphones for music, other voices, clipped syllables, and watery or metallic artifacts.

Remove backing vocals only if present. For songs with harmonies or a chorus underneath the target, use a lead-versus-backing separation option on the vocal stem. Keep the lead output. If the singers still overlap or the lead has holes, use a clean section or a different take.

Reduce reverb only where audible. If the voice has a wide stereo reverb tail, first test a stereo de-reverb option on a copy. For remaining room reflections, compare a room de-reverb pass. You can skip either stage. Listen for truncated consonants and breaths at each pass.

Remove echo only if it repeats the voice. An audible delayed repeat calls for a separate short test. Keep the original or replace that take if removal strips out words. Avoid stacking passes on otherwise clean audio.

Prepare the final clips. Trim unusable noise and long empty sections in an editor such as Audacity, while keeping useful breaths and natural phrasing. Export clean WAVs. Put the approved files together in a ZIP and keep a few clean clips outside it for evaluation.

Test the full cleanup chain on a few seconds before treating the entire dataset. A model can learn artifacts that are left in its training audio. Check several clips from different sessions before uploading.

l: Clean a dataset locally with Ultimate Vocal Remover (UVR)
p: UVR separates an audio file into tracks called stems. Use it when the target voice is mixed with music, sound effects or other vocals. If you already have a clean voice recording, keep the original. UVR processes audio on your computer after the required models are downloaded. Cloud runs the later RVC training job separately.

l: Install UVR and prepare a test clip
p: Download the installer or package for your operating system from UVR releases. Launch the desktop app after installing it.
Make a 15–30 second copy of an example that contains a clear line and a section where the music overlaps it. Keep the original safe.
Click Select Input and choose that test clip. Use Select Output to choose a new writable folder, such as uvr-test. Choose WAV for the output format.

Select a Process Method and a model that separates vocals from instrumental, for example a vocals model under MDX-Net. If the list is empty, open the settings Download Center, select the corresponding model family and download a suitable model. Return to the main window and select it.

Enable GPU Conversion only if your installed build recognizes a supported device. If that option causes an error, turn it off and test on the CPU. CPU processing can be slower, so start with a short clip.

Click Start Processing. When it finishes, find the vocals stem in the output folder. Some models also write an instrumental stem. Play the original and the vocals stem at similar volume. Check consonants, breaths, held notes, and sections where the accompaniment is loud. If you still hear instruments or the voice sounds watery or metallic, compare another model on the same test clip before processing the full dataset.
If you've selected the wrong stem, check the filenames or listen to each output. Keep the one that contains your target lead voice.

p: What remains
What to try in UVR
Backing vocals or harmonies
Feed the isolated vocal stem into a model intended for lead and backing separation, if your installation offers one. Keep the lead output and verify that the target vocal is complete.
Reverb tails between phrases
Try a model intended for de-reverb if available. Compare before and after on the same passage. Keep the original stem if de-reverb damages consonants or held notes.
Audible delayed repeats
Test an echo-removal model if available. If it removes words or distorts breaths, use another take or exclude the affected section.
Room hum, clipped peaks or other voices
Check the original. If treatment keeps damaging the voice, replace or exclude the clip. Separation cannot reconstruct peaks lost to clipping.

Process the full set only after a short comparison sounds right. Use Audacity or another editor to trim unusable material. Keep natural pauses and breaths, export the approved clips as WAV, and pack only those clips into the dataset ZIP. Keep the instrumental and rejected stems out of the ZIP. Next, upload it in Training on Ilaria RVC and confirm Path to Dataset points to the imported recordings.

Your dataset is the single biggest factor deciding how natural, clean, and expressive your RVC voice model will sound. Even the best training settings cannot fix noisy, reverberant, or distorted source recordings.
Golden rule: Quality always beats quantity. 10 minutes of dry, clean, varied single-speaker audio will train a much better voice model than 60 minutes of echoey, noisy, or repetitive clips.

l: 1. What makes a great RVC dataset

p: Minimum usable length: Around 5 to 10 minutes of pure speech or singing (excluding silence) can produce a working voice if the audio is very clean.
Recommended target: 15 to 30+ minutes of clean, varied audio gives the model enough phonetic coverage to handle different words, pitches, and emotions naturally.

Vocal variety matters: Include calm speech, energetic speech, different pitches, soft and loud phrases, and clear consonants (s, f, t, k). If you only train on monotone speech, the model will struggle when you sing or speak expressively.
One speaker only: Never leave overlapping voices, crowd noise, or backing harmonies in the dataset.
Dry room (minimal reverb): RVC learns room echo as part of the voice timbre. Close-mic studio recordings or dry voiceovers work best.
Lossless format: Prefer PCM .wav (or .flac) over low-bitrate .mp3 files whenever possible, so compression artifacts are not baked into the model.
No music or sound effects: Remove all background music, game audio, and SFX before preprocessing.
Separate vocals from music/SFX: If your source comes from songs, videos, or games, extract dry vocals first using UVR5 or MVSep.

Be careful with heavy denoising or dereverb: Only apply noise or reverb removal when truly needed. Aggressive filters can strip crisp high frequencies and create watery, metallic artifacts. Always A/B listen to the original vs processed clip.
Trim dead air and bad noises: Cut long silent pauses, loud mic bumps, coughs, clicks, and extreme clipping. Keep short, natural pauses between words so phrasing stays human.
Keep clip lengths reasonable: Split very long recordings into clean segments (roughly 3 to 15 seconds each), or let Ilaria RVC's preprocessing slicer segment them cleanly.
Use simple file paths: Store your dataset in a short folder path without spaces, accents, or special symbols (for example C:\RVC\datasets\my_voice\).
Before spending GPU time training, run Ilaria RVC's built-in Dataset Checker to catch hidden audio problems early:
Clipping detection: Finds segments where peaks hit 0 dBFS and flatten out, which can cause harsh distortion or NaN loss during training.
Long silences: Flags clips that are mostly empty air so you can trim or remove them.
Unreadable or broken files: Catches corrupted headers, zero-byte files, or clips shorter than 1 second that would crash preprocessing (zero-size array).
Inconsistent active levels: Highlights clips that are dramatically quieter or louder than the rest of the dataset.
Recommended workflow:
Point the Dataset Checker to your dataset folder and run the scan.
Listen to every flagged file before deleting or editing it.
Preserve natural quiet delivery and intentional pauses when they belong to the voice, and remove or re-clean only genuinely broken, clipped, or noisy clips.
Use the Audio Analyzer to inspect why a recording or conversion sounds wrong:
Waveform peaks: Flat-topped waves indicate hard digital clipping. Lower the gain or replace the clipped recording.

Spectrogram: Look at silent gaps between words. A constant horizontal line at 50/60 Hz points to electrical hum; bright vertical smudges or wash across frequencies indicate leftover music bleed or room reverb.
Pitch & active levels: Check whether the speaker's pitch jumps unnaturally (tracking error) or whether levels drop too low.

Before vs After comparison: Load the exact same region of both the original input and the converted output to tell whether an artifact came from the dataset, the separation step, or inference settings.
Add more varied phrases and stop training earlier (fewer epochs).

Every option produces a FAISS retrieval index. The selector changes which extracted feature vectors go into the index, independently of the training of the voice model. A feature vector represents a short audio frame. The thresholds below count vectors, not clips, epochs or minutes.
Option
What Ilaria RVC does
When to try it
Auto
Keeps all vectors up to 200,000. Above that it attempts to reduce them to 10,000 cluster centers. If clustering fails, it retains the original vectors.
Start here for a first index. Check the Train Index log to see which path Auto took.
Faiss
Keeps all extracted vectors and builds the FAISS index without a KMeans reduction pass.
Try it when you want to preserve examples that a smaller index might average out and have enough RAM and disk space.
KMeans

Uses MiniBatchKMeans to represent similar vectors with shared centers. It normally keeps about one center per ten vectors, within a range of 39 to 10,000 centers and always fewer than the input count. It keeps all vectors for inputs of 39 or fewer, and reports a clustering error rather than silently falling back.
Compare it when you want a smaller index. The clustering pass takes extra work, and the reduced index can lose fine detail.

A smaller index is usually lighter to store. It does not guarantee a faster build or better conversion. Clustering still requires loading the extracted features. If Auto falls back on a large dataset, building from all vectors can still run out of memory.
Finish Feature Extraction, then run Train Index. Check the log for the vector or center count. Make a copy of the resulting index before generating a second one with another setting.
Use the same inference .pth and a clean held-out recording. Set Index Ratio to zero first to hear the checkpoint alone. The index is optional for conversion.

Compare the two matching indexes at the same nonzero Index Ratio, with pitch and effects held constant. Listen to clear consonants, sustained vowels, unusual sounds and how much target voice character is retained. Keep the one that sounds better on several clips.

Keep the chosen index with the model and the feature configuration that produced it. If you change the algorithm, rebuild the index from the existing compatible features. If you change the training embedder, extract matching features for that experiment instead of reusing the old index.

In Ilaria RVC, the Voice Blender feature is located in the Other tab under Merge models. It lets you combine the weights of two compatible .pth voice models into a brand-new hybrid voice without having to train a new model from scratch.
Two voices sounding similar does not guarantee they can be merged. Both source models must match technically:
Inference .pth files only: Use exported inference models from weights/. Never use raw training checkpoints (G_*.pth / D_*.pth) or .onnx files.
Same RVC version: Both models must share the same architecture (v1 256-d vs v2 768-d).
Same sample rate: Both models must be trained at the same sample rate (for example both 40k or both 48k).
Same embedder / hidden dimensions: Both must use compatible tensor shapes.
Always click Check model compatibility in Ilaria RVC before merging. If the check fails, the two .pth files cannot be blended together.

l: How to blend two voices in Ilaria RVC
p: Open the Other tab and scroll to Merge models.
Select Model A and Model B from your model dropdowns (click Refresh first if you recently added a .pth file).
Click Check model compatibility and confirm the log says the two models are compatible.
Set Model A contribution (%):
50 gives an equal 50% / 50% blend of Model A and Model B.
70 gives 70% Model A and 30% Model B.
100 outputs purely Model A; 0 outputs purely Model B.
Choose Sample rate (Auto if available, or match the exact sample rate of both models).
Choose Output precision:
fp16 creates a smaller file and runs faster on modern NVIDIA CUDA GPUs.
fp32 is larger but works on all setups, including older GPUs, DirectML, and CPU.
Enter a descriptive Output model name (for example Alice70_Bob30) and optional notes.
Click Merge and save model and check Merge Log to confirm the .pth was saved.
No .index file is created: Merging combines the .pth weights only and does not generate a new .index file.
Test with Index disabled first: Switch to Inference, click Refresh, select your new merged .pth, and test it on a clean 10-20 second .wav clip with Index Rate = 0.

Compare side by side: Listen to the same test clip through Model A, Model B, and the merged model at equal volume. Adjust Model A contribution (%) in small steps (for example 40%, 50%, 60%) until you find the balance you want.

Optional index testing: Once the .pth blend sounds good, you can test pairing Model A's or Model B's .index at a low Index Rate (0.2 to 0.4) to see if it improves clarity without pulling the voice too far back toward one source.
Keep your original models: A merged .pth is strictly for inference (converting audio). It does not contain training state and cannot be used to resume training.
Complete beginner-friendly guide to Ilaria RVC's Safetensors and PTH model converter in the Other tab, including metadata preservation and Move .pth to models.

Starting in Ilaria RVC 2.4.5, the Other tab includes Convert model weights, a built-in converter that turns .pth voice models into .safetensors files and .safetensors files back into .pth models.
When you download AI voice models, you usually see .pth files, and sometimes .safetensors files:

.pth (PyTorch format): The classic RVC model format. It stores the neural network weights plus RVC's voice configuration (sample rate, pitch guidance, RVC version, embedder info). However, .pth uses Python's pickle format, which is why modern PyTorch (2.6+) restricts how .pth files are loaded for security.

.safetensors (SafeTensors format): A modern format created by Hugging Face that stores model weights without executable code. It is much safer to share or download from strangers and loads very cleanly.
Why convert between them?
Convert .pth → .safetensors when you want to archive or share your voice model in the safer .safetensors format while keeping its RVC settings intact.
Convert .safetensors → .pth when you downloaded a .safetensors voice model and need a .pth file that Ilaria RVC (or another RVC app) can load in Inference.
Inside Other → Convert model weights, Ilaria RVC runs the conversion safely on your CPU (no GPU/VRAM needed):

First-time automatic setup: If safetensors is not installed yet, Ilaria RVC automatically downloads and installs safetensors==0.8.0 into assets/weight_converter/dependencies on first use (requires an internet connection the very first time).

RVC metadata preservation: When converting an exported RVC .pth to .safetensors, Ilaria RVC saves the voice configuration inside a special metadata tag (ilaria_rvc_checkpoint). When you convert that .safetensors back to .pth, it restores the full RVC voice configuration automatically so it works right away in Inference.

Tensor-only files: If you convert a .safetensors file that came from another tool without RVC metadata, Ilaria RVC still converts it into a tensor-only .pth, but it will not have the voice settings needed for automatic Inference or Move .pth to models.
Training checkpoints are blocked: Raw training checkpoints (G_*.pth or D_*.pth from logs/) contain training optimizer state and cannot be converted here. Export your finished voice model first.
Open Other and expand Convert model weights.
Drag and drop your .pth or .safetensors file into Choose or drop a .pth or .safetensors file.

Watch Conversion Log (5% | Preparing Safetensors... → 10% | Reading weights on CPU... → completion).

What Audio Analyzer measures vs. what it suggests: Audio Analyzer directly plots and measures signal levels, silence intervals, spectral energy, and estimated F0 contours. It does not automatically diagnose "good" vs. "bad" voice timbre on its own. Always listen to the selected region in the built-in player before treating a visual difference as a problem.
What it directly shows
Where are loud peaks, flat-topped clipping, quiet passages, or abrupt joins?
Which frequencies are present at the exact moment hiss, buzz, or an artifact starts?

l: Practical examples: what to look for
p: Clipping: Flat-topped peaks hitting the maximum amplitude in the Waveform (often heard as harsh crackle). Lower input gain or normalize the source before training or conversion.
Background noise / hiss: A constant horizontal band or bright floor across mid/high frequencies in the Spectrogram during pauses. Clean the source with UVR5 or MVSep before training.
Excessive silence or dead gaps: Long flat sections in the Waveform and high silence ratios in the Level and silence tables. Trim long pauses in datasets so training does not waste steps on silence.
Too quiet / too loud volume: Very thin waveform amplitude (risks noisy amplification) or near-max peaks. Check the Level and silence tables so A/B comparisons are judged at matched loudness.

Distortion & reverb: Blurry, smeared horizontal tails extending after words end in the Spectrogram indicate room reverb; harsh vertical spikes or smeared harmonics suggest distortion or over-processing.

Dataset quality check: Inspect raw source clips before training, then compare the same phrase across checkpoints. When pitch estimation looks erratic during breaths or unvoiced consonants (s, f, t), listen first: unvoiced sounds naturally have no stable pitch.

Choose a matching time range and channel view, and keep the same FFT window, frequency scale, and silence threshold across comparisons. A larger FFT window improves frequency detail while smoothing fast time events. Export CSV or JSON for numeric measurements, or a ZIP with charts for later review.
