l: 1. What GPU Clock Locking Is (Beginner Introduction)
p: What a GPU frequency (clock speed) is: Inside your NVIDIA graphics card, the main processor (the GPU core) performs millions of small math calculations every second. Its clock frequency is how many calculation cycles it completes per second.
What MHz means: MHz stands for megahertz (1 million cycles per second). For example, 1500 MHz means 1.5 billion cycles per second, and 1800 MHz means 1.8 billion cycles per second.

How NVIDIA dynamic clocks work: Modern NVIDIA GPUs do not run at one fixed speed. When your PC is idle on the desktop, the GPU drops to a low speed (for example 210 MHz or 300 MHz) to save electricity, stay quiet, and stay cool. When heavy work starts, it raises the speed.

What NVIDIA GPU Boost is: NVIDIA GPU Boost is the built-in automatic system that constantly adjusts your GPU's frequency up and down based on workload, temperature, power limits, and voltage headroom.

Why clocks fluctuate during Vonovox: Real-time voice conversion processes audio in discrete chunks (the exact chunk duration depends on your Block Size and audio settings) rather than a continuous heavy 3D render. Between chunks, the GPU may briefly see low load and drop its clock speed, then ramp back up on the next chunk.

What locking a clock means: GPU Clock Locking (nvidia-smi -lgc) tells the NVIDIA driver to keep the GPU core inside a specific supported frequency range (or at one supported frequency, when min and max are equal) instead of letting it drop down and ramp up constantly. Think of it like cruise control on a highway: the car holds a steady speed instead of slowing down and accelerating over and over.
GPU Clock Locking vs. Overclocking:
Overclocking pushes a GPU beyond its factory-rated limits or alters voltages/power curves to chase higher peak speed.
GPU Clock Locking only picks a frequency that NVIDIA already built into your card's official supported clock table. It does not raise voltage, unlock power limits, or force unsupported speeds.

Why a stable clock can help real-time audio: If your GPU takes 8 ms to process an audio block at a higher clock, and 18 ms when it temporarily downclocks, that sudden jump can cause uneven processing times. Holding a steady supported clock can make block processing times more consistent.

Why the maximum clock is not always best: Running at the absolute highest supported MHz increases heat, fan noise, and power draw. If your GPU hits its temperature or power limit, it will automatically throttle (force its own speed down), creating worse stutters than a moderate, steady clock.
Vonovox processes live microphone audio through CUDA on your NVIDIA GPU. Every audio chunk (determined by Block Size) must finish processing before the next chunk arrives.
GPU Delay & processing time variance: In Vonovox, GPU Delay shows how long the GPU takes to convert each chunk. If GPU clocks bounce between idle and boost states, GPU Delay can spike unexpectedly.

Audio crackling, popping, and stuttering: If even one audio chunk finishes late because the GPU was still ramping up its clock, the audio buffer runs dry and you hear a click, pop, or robotic stutter.

Buffer Size and Block Size: Larger Block Size values give the GPU more breathing room at the cost of higher overall latency. Smaller Block Size values feel more responsive but are much more sensitive to sudden GPU Delay spikes.

WASAPI and WASAPI Exclusive Mode: WASAPI (Windows Audio Session API) handles audio routing between your mic, Vonovox, and your virtual cable. WASAPI Exclusive Mode (when supported by your device and app) can reduce Windows mixer overhead, while shared mode offers broader compatibility. Neither fixes a GPU that is late delivering converted audio, and GPU Clock Locking does not fix Windows audio driver/sample-rate mismatches.

Vonovox + gaming simultaneously: When you play a 3D game and run Vonovox at the same time, both compete for the same GPU. If the game saturates 95-100% of GPU compute, Vonovox waits in line regardless of clock locking. In that case, lowering in-game graphics/FPS caps or raising Vonovox's Block Size helps far more than locking clocks.

GPU vs. CPU or audio driver issues: Audio glitches can also come from CPU overload, mismatched 48 kHz sample rates, USB mic power saving, or virtual cable misconfiguration. GPU Clock Locking only targets GPU frequency transitions.
Possible benefits (not guaranteed)
What GPU Clock Locking does NOT guarantee
More predictable GPU clock behavior during bursty audio loads
Faster overall voice conversion speed
Fewer sudden GPU Delay spikes on some desktop/laptop setups
Elimination of all crackling, popping, or dropouts
Easier A/B troubleshooting when isolating latency jitter
Better voice quality, timbre, or pitch accuracy
Having nvidia-smi installed does not guarantee that -lgc (Lock Graphics Clocks) is supported on your hardware and driver combination.
Desktop GeForce GPUs: Many modern desktop GeForce cards support -lgc on recent drivers, though exact clock granularity and behavior depend on architecture and driver version.

Laptop NVIDIA GPUs: Many laptops restrict clock locking in firmware/BIOS, power management, or Optimus/hybrid graphics paths. Even when -lgc is accepted, laptop thermal and power limits frequently override the requested clock.
Workstation / Datacenter GPUs (Quadro, RTX A-series, Tesla, L4/T4): Broadly support nvidia-smi clock controls on standard enterprise/studio drivers.

Older hardware generations & drivers: Older architectures (such as Maxwell/Pascal or legacy drivers) may return Not Supported for -lgc or SUPPORTED_CLOCKS. Do not assume every GTX or RTX card supports clock locking.

p: There is no single "best MHz" for every GPU model, PC case, or room temperature. Follow this safe selection process:
Observe your GPU's normal clocks first: Open Vonovox, start live conversion, and run nvidia-smi -i 0 -q -d CLOCK in CMD to see what Graphics MHz your card naturally uses.
Check SUPPORTED_CLOCKS: Pick a value from your Graphics list that sits comfortably around or slightly below your typical boost range.
Do not automatically choose the maximum: The highest listed clock draws the most power and generates the most heat. A slightly lower supported clock often stays cooler and avoids throttling.
Watch temperatures and power draw: Keep an eye on nvidia-smi while testing. If temperatures climb rapidly or fans run at full blast, pick a lower supported clock.
Check for thermal or power throttling: Run nvidia-smi -i 0 -q -d PERFORMANCE during load to see if SW Thermal Slowdown or HW Thermal Slowdown becomes Active.
Test 2-3 supported values if needed: Compare them using the A/B test.
Keep it only if it helps: If you do not see measurably steadier GPU Delay or cleaner audio, reset to defaults.

l: Verify the clock lock was accepted vs. actually observed
p: It is important to distinguish between:
Requested frequency: The MHz value you passed to -lgc.
Configured range (min,max): The bounds accepted by the driver (note that some drivers/devices may snap to the nearest supported clock).
Actually observed frequency: The real clock your GPU runs at under load.

After running -lgc, CMD only confirms that the driver accepted the request. Acceptance does not guarantee the GPU will stay locked at that exact MHz. To check the actually observed live clock while Vonovox is converting audio, run:
Or watch it update every second (press Ctrl + C to stop watching):

Look at Clocks → Graphics in the output. Thermal limits, power limits, and driver or laptop firmware restrictions can still prevent the GPU from holding the exact requested MHz, and -lgc does not always keep a perfectly fixed frequency under all conditions.
Always restore dynamic clock management when you finish testing, when you close Vonovox, or if you see no benefit (replace 0 with the GPU index you configured if you have multiple GPUs):
What it does: -rgc (Reset Graphics Clocks) removes the clock lock and hands control back to NVIDIA GPU Boost.
Why restore defaults: Dynamic clocks keep your GPU cooler, quieter, and more power-efficient during normal desktop use, video playback, and gaming.
How to verify restoration: Run nvidia-smi -i 0 -q -d CLOCK while idle on the desktop; after a few seconds, the Graphics clock should drop back down to low idle speeds.
Reboots and driver resets: nvidia-smi -lgc is not permanent. Rebooting Windows or restarting the graphics driver normally resets clocks to default automatically.

If -rgc returns an error: -rgc is not guaranteed to succeed if the NVIDIA driver itself is in an error state. Ensure CMD is running as administrator, confirm the -i GPU index matches nvidia-smi -L, or reboot Windows to restore dynamic clocks.
These two Windows .bat scripts use built-in Windows PowerShell (no external software required) to automate the safe workflow above:

What the scripts do: Lock-GPU-Clocks.bat temporarily locks only your NVIDIA GPU's core Graphics clock until you reset it or reboot. Reset-GPU-Clocks.bat removes that lock and returns control to NVIDIA GPU Boost.
No risky changes: Neither script overclocks, touches voltages, modifies power limits, disables Windows security features, or makes permanent system changes.

Strict input & frequency validation: Lock-GPU-Clocks.bat checks administrator privileges independently of the Windows Server service, verifies that your chosen GPU index exists in nvidia-smi -L, parses only Graphics clocks from SUPPORTED_CLOCKS (ignoring Memory clocks), rejects arbitrary or unverified numbers (like 50000), and never auto-selects the maximum clock.

Safe error handling: If -lgc fails, the script does not run -rgc automatically, displays the NVIDIA exit code, and tells you how to inspect your current clocks before proceeding. It also uses structured nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks.gr telemetry to distinguish between driver acceptance and the actually observed clock.

l: How to create and run the .bat files safely
p: Open Notepad (search notepad in the Start menu).
Copy one of the complete scripts above and paste it into Notepad.
Click File → Save As....
At the bottom, change Save as type from Text Documents (*.txt) to All Files (*.*).

Name the file Lock-GPU-Clocks.bat (or Reset-GPU-Clocks.bat) and save it to an easy-to-find folder such as your Desktop. (Changing Save as type to All Files prevents Windows from accidentally naming it Lock-GPU-Clocks.bat.txt.)
Right-click the saved .bat file and select Run as administrator.
Read the output carefully:
[ACCEPTED] / [DONE] means nvidia-smi accepted the command and shows the observed Graphics clock right afterward.
[ERROR] or [STOPPED] explains what failed and confirms no unverified clock was applied. If your GPU shows Not Supported or cannot be parsed, skip this optimization.

Locking within NVIDIA's supported clocks is not overclocking, but it still has trade-offs:
Higher temperatures and fan noise: Holding higher clocks at idle or light load generates extra heat and keeps fans spinning faster.

Higher power draw and shorter laptop battery life: A locked graphics clock can limit or reduce how often your GPU drops into low-power idle states, which can increase idle power draw and drain laptop batteries faster.
Thermal throttling or power throttling: If a locked clock pushes your cooling or power budget too hard, the GPU will throttle itself down anyway, sometimes causing worse stutters.
Limited compatibility and third-party tool conflicts: Tools like MSI Afterburner, Armoury Crate, or OEM laptop control centers may override or conflict with nvidia-smi clock settings.
Do not modify BIOS, voltages, or thermal protections: Never flash custom VBIOS files, disable thermal limits, or force overvolting for voice conversion.

l: 12. Advanced Note: GPU Memory Clock Locking (-lmc)
p: nvidia-smi also provides memory clock commands:

-lmc locks VRAM (memory) frequency, whereas -lgc locks GPU core (graphics) frequency. Memory clock locking is not part of the standard Vonovox workflow because there is insufficient evidence that locking VRAM clocks improves live RVC audio performance, and keeping VRAM at high clocks continuously increases idle heat and power draw.

l: 13. Alternatives When Clock Locking Does Not Help
p: If -lgc returns Not Supported or does not improve your audio, try these safer, often more effective steps:

NVIDIA Control Panel → Power Management Mode: Set Power management mode to Prefer maximum performance for the Vonovox executable (Manage 3D settings → Program Settings). Note: this is not the same as -lgc and does not guarantee fixed clocks across all CUDA workloads, but it can reduce aggressive downclocking on some systems.
Verify Vonovox uses your NVIDIA GPU: On laptops with hybrid graphics, make sure Vonovox runs on the NVIDIA GPU rather than integrated graphics.
Adjust Block Size in Vonovox: Increasing Block Size by one step is the most reliable way to eliminate crackling when the GPU is busy.
Match 48 kHz audio formats & WASAPI setup: Follow Route and tune Vonovox to align sample rates and avoid duplicate monitoring.
Reduce competing GPU workloads: Cap in-game frame rates or lower heavy GPU settings when running Vonovox alongside games.
Check drivers & cooling: Update to a clean Studio/Game Ready driver and clear dust from laptop/PC vents if thermal throttling occurs.

Can I use 50000 MHz? No. Never enter arbitrary numbers. Out-of-range values can fail with Invalid Argument and are not guaranteed to clamp safely.
Can I use Vonovox while gaming? Yes, provided your GPU has enough headroom for both. If the game hits 95-100% GPU load, cap FPS or increase Vonovox Block Size.
Do I need to apply it every time? Yes, if you decide to keep using it, because nvidia-smi clock locks reset on reboot or driver restart.
Does it work on every NVIDIA GPU? No. Support depends on the GPU generation, board/laptop firmware, and driver version.
Does it work on laptops? Sometimes, but many laptops restrict -lgc in firmware or hit thermal/power limits quickly. Always keep laptops plugged into AC power when testing.
Does it work with RTX GPUs? Many desktop RTX cards support -lgc on modern drivers, while some laptops or specific configurations may return Not Supported. Test with SUPPORTED_CLOCKS first.
How do I restore everything to normal? Run nvidia-smi -i 0 -rgc as Administrator, run Reset-GPU-Clocks.bat, or reboot Windows.
Is GPU Clock Locking safe? Yes, when you only use official frequencies from SUPPORTED_CLOCKS and monitor temperatures. It does not change voltages or bypass hardware thermal protections.
Is this overclocking? No. Overclocking pushes hardware beyond factory limits. Clock locking only selects frequencies already defined by NVIDIA in your card's supported table.
Should I always select the maximum clock? No. Maximum clocks create maximum heat and noise and can trigger thermal throttling. Moderate supported clocks are often more stable.
Should I lock the VRAM clock too (-lmc)? No. There is no solid evidence that locking memory clocks helps Vonovox, and it increases idle heat and power draw.

What happens if my GPU overheats? NVIDIA's hardware thermal protection will automatically throttle the card down (or shut down in extreme cases). If temps climb too high, run nvidia-smi -i 0 -rgc immediately.
What should I do if I see Not Supported? Skip GPU Clock Locking completely and use the safer Alternatives such as Block Size tuning and NVIDIA Control Panel power settings.
Will it improve Vonovox voice quality? No. Voice quality depends on your model, microphone, pitch/F0 extractor, and audio routing, not GPU clock locking.
Will it reduce latency? It does not lower minimum latency below what your GPU can already compute, though it may reduce sudden latency spikes caused by clock ramping on some setups.
Will the settings survive a reboot? No. Rebooting Windows automatically clears -lgc and returns your GPU to normal dynamic clocks.
Will this increase my FPS in games? Usually no, and it is not meant for that. If a locked clock is lower than your normal boost clock, gaming FPS may even drop slightly.

l: Install Applio and check the engine
p: GitHub · Hugging Face
Applio has two download options that run the exact same engine - only the UI and installation method differ:
Desktop App: opens a native installed application window and manages its Python engine environment on first launch.
Gradio Web Interface: runs the Python application and opens a local web UI in your browser (available as a compiled Windows ZIP or Python source install).
Open the official Desktop downloads. Find Assets and expand the list if the installer you need is hidden. Choose the asset for your operating system. The source-code archives are for developers.

On Windows, run the setup executable and choose a folder your account can write to. The packaged app uses a data directory beside its executable. On macOS, use the disk image for your processor, ARM64 for Apple Silicon or x64 for Intel. On Linux, install the available Debian package or make the AppImage executable and open it.

Start the app and review the first-run terms. Keep the app open while it sets up Python, installs the engine requirements, fetches assets and verifies the installation. Use Install / Repair if your build offers it when a check fails.

When verification completes, check the compute device detected in setup. Record the backend and hardware the app reports. A machine with more than one GPU can report a different device from the one you expected.
Open Models. If it opens and the engine is ready, continue to install a voice. Run the short conversion before trying live mode or training.
You can install an official Desktop package without Node.js or pnpm. Those tools are for building the app from source.
Windows compiled package: download a Windows ZIP from the compiled Gradio downloads, or clone the GitHub repository for a manual Python/source install.
Extract the complete ZIP to a simple path you own, for example C:\Applio-Gradio. Open that folder in Explorer. If you see a second folder containing the launcher, open it.

Run run-applio.bat (or python app.py on a manual Python install; python app.py --help lists server options). Leave the console running, wait for it to print a local address, and open that exact address in your browser.
Find Models or Download, depending on the release. Then open Convert Audio or Inference. If the browser loses its connection, check whether the launcher is still running before reopening the page.

l: Confirm that the engine can use it
p: Use an isolated clip of speech that lasts about ten seconds. Start with pitch at 0, effects off and a retrieval ratio of 0. If the model has several speakers, select the intended speaker ID.
Choose the documented embedder and run a single conversion. Confirm that the result is playable and you can recognize the words you supplied.
If you have a matching index, save the baseline first. Select the index, raise the retrieval ratio a little and run the same clip again. Keep whichever result works better for that voice.

If a model disappears after refresh, verify its file extension and check where the selected installation keeps models. If the voice is listed but produces an error at load time, read the first model-loading error. Verify that you supplied an inference export and that your build supports the architecture. If a file came from a browser download, check that the browser saved the actual model archive and did not save an HTML login page.
Start with one short recording you can recognize instantly. Spoken test material could be “Could you put the blue book by the window?” followed by a quiet pause.

Start with one short recording you can recognize instantly. Spoken test material could be “Could you put the blue book by the window?” followed by a quiet pause. For a song, use a few seconds of an isolated lead vocal. The engine receives the sound present in that file, including room noise, accompaniment or other speakers.
Open Convert Audio. In older Gradio versions, look for Inference. Select the single-file mode.
Select the inference voice you installed, and confirm the embedder and speaker ID. If settings restored when you changed voices in Desktop, inspect them before using the new voice.
Add your audio recording. Use Pitch at 0 and disable extra processing and effects. Start with retrieval influence at 0. Select WAV or FLAC so you can compare lossless results.
Start the conversion once. In Desktop, look at the job status if the result is queued. In Gradio, leave the launch console open to see errors that do not fit in the browser.
Play both files. Check that words land in the same places and that the output contains the target voice. Save the output to a folder you control and record the settings you used.

l: Change one control at a time
p: Control
A useful first experiment
Pitch shift

Try a small semitone shift if the source lies outside the target voice’s comfortable range. +12 doubles frequency and −12 halves it. Replay a high and a low phrase before applying the change to a song.
Pitch extractor
Compare available estimators when a note jumps or a soft phrase loses voicing. Keep the model, transposition and input fixed.
Search Feature Ratio
With the correct index loaded, increase influence in small steps. Listen for stronger target character, muffled consonants or unwanted source leakage.
Volume Envelope
A value near 0 follows the source dynamics more closely. A value near 1 retains more of the generated dynamics. Compare quiet and loud syllables at a matched playback volume.
Protect Voiceless Consonants
On the current pitch-guided engine, settings below 0.5 activate protection. Lower values increase it. Try a phrase with breaths and consonants such as S, F or T.

Split Audio can help process a long file in pieces. Listen across the joins. Clean Audio can reduce unwanted noise, so compare it against a clean baseline for changes to detail. Proposed Pitch derives a target-directed shift and can interact with manual transposition. Test each by itself. Effects activated through Post-Process apply to the generated audio and can mask a conversion issue.
Put two working files and one quieter or longer example in a test input folder.
Choose batch mode. Select the input, and use a different destination where the engine can write. For Gradio running on another machine, paths must exist on that machine.
Copy the tested model, embedder, index and pitch settings. Start the test and inspect the results before processing an entire collection.

If an input fails, convert that file alone using the same settings. If it fails only in the batch, check the path and output naming. Store the files you want to keep outside temporary working storage.
The job produced no audio. Read the error first. Verify the input plays, the engine verifies, and the selected model is an inference export.
Pitch sounds jumpy or electronic. Test the correct embedder, one pitch estimator and a clean input without effects. Replay the original to see whether the noise or jump was already present.
Speech is present but the target voice sounds weak. Check speaker ID, then compare retrieval only if you have the right index.
The file clips or pulses. Test at a lower source level and turn off processing that changes gain. For singing, compare the isolated vocal before mixing it back into the backing track.
A first run proves that your recordings, configuration and hardware can produce an export you can convert with. Work on copied recordings you have permission to use.

l: Train, evaluate and export a voice in Applio
p: A first run proves that your recordings, configuration and hardware can produce an export you can convert with. Work on copied recordings you have permission to use. Keep two or three phrases outside the training folder so you can check behavior on recordings the model has never seen.
Create a short, recognizable experiment name such as speaking_trial_01. Keep scratch tests under their own names so you can find later checkpoints.

Check the recordings by ear at the beginning, middle and end. Remove clips with another speaker, music, clipping or long silent sections. If Desktop has dataset review tools, inspect flagged clips and prepare a training copy there. Trimming silence and adjusting level cannot repair audible distortion.

Select the copied dataset in Training. If Gradio asks for a folder path, use one on the machine running the engine. For a supported multispeaker workflow, preserve numeric folders such as 0 and 1 and record which person each ID represents.

Choose a vocoder and sampling rate supported together. Select a compatible generator/discriminator pair if using pretraining. Match rate, pitch guidance, architecture and the publisher’s embedder requirements. Record the exact embedder and any custom files for inference later.
Choose a batch size that fits GPU memory and save some intermediate exports. Pick an initial epoch target for a pipeline test. Extend it later if held-out tests improve.
Applio builds optional retrieval data from the experiment.
Applio builds the model’s content features and any pitch information needed by the configuration.
Applio reads the dataset, prepares clips and resamples for the chosen rate.
Epochs progress and the configured checkpoint or export files appear. On out-of-memory errors, stop other GPU work, lower batch size and consider disabling dataset caching.
Extract
Generate Index

In Desktop, you can choose Automatic Training after reviewing the dataset, model configuration, epochs and save settings. Start the job once and follow its console. For separate control of each stage, use Manual Training Setup. Gradio exposes the corresponding steps in its Training workspace.
Keep the generated index with the matching export. If you chose to skip this stage, leave retrieval disabled during your test.
Preprocess
Stage
The experiment learns voice characteristics from those features.
The intended embedder loaded and extraction finished. If you change encoders, run extraction again for that choice.
The log shows usable audio from the intended folder. If your build offers Post normalization, it adjusts each slice after splitting. Use it only when you want that treatment.
Train
What happens
What to confirm before continuing

When a stage fails, copy its first error and confirm its inputs before rerunning it. If recordings, rate or architecture change materially, a fresh experiment helps keep incompatible files apart. Stop realtime before starting Desktop GPU training.

l: Compare checkpoints before choosing a winner
p: Open Models → Export in Desktop, or find the training export control in Gradio. Save an inference .pth from an intermediate checkpoint and a later one, plus the index if generated. For each export, convert the same held-out phrases with the same speaker ID, embedder, pitch settings and volume. Listen for intelligibility, voice consistency on soft and loud syllables, and artifacts on breaths. Training metrics can reveal failed progress. Listening helps decide which export to keep.

Keep the experiment directory together with its preprocessing files, features and G_*.pth and D_*.pth training checkpoints. Keep the same name, architecture, rate and embedder on continuation. Choose a new total epoch target higher than the completed epoch count. In Desktop, leave Fresh Training off. Check the first log lines to see which checkpoint loaded and stop if the run unexpectedly starts over. The small inference export is the file you use in the converter. Continuing training requires the experiment’s training state.
Prove that your model works with one recorded clip before setting up live audio. Use headphones for monitoring so the microphone cannot re-capture the speakers.

Prove that your model works with one recorded clip before setting up live audio. Use headphones for monitoring so the microphone cannot re-capture the speakers. Stop training or file conversion jobs that use the same GPU.
Open Realtime. In Desktop, give microphone permission when asked, then select Input Device and Output Device. Refresh the list if you connected a device after opening Applio.

Use your physical microphone as input and your headphones as output or monitor for this first test. In Gradio, choose the devices in Audio Devices. PortAudio device names may differ from Windows names or the labels shown in Desktop.

Select the tested model, its matching embedder, and the optional index if you use it. Start the stream and wait for the ready state. In Desktop, enable Hear myself to monitor and set a comfortable volume.

Say “one, two, three,” pause, then repeat at your normal speaking level. Listen for the converted voice, missing syllables or clicks. If you hear your unchanged voice, check Passthrough and check whether the microphone is monitored elsewhere.

l: Route it to your chat or streaming app
p: 1. Inside the Voice Changer
2. Inside Discord, Games, OBS, or Other Applications
Audio coming from Discord, your game, or other apps must play directly to your headphones (never back into the virtual cable).
Correct Audio Routing
If headphones sounded correct but the receiving app is silent, troubleshoot the device names, destination level and input selection before changing the voice or index.
In the receiving app, select the cable’s recording endpoint as the microphone. If you need monitoring, use headphones. Disable monitoring paths that send the cable back into itself.
Input Device: Line 1 (VAC, recommended) or CABLE Output (VB-CABLE).
Input Device: Your physical microphone.
Keep Applio’s input on the physical microphone and select the cable’s playback endpoint as its output.
Monitoring: Hearing your own converted voice in your headphones is a separate optional feature to enable only when needed. Avoid duplicate audio paths, echo, and loopback.

Once the headphone test works, stop the stream and choose an installed virtual audio cable or equivalent operating system device. The virtual cable has one endpoint that receives playback and another that exposes that signal as a recording input.
Output Device: Line 1 (VAC, recommended) or CABLE Input (VB-CABLE).
Output Device: Your headphones (strongly recommended over speakers).

Speakers & Headset Bleed: Avoid using speakers; sound from speakers can leak into your microphone and cause double audio, echo, or other people's voices being converted too. This can also happen with headsets if the volume is too loud or the earcups are not closed and isolated enough.

Start Applio, then use the receiving application’s microphone test or make a private test recording. Check that it hears the converted signal. Turn off duplicate physical-mic inputs if you hear two voices.

VAC vs. VB-CABLE: VAC (Line 1) is always recommended. If you have VB-CABLE installed as well (or instead), remember that the voice changer outputs to CABLE Input while Discord / games listen to CABLE Output.
c: Your Microphone → Voice Changer → Line 1 (VAC) or CABLE Input/Output (VB-CABLE) → Discord / Game / OBS

Physical microphone
  → Applio Realtime input
  → virtual cable playback endpoint
  → virtual cable recording endpoint

p: Use automatic chunk sizing first where available. If audio breaks up, increase Chunk Size, then repeat exactly the same phrase. Smaller chunks can reduce delay while leaving the engine less time to finish each block. Crossfade Overlap smooths joins, and Extra Conversion Size gives more context at a compute cost. Change one control per test. Keep a stable setting you can return to.

If quiet starts or word endings disappear, check VAD or Silence Threshold. If loud vowels crackle, check the raw microphone and lower its input gain. If the stream only fails with a particular game or GPU job running, retry with that job closed. Stop live mode before returning to training or queued GPU work.
Applio uses an online Edge TTS voice to read your text and an RVC model to change the generated voice.

l: Turn a short script into converted speech
p: Applio uses an online Edge TTS voice to read your text and an RVC model to change the generated voice. The source voice determines pronunciation, pacing and the language it reads. Use text you are comfortable sending to the online synthesis service.
Open the text-to-speech workspace after the engine is ready and the voice model works.
Enter one short sentence with punctuation. Choose a source TTS voice for the language of that sentence. Start with its ordinary speaking rate.
Select your RVC inference voice, the matching embedder and its index if you use one. Start with pitch shift at 0 and effects off.

Generate speech and listen to the output. If your interface makes the synthesized source available, play it too. If the source misreads an acronym or pauses oddly, change punctuation, spell out the acronym or select another source voice first.

When the phrase sounds right, save the audio and write down the source voice, speaking rate, RVC model, embedder and pitch. For longer scripts, use small sections with natural breakpoints and keep their settings consistent.

If the speech generation step fails, test a different source voice and check the engine’s connection to the speech service. If speech generation succeeds and only conversion fails, run a short recorded file through the same RVC model. That test exposes model or embedder problems without changing the script.

GitHub · Hugging Face

RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) is the upstream Retrieval-based Voice Conversion WebUI. Use its browser interface for file conversion and training. For microphone conversion, use the separate desktop interface described in the real-time guide.
Your setup
What to use
Windows and a supported GPU
Start with a matching prebuilt Windows archive. This is the shortest route.
Windows and an NVIDIA RTX 50-series GPU
Use a package explicitly marked for the 50 series or the source setup with the CUDA 12.8 Torch build. Older NVIDIA archives can start but fail when they try to run GPU operations.
Windows and an AMD or Intel GPU
Choose the matching AMD/Intel archive. DirectML support depends on the release and operation. Test file conversion first.
Ubuntu or a custom Windows setup
Install the current source branch into a separate Python environment.

Open the RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) Windows package and asset downloads and choose the archive matching your GPU. For the current package family, look for the 20260718 NVIDIA, NVIDIA 50-series, or AMD/Intel variant. If you already have an older release that works, leave it in its own directory.

Extract the entire archive to a writable local folder such as C:\RVC\Mainline. Allow space for both the download and the extracted files. In File Explorer, open the resulting folder and look for the launcher, assets, and the Python runtime. If you see one more enclosing directory, open it.

Run go-webui.bat if present. Older archives may call it go-web.bat. Keep the command window open and wait for the local address. If the browser does not start, open the address shown in the terminal. A common default is http://127.0.0.1:7865.
Confirm that the page opens and that the terminal remains running. Keep the archive intact until the first conversion succeeds.

Recommended on Windows: download the ready-to-use Windows archive for your GPU. Installing from source is discouraged for most users because you have to configure Python and its dependencies yourself.

Download and extract the RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) source ZIP. Open a terminal in the directory containing webui.py and the requirements files. The source setup below applies to the Python 3.12 branch. Run each snippet from that directory using a 64-bit Python 3.12 interpreter.
Windows PowerShell
If PowerShell blocks the activation script, open Command Prompt in the same directory and run .venv\Scripts\activate.bat. On Windows, put ffmpeg.exe and ffprobe.exe beside webui.py.
Ubuntu 24.04
Choose one dependency set. The filenames contain requirments as spelled in the repository. Run the matching block from top to bottom.
CPU, AMD, or Intel
NVIDIA RTX 50 series
Supported older NVIDIA cards
Check which interpreter and Torch build the terminal is using:
Expect the interpreter path to contain .venv. CUDA availability should be True for working NVIDIA CUDA inference. CPU and DirectML installations can show False in this CUDA check.
Install the shared feature and pitch models before your first conversion:

Generic HuBERT checkpoints are not recommended as the default encoder for voice conversion. Their speech prediction training does not explicitly remove speaker identity, so the features can carry source timbre into the output. For RVC, use the encoder expected by the model, such as ContentVec when the voice was trained with it.
Windows DirectML setups that use the ONNX pitch model also need hf download lj1995/VoiceConversionWebUI rmvpe.onnx --local-dir assets/rmvpe. The training guide lists the additional training assets.

Run python webui.py from the same directory. The feature encoder should be a folder named assets/hubert_base containing the config, preprocessing config and weight file. If you installed a legacy archive, keep its bundled files and naming conventions together.

l: If the WebUI will not open
p: What you see
What to check first
No browser tab
Read the last lines in the terminal and copy the actual local URL. If the default port is busy, a build may choose another one.
The launcher opens and immediately closes
Run it from an existing Command Prompt inside the extracted folder so you can read the first error. Check that extraction finished before changing dependencies.
ModuleNotFoundError on a source install
Confirm that you launched from the virtual environment used for installation. Complete the matching requirements installation.
CUDA is unavailable on an NVIDIA setup
Check the GPU model, driver and Torch wheel together. An RTX 50-series system needs the matching build.
Missing HuBERT, RMVPE or FFmpeg
Check the asset folders and executable paths above. Retry with a simple local WAV after correcting the missing file.
When the interface opens, continue with your first file conversion.
Interactive RVC Compatibility Matrix
Start with a short recording that you can hear clearly in a normal media player, plus an exported RVC model you have permission to use.

l: Convert recordings in RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC)
p: Start with a short recording that you can hear clearly in a normal media player, plus an exported RVC model you have permission to use. The model changes the voice in the recording. The source provides the words, rhythm and delivery. For a song, use a separately recorded or isolated vocal track for the first pass.

l: Put each file in the right place
p: What you received
Where it goes
A ZIP or 7z with a model inside
Extract the files before adding them to RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC).
An inference .pth file
Copy it to assets/weights/ inside the RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) folder. If you trained it yourself, use the exported small model.
A populated .index for that exact model
In current builds, copy it to assets/indices/. Older builds commonly discover indexes under logs/. If auto-detection fails, select it or enter its full path manually.
A G_*.pth or D_*.pth training checkpoint
Keep it with the experiment in logs/. Use the training guide to identify or export a model for inference.

Use added_*.index when training produced both trained_ and added_ files. The latter contains the searchable feature vectors. Your model can work with no index. Set Index Rate to zero when you skip the index or cannot identify its matching file.

Open the WebUI and find the Model Inference tab. Refresh the model and index lists after copying files, then select the inference .pth in the voice dropdown. Give the interface time to read the checkpoint.

Choose a short WAV with one voice speaking or singing on its own. Newer builds expose an upload control. If your build shows a path box, give it a full path such as C:\RVC\test\voice.wav. Try a short local path when diagnosing file access in an older package.

Set pitch shift to 0 for the first pass. Set Index Rate or Search feature ratio to 0, and leave extra settings as they are. Select rmvpe if available and its weights are installed. With a single-speaker checkpoint, start with speaker ID 0.

Click Convert once and wait for the status and playback panel. Play the result from the beginning. If it sounds usable, use the audio player's menu to download it. If conversion fails, read the status or terminal before changing settings.
Replay the same source and output back to back. Check the first word, the highest and lowest notes, and several pauses. Change one control and rerender the same input to tell which change helped.

l: Understand the controls you are likely to touch
p: Changes how closely the result follows loud and quiet moments in the input. Closer to zero follows the source more.
Control

Controls how much the conversion preserves unvoiced detail, such as breaths and consonants. Lower values strengthen protection in the usual RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) 0–0.5 control. Try a small adjustment after index retrieval works.
Estimates the pitch contour used in pitch-guided conversion. Try another method when voice breaks appear on certain notes. Compare the same clip and keep everything else constant.
How to use it
Index Rate
Mixes in nearby features from the target voice when a matching index exists. Increase it gradually if the result keeps too much of the source timbre. Back it down if diction gets muddy.
Pitch extraction
Pitch shift
Protect
Resample output
Selects a voice within a multi-speaker checkpoint. Choose an ID actually present in that model.
Sets the exported audio sample rate where the build exposes it. Leave it at the model default during your first test.
Speaker ID
Transposes the source in semitones. +12 raises it an octave, -12 lowers it an octave. Make small moves first when words or notes sound strained.
Volume envelope

Save an unprocessed 10-second source as test.wav. Convert it with zero pitch shift and no index to get baseline.wav. Load the matching index and raise its rate for retrieval.wav. Compare those two files at similar volume. Once you choose a retrieval setting, try a pitch adjustment and save a third file. Keep whichever setting improves the same troublesome line without degrading the rest.
Finish a successful single-file test using the same voice and settings.
Create separate input and output folders. Put only the audio you want converted in input.
Under Batch Inference, choose your files or enter the full input-folder path. Set the output-folder path explicitly and choose WAV if you plan to edit the audio later.

Start with two short files. Confirm that each result appears in the output folder and plays to the end. Then run the full set. Check status for individual failures so you can retry just the affected files.
Symptom
Next test
Model list is empty
Confirm the .pth is extracted, under the active installation's assets/weights/, and visible after refresh.
Model shows up but cannot be loaded
Check that the file is a compatible inference export. A training checkpoint or a model from a different voice engine can show up in the list without being usable.
Index fails or there is no audible result
Set retrieval to zero, run a conversion and confirm the checkpoint works. Then select the matching populated index and try again.
Output is gritty or syllables wobble
Listen to the input first. Retest a clean vocal with index off. Then compare pitch methods and a modest change in transposition.
Output is missing in batch mode
Verify that the input files open, the destination folder is writable, and the terminal reports success for the relevant filename.
For more background, see RVC models and files and audio quality.
Start with a single speaker and a fresh experiment name. Training produces a model you can test on new performances in the inference interface.

l: Train and export a RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) model
p: Start with a single speaker and a fresh experiment name. Training produces a model you can test on new performances in the inference interface. Keep raw audio and the experiment log so you can reproduce your result.

Put clean voice recordings in a local folder such as C:\RVC\datasets\voice_a. Keep backups elsewhere. Use recordings you have permission to train with. Check that you can play several files and that they contain the intended voice without backing music or unrelated speakers.

Keep one or two short recordings of different phrases outside the dataset. Use these as test inputs for every checkpoint. For a dataset intended for singing, make sure you have material with the relevant vocal range and test with an isolated vocal.
If you installed from source, open the same environment used to run the WebUI and get the matching pretrained weights and silence assets. Packaged releases may already contain them.
See dataset preparation for recording and cleanup details.

c:
hf download lj1995/VoiceConversionWebUI --include "pretrained/*" "pretrained_v2/*" --local-dir assets
hf download lj1995/VoiceConversionWebUI mute.zip --local-dir .model-downloads
python -m zipfile -e .model-downloads/mute.zip logs

l: Configure the experiment and process audio
p: Open Train. Use a fresh name such as voice_a_v2_40k so RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) creates a separate folder under logs/.

Choose a target sample rate and architecture version supported by your release. V2 is a reasonable starting point when you plan to use a compatible V2 inference client. Rate, architecture, and pitch guidance must agree with the generator and discriminator pretrains. Use pitch guidance for a normal pitch-guided voice model.

Select a single-speaker dataset, where the build offers a choice. Use speaker ID 0 for the first run. Paste the complete dataset folder path, then click Process Data or the equivalent preprocessing button.

Wait for preprocessing to finish. Review warnings in the output and check that the experiment has produced processed audio. If the run produces nothing, verify the path and test whether the included audio files decode. Fix this before starting extraction.

For a multi-speaker experiment on a build with Multi-speaker Dataset Helper, keep each speaker's files separate and assign stable speaker IDs. Check the generated manifest and use those same IDs later during conversion. Complete a single-speaker pass first so you have a working baseline.
Choose the GPU index shown by the interface. For one GPU the ID is commonly 0. Device fields for different operations may be separate. Copy the available IDs instead of assuming a specific slot.

Select a pitch extractor that the build can run. If a GPU RMVPE option is available and works on your system, start there. A CPU option can help isolate a backend problem. Feature extraction also requires the shared HuBERT assets installed in setup.

Run Feature extraction and wait for both the required pitch and the content-feature stages to finish. If a stage logs no usable files, stop and correct the cause. Changing the dataset, model version, or target rate changes the experiment. Use a new experiment name when comparing incompatible settings.

Generic HuBERT checkpoints are not recommended as the default encoder for voice conversion. Their speech prediction training does not explicitly remove speaker identity, so the features can carry source timbre into the output. For RVC, use the encoder expected by the model, such as ContentVec when the voice was trained with it.

Check the generator and discriminator fields in the training panel. They should refer to a matched pair for the version, sample rate and pitch mode you selected. If a log says the files were skipped, make sure you are training with the intended setup before continuing.

Start with a batch that fits memory and leave dataset caching off for the first test. If the GPU runs out of memory, stop the failed job and lower the batch size. Avoid running a live conversion alongside the first training run.

Set a finite trial target and an interval that saves multiple checkpoints you can compare later. If you want intermediate models ready for inference, enable small model exports at save time where available. Keeping only the latest training checkpoints saves space but limits resuming from earlier versions.

Click Train model. Watch the experiment status and confirm the training log advances across epochs. Use the application's stop control when available and wait for it to finish writing files before closing the process.

Training curves reveal whether the job is running or producing errors. Choose the final model by converting the same test recordings with several saved inference exports. Compare words, consonants, pauses and difficult notes at similar volume. More epochs can help, plateau or make results worse depending on the dataset.
Back up the small inference model and its matching index to use or share. Keep the experiment folder, including matching G_*.pth and D_*.pth, configuration and logs, if you plan to resume training.
Check the dataset path, permissions, supported formats and whether the WAV files open outside RVC.

Click Train feature index after successful extraction if you want a retrieval index. Look for the populated added_*.index in the experiment output, with a discoverable copy or link if provided by your build. Skip retrieval if you only want to evaluate the checkpoint itself.
Confirm you selected an exported inference model. Test a known working checkpoint with the same input and no index.
Convert a held-out clip at zero index rate. Once that works, try the matching populated index. Save both outputs for comparison.
Feature extraction stops

Find the small exported model under assets/weights/. If you have only a generator checkpoint, use ckpt Processing and the small model extraction tool, supplying the matching rate, pitch flag and version. Refresh the model list in inference and select the small export.
Identify whether content or pitch extraction failed. Check model assets and try a supported backend.
Index generation finds no features
Inference fails with a checkpoint
Preprocessing finishes with no audio
Reduce batch size, switch off caching and free VRAM before retrying.
Revisit successful feature extraction for the same experiment. Check version and folder names before trying to reuse files.
Symptom
Training starts and then runs out of VRAM
Where to look
This guide applies to the separate real-time GUI included in supported RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) builds.

l: Use the RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) real-time voice changer
p: This guide applies to the separate real-time GUI included in supported RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) builds. It can run a microphone through a model continuously while the WebUI is used for recordings and training. Start by listening directly through headphones, then send the processed audio to your other app.

l: Open the interface and select your files
p: Finish installation and check the model with a short file conversion. This gives you an independent test if a microphone problem comes up.

In a Windows package with go-realtime_gui.bat, launch it from the unpacked program folder. In the current source branch, activate the environment from setup and run python realtime_gui.py from the repository directory. Package launcher names vary.

In the real-time window, select the small inference .pth. If you have its matching populated .index, choose it here. Leave Index Rate at 0 for the first listening test. If your build requires an index in its file picker, supply the one for the selected model.

Choose a sound host interface, then select your physical microphone as input and headphones as output. Choose the normal values for pitch and sample rate offered by your build. Start with default performance settings.

l: Verify the microphone before connecting an app
p: Lower the headphone volume before starting. If the GUI offers Input voice monitor, use it to confirm the selected microphone. Speak a short sentence and pause. Check that you hear one direct voice and silence during the pause.

Switch to Output converted voice and start conversion. Wait for initialization. Repeat the same sentence at an ordinary speaking level and listen to consonants and word endings. Check for feedback before raising the volume.

If the stream starts but clips words, check the device selection and input level. If there are repeated gaps, return to the default processing block length. A clean, slightly delayed voice is a better baseline than a low-latency signal that keeps breaking up.
Stop the stream before changing audio devices or loading a different checkpoint. Restart and repeat the same listening test.

p: 1. Inside the Voice Changer

Audio coming from Discord, your game, or other apps must play directly to your headphones (never back into the virtual cable).
Correct Audio Routing
If the destination app cuts quiet syllables, compare a short sample with automatic noise processing off for diagnosis. Restore any processing that improves the result without losing words.
In the destination app, choose the cable's recording end as its microphone. Select your headphones for that app's playback so sound from the call does not travel back through the cable.
Input Device: Line 1 (VAC, recommended) or CABLE Output (VB-CABLE).
Input Device: Your physical microphone.
Monitoring: Hearing your own converted voice in your headphones is a separate optional feature to enable only when needed. Avoid duplicate audio paths, echo, and loopback.
Output Device: Line 1 (VAC, recommended) or CABLE Input (VB-CABLE).
Output Device: Your headphones (strongly recommended over speakers).

Set up a virtual cable or other pair of connected playback and recording devices. The playback end receives sound from RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC). The recording end supplies that sound to your call or recorder.

Speakers & Headset Bleed: Avoid using speakers; sound from speakers can leak into your microphone and cause double audio, echo, or other people's voices being converted too. This can also happen with headsets if the volume is too loud or the earcups are not closed and isolated enough.

Start conversion and make a private recording or use the app's microphone test. Confirm that it captures the converted voice once. If you also need local monitoring, use the destination app's monitoring where available and keep it separate from the cable input.
Stop conversion and set the RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) output device to the cable's playback end. Leave the physical microphone selected as RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC)'s input.

VAC vs. VB-CABLE: VAC (Line 1) is always recommended. If you have VB-CABLE installed as well (or instead), remember that the voice changer outputs to CABLE Input while Discord / games listen to CABLE Output.

p: Check first
Confirm you chose the two ends of the same cable. Test both endpoints with a local recording app.

Decrease Sample length or the equivalent block control one increment at a time. A shorter block reduces waiting but gives the engine less time to finish. Repeat a quiet phrase and a louder phrase after each change. If there are clicks, dropouts or repeated syllables, go back to the last stable value. Once the block size is stable, adjust one other setting at a time if your build exposes it:
Device is missing
Extra inference time gives the model more context around the current block. Reduce it cautiously and listen for instability.
Fade length blends overlapping chunks. A change can help with clicks at chunk boundaries.
Good monitor sound, silent destination
Howl or doubled voice
Index rate and noise reductions add processing. Try a stable baseline with the optional features off before tuning each one.
Model will not start
Pitch extraction affects both pitch quality and workload. Compare a supported alternative when difficult notes wobble or processing takes too long.
See real-time conversion basics for other supported apps and general routing terminology.
Set the downstream microphone to the cable's recording end. Disable a second capture source if the app mixes both.
Stop the stream, reload the device list, and try another host interface that exposes the microphone and output. Check system microphone permission.
Symptom
Test the same inference export in the WebUI and confirm the matching assets. Check the first GUI error before changing device and model settings together.
The downstream app receives the raw voice
Use headphones, check that no input points to the cable's own return, and switch off duplicate monitoring.

Use the same test with your call, game or recording workload running. The round-trip delay you hear also includes drivers, the virtual cable and the destination app. A timing figure shown by the converter accounts for only part of that path.

VCClient converts live microphone audio. The interface is the client and the conversion process is the server. For your first test, run both on the same computer. The client version (v1 or v2) and the model version (RVC V1 or V2) identify different things. Check the package's model support before choosing a file.
Check your operating system and processor architecture. On Windows, open Task Manager → Performance and read the GPU model. On Mac, open About This Mac and look for an Apple chip or Intel processor.
Plug in your microphone and headphones. Make a short recording in the operating system to check the microphone independently of VCClient.

Keep one known-working RVC inference model available. A .pth is a PyTorch model, while an .onnx uses an ONNX runtime. Use the optional matching .index only with the model it belongs to. See Models and files if you received a ZIP or a set of training checkpoints.

In the documented v1 Windows setup, AMD and Intel GPU acceleration is for ONNX models. Select CPU if your standard package does not detect a usable GPU provider for your model.

l: Convert your microphone in w-okada VCClient
p: Start with headphones and a single local audio path. When you hear a clean converted voice in the headphones, connect it to a call or recorder. This order lets you locate issues before adding the virtual cable.

l: Add a model and hear the first result
p: Plug in your microphone and headphones before opening VCClient. In the operating system, speak into the microphone and check that the input meter moves. Pause Discord, OBS and other capture apps during this test.

In Model Selection, choose a compatible sample model if one is available. For your own model, use Edit, pick a spare slot and choose Upload. Select RVC when the dialog requests a model type. Supply the inference file accepted by your release and an optional matching index. Wait for the upload and then select the filled slot in the main view.

In the audio controls choose Client for a first browser-side test. Select the exact name of the physical microphone and the exact name of the headphones. If the browser asks for permission, allow microphone access for the local page.
Turn off passthrough, leave pitch and index at zero, and keep the default chunk, context, crossfade and pitch estimator. If you imported an index, you can evaluate it after hearing the baseline.

Press Start, wait for model warmup and speak for at least 30 seconds. Include a quiet sentence, a normal sentence, a louder phrase and a brief pause. With conversion enabled you should hear the selected voice. Press Stop when making changes that require restarting the stream.

If you hear silence, test the same devices in a plain recorder. If you hear your original voice twice or hear it alongside conversion, disable direct microphone monitoring on your interface or remove the duplicate software path.

l: Understand client and server device mode
p: Client uses devices available to the client/browser. Microphone permissions and the browser's output selection can affect the device list. Server opens devices on the computer running the conversion engine. This matters on two computers: a USB microphone plugged into the client does not automatically appear on the server.

On one PC, test the simpler client path first. Switch to Server if your build exposes a separate monitor or the browser cannot select the desired output endpoint. In Server mode, choose the host API and device names offered by the server. If several entries share a name, try using the same audio API for input and output. Once the signal is stable, you can test alternatives for latency.

Select the cable's recording endpoint as the target microphone. With VB-CABLE, that is commonly CABLE Output. In OBS, select that device for the audio input capture and mute any second capture of the physical mic.

Use a test call or make a short local recording in the target app. Test quiet and loud speech. Confirm that stopping VCClient or muting the converted source makes its meter stop. If it continues, the target has another input active or is receiving an unintended route.

l: Tune a setup that already works
p: Check the selected package, model format and compute provider separately. Test with the same known-working model on each device.

Choose a pitch estimator that handles your normal speaking range. Compare the same phrase at each setting. Pitch changes the register, while index blending changes how much the inference uses features retrieved from the matching training index. Increase either one gradually and record the result. Hold the model and microphone gain steady during the comparison.
Compare the input threshold and destination voice activation. Try a recording with voice activation disabled to isolate the stage.
Conversion falls behind when a game opens
Distortion is already present in the plain mic recording
First syllable disappears after a pause
GPU conversion fails and CPU works
Increase chunk size or reduce the competing GPU workload. Repeat a longer recording before going live.
Keep the working package name, model, audio mode, device names, pitch method and buffer controls in a note. That gives you a reliable baseline after a device or software update.
Local monitor is fine, but cable audio crackles
Lower the physical input gain before tuning the model.
Match supported sample rates in the OS sound panel and reopen both streams. Check for a second application holding the endpoint in exclusive mode.
Original voice reaches the call
Specific test

Start from the default chunk and test under your actual workload. When the UI shows chunk duration and conversion time, compare them in matching units. Each block needs enough time to finish. Leave margin for spikes while running a game or streaming. Reduce the chunk one step at a time and listen for dropouts before keeping the change. If words cut out, increase it again or reduce extra context. Crossfade helps soften boundaries but also consumes part of the available processing budget.
Symptom
Turn off passthrough and choose the cable as the only microphone in the receiving app.

On the releases page, expand Assets for one release. Download the DirectML ZIP or every CUDA part. A split example includes .001 and .002. The parts must stay beside each other with their downloaded names.

For CUDA, use an archive tool that supports split files and extract from .001. It reads the later parts during extraction. For DirectML, extract the single ZIP. Choose a folder you can write to and keep the extracted folders intact.
Open the extracted package, then MMVCServerSIO, then launch MMVCServerSIO.exe.

Leave the startup window open while any required weights download. When the browser opens, keep that console available for diagnostics. If the page does not open automatically, use the local address printed by the server.
The first CUDA conversion may take a few seconds to start. Wait for warmup before repeatedly pressing Start or changing devices.

On macOS, unpack the archive for your exact chip architecture and open the bundled MMVCServerSIO executable. If macOS blocks launch, confirm the file came from the official release and examine the block before making system changes. Grant microphone access to the browser for browser capture, or the local app when it opens the microphone directly.

For a Linux source install, use the fork's own source archive and the documented Python 3.10 environment. Open a terminal in the repo's server folder. The installer is vc_install.sh; choose the backend that matches your system when it prompts. Use the startup script included by that version and open the local address printed to the terminal. Script names differ across snapshots. To identify the supplied entry points, list the files in the server folder before running one. For a release binary, unpack the package for your architecture and start its included executable. The Windows DirectML archive is a separate runtime.

l: Set up live audio in Okada TG Developed Fork
p: Use a compatible RVC inference checkpoint and a working microphone. First prove that the converted signal reaches your headphones. Then send that signal to another application and make a recording from the receiving end.
Stop conversion if it is already running. Open Edit in the model selection area and pick an empty slot.

Choose Upload and select the RVC inference model file. When the dialog exposes a separate field for the index, add the matching .index if supplied. Use only compatible inference files. An index by itself cannot produce a voice.
Wait for the upload and click the newly loaded slot in the main view. Check the model name before pressing Start.
Set pitch and retrieval to zero. Make sure Passthrough is off. Its enabled state sends the dry microphone, so the microphone can reach a call even if conversion is bypassed.

l: Test the microphone and the compute device
p: In Audio, choose the mode for the devices you intend to use. In a local browser test, use Client and grant the site access to your microphone. In Server, choose the input and output devices visible to the process that runs TGR.
Name the endpoints before starting. Input is the physical microphone, Output is the headphones for the first test, and Monitor is optional if your build offers it.

Pick your intended GPU or CPU in the device selector. For a DirectML baseline, try rmvpe_onnx if listed. Supported DirectML pitch detectors documented by the fork also include fcpe_onnx, crepe_tiny_onnx and crepe_full_onnx. The CUDA build can expose a different list.

Press Start at the default chunk size. Give the model time to initialize, then say a quiet sentence and a longer louder one. Pause between both. Check that the output changes when selecting the model and that the audio remains stable across a minute.
If you hear a dry copy as well, turn off hardware sidetone or remove the other mic loop in the OS. Keep headphone levels moderate during tests.

Chunk controls the block of incoming audio. Extra supplies context around the current block. Crossfade controls overlap where blocks join. Change one control at a time and make a test recording. If processing time is getting close to the chunk duration, start by increasing the chunk or reducing extra context. If a changed chunk behaves oddly, stop and start conversion again.
Clicks start after the cable is connected
Compare the mic and cable sample rates and host API selections. Retest without the cable to confirm which stage introduces the click.
Fault

If you need help diagnosing further, keep the release identifier, backend, microphone and cable device names, chosen detector and first console error. Confirm whether the problem also occurs in a local headphone test.
Next action

On the documented DirectML build, changes to Chunk, Extra and Crossfade can require selecting CPU and then reselecting the intended GPU. Do that after stopping, restart the stream, and repeat the same test before evaluating latency. On CUDA, allow first-start warmup before measuring. Some Server audio and protocol combinations show perf without other timings. Judge the full call path with a recording in the receiving app.
Only one pitch method crashes or stalls
Restore the last stable chunk, reduce context or competing load, and retest. Keep the setting that works with both apps open.
Return to a method listed by your backend. On DirectML, compare the ONNX pitch options with the same short phrase.
Stop TGR and check the meter again. A meter that still follows your mic points to an extra route or the wrong recording endpoint.
Test the input threshold and the destination app's voice detection separately. Check a plain recording for actual silence.
The mic passes through unchanged
Turn off Passthrough, check the selected slot, and select the cable as the receiving app's only microphone.

l: Okada TG Developed Fork on Cloud
p: If your computer does not have a compatible NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel GPU, you can run Okada TG Developed Fork on a cloud GPU using Google Colab, Kaggle, or Lightning.AI, then connect from your browser.

Why "Server audio not available" appears: Cloud virtual machines have no physical sound card. That message is completely normal. Always use Client mode so your browser captures your local microphone and plays the converted voice through your own headphones or virtual cable.

Latency expectation: Cloud conversion adds network round-trip time on top of GPU inference. Choose the closest Ngrok region (or Port Viewer on Lightning.AI) and keep a stable wired or 5 GHz connection for the lowest delay.

l: 2. Set up a Virtual Audio Cable (for Discord, OBS, or games)
p: To route the converted browser output into Discord, OBS, or a game, install a virtual audio cable on your computer:

Windows: download VAC Lite (or VB-CABLE). Run setup64 on standard Intel/AMD PCs, or setup64a on ARM Windows laptops (such as Snapdragon). If Windows switches your default sound device after install, press Win + R, run mmsys.cpl, and restore your normal Playback and Recording devices (including Default Communication Device).
macOS: install BlackHole or VB-Audio Cable.
Linux: install PortAudio (sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y portaudio19-dev on Debian/Ubuntu, sudo yum install -y portaudio on Fedora/RHEL, or sudo pacman -Syu portaudio on Arch).
For step-by-step Discord and OBS routing, see the virtual cable walkthrough.

Important Terms of Service warning: Running Web UIs on the Google Colab Free Tier violates Google's Disallowed Activities policy. Google's detection runs mid-session as well as at startup, and repeated violations can lead to GPU restrictions or account bans. Use Colab Paid Tier for Web UI workflows.

In the right sidebar:

Under Accelerator, select GPU T4 x2.

Run the first installation cell until it prints Done! Proceed with the next steps, then run the third cell.
Paste your Ngrok authtoken into the last cell, run it, and open the generated public URL.
Create a Lightning.AI account and verify your phone number (account verification can take 2-3 business days).
Clone the Wokada-TgDevelop-Fork Studio.
Switch to a GPU environment via Studio Environment → Switch To GPU.
Run the first cell to install dependencies and the second cell to configure the server.
In the third cell, pick your tunnel (Port Viewer is recommended for stability and low overhead) and run it.
Use Teamspace Drive on the right sidebar to upload your .pth and .index voice models.

Once the Web UI opens in your browser, model loading, pitch settings, and Client mode audio setup are identical to a local install. Continue with Model, microphone and cable.
If the cloud server crashes or refuses to start, append --log-level debug to the launch command in the final cell and re-run it:
Google Colab: !./ML_Program --log-level debug
Kaggle & Lightning.AI: !./VoiceChanger --log-level debug
Copy the printed error output (avoid warning, error, or critical log levels, as they hide the context needed for troubleshooting).

W-Okada stores imported models inside model_dir as .safetensors. If you need to recover a .pth file from a cloud session, you can run a quick torch + safetensors conversion script (!pip install torch safetensors) or use Ilaria RVC's built-in Safetensors Converter locally.

l: 2. Load a model and tune settings
p: Upload or select an inference RVC .pth model and its optional matching .index file.

Chunk / Block size: start around 0.3s to 0.5s (or 192 / 256+ samples/frames depending on the UI slider) to balance delay and audio smoothness. Lowering Chunk too far causes robotic stutter or dropouts.
Extra Data / Context: keep moderate (0.5s to 1.0s) for stable tone without overloading the GPU.
F0 / Pitch detector: use RMVPE (most accurate) or FCPE (lighter/faster for real-time); avoid heavy Crepe Full in live mode if inference time exceeds chunk time.
Tune (Pitch): +12 for male to female, -12 for female to male, 0 for same range.
Index ratio: start at 0.0 to test clean conversion, then raise gently (0.3 to 0.6) if needed.

High latency or robotic stutter: close GPU-heavy games/browser tabs, raise Chunk one step, and optionally test disabling Hardware-accelerated GPU Scheduling (HAGS) in Windows Graphics Settings (restart and compare before/after; re-enable HAGS if it makes no difference).
PortAudio / device error: match all audio devices to the same sample rate (48000 Hz) in Windows Sound settings and close apps holding exclusive device control.

This guide covers Tiger14n's archived desktop app for converting audio files. Prepare a voice checkpoint and a short, dry WAV recording before you start.
Open the project's Windows package. Download the packaged asset from the release, and extract the contents to a writable folder. Keep the runtime and model assets in the extracted layout.

Open the included launcher. A source checkout can be started with RVC-GUI.bat on Windows or python rvcgui.py once the runtime is set up. The archived source expects a compatible Python and PyTorch environment plus hubert_base.pt in its project root. Use a separate environment if you are testing the source so other RVC installations retain their dependencies.

If the packaged app closes immediately, run its launcher from an open terminal and read the first error. An archive that contains source files only will not have the packaged runtime. If the error names HuBERT in a source install, place the project's HuBERT weights in the project root.

Generic HuBERT checkpoints are not recommended as the default encoder for voice conversion. Their speech prediction training does not explicitly remove speaker identity, so the features can carry source timbre into the output. For RVC, use the encoder expected by the model, such as ContentVec when the voice was trained with it.

Click Import model from .zip and select a ZIP containing an inference .pth and its matching .index if supplied. For manual placement, put the files in a per-voice subfolder under the app's models directory. For example:

Select the imported voice in the GUI. If it is absent, reopen the model list or restart the app after checking the folder. Use an inference model compatible with the archived build. A model created with an encoder or architecture the build cannot load should be tested in a compatible app.

In Input audio file, click Browse and select a short, dry vocal recording with a clearly voiced vowel and a consonant. Use a full WAV file as your baseline; separate a vocal stem first if the source is a full song.
Select the voice from the model controls. If your model has several supported speaker slots, choose the documented slot; otherwise use the default.
Leave Pitch at zero and set Feature retrieval rate to zero for the baseline. Leave F0 method at the default for this test.

Click Convert once and wait for Output path to show the generated file. Click Open to play it and compare it with the original at a similar volume. Copy the generated file to a distinct name if you want to keep it for comparison. Compare the same sentence before making another adjustment.
If you want stronger target character and have the matching index, try a small retrieval blend. If words become less clear, return to the baseline.
