l: Train RVC Models in Redpanda-vc - EMA & Step-Based Saving
p: Checkpoint (G_*.pth / D_*.pth): A saved training snapshot used to pause and resume training later.
Discriminator (D): A helper network used only during training to judge how realistic the generator's audio sounds compared to the real recordings.
EMA (Exponential Moving Average): A smoothed, running average of the generator's weights maintained during training.
EMA does not edit or clean your dataset files.
EMA does not guarantee better audio quality on every voice.
EMA does not remove all randomness from training.
EMA does not repair clipped or noisy recordings.
EMA helps smooth out changes in the generator's weights during training. Instead of exporting only the latest generator weights, Redpanda-vc can export a running average of them.
EMA is not an audio filter or denoiser.
Epoch: One full pass through your prepared dataset.
Generator (G): The part of the model that actually creates the converted voice audio.
Optimizer: The math engine that updates the model's weights after each training step.
Redpanda-vc on GitHub · Set up Redpanda-vc · Redpanda-vc vs other RVC versions · General RVC Training Guide
Step: One single weight update after processing one small group (batch) of audio clips.

Training a voice model teaches a program to reproduce a target voice from a collection of clean audio clips. If you are new to RVC, you do not need to memorize technical jargon before starting. Here are the key terms in plain English:

Training does not produce a finished voice instantly, and final quality depends heavily on your source recordings, dataset preparation, and training settings. Before diving in, keep in mind what EMA does not do:
Weights: The internal numbers inside the model that adjust bit by bit as it learns a voice.

Imagine a student practicing how to pronounce a difficult word. One individual attempt might sound slightly clearer or slightly rougher than the one right before it. Looking at the trend across many recent attempts gives a steadier picture of the student's progress than judging solely by the very last attempt.
(Keep in mind this is only an analogy: EMA does not listen to audio, judge pronunciation, or pick "better" recordings on its own.)
In rvc/train/train.py, Redpanda-vc maintains EMA in memory while training runs:
The generator trains normally on each batch.
The optimizer updates the generator's live weights.
Immediately after each generator optimizer step (on rank 0), GeneratorEMA.update() updates a separate averaged copy of the generator's weights (excluding enc_q, which is only used during training).
That running average stays in memory and is saved inside the G training checkpoint.
When EMA is enabled (Generator EMA Decay 0), Redpanda-vc exports inference .pth models from those EMA weights instead of the raw live generator weights.
EMA updates every training step, not once per epoch. Redpanda-vc does not average multiple .pth files already saved on disk; it maintains one continuous running average in memory during training.

l: Optional math details: standard EMA vs. Redpanda-vc's bias-corrected formula
p: The intuitive standard EMA update is:

In rvc/train/train.py (GeneratorEMA.update(), lines 199-205), Redpanda-vc does not apply a constant decay from the very first update. Instead, it computes a bias-corrected effective decay based on the number of updates (updates):

where beta is your ema_decay setting. This warm-up correction reduces the influence of the initial weights during the earliest updates, then approaches beta as updates grows. Floating-point parameters are blended via torch._foreach_lerp_, while non-floating-point buffers are copied from the live generator.
In Training → Advanced Settings, Redpanda-vc exposes Generator EMA Decay (tabs/train/rvc.py, lines 809-819):
Minimum: 0
Maximum: 0.9999
Default: 0.999
Slider step: 0.0001
Generator EMA Decay = 0: Disables GeneratorEMA completely. Inference .pth models are exported directly from the live generator weights.
Generator EMA Decay = 0.999 (Default): Maintains an exponential running average that gives meaningful weight to recent generator updates while smoothing step-to-step fluctuations.

Generator EMA Decay = 0.9999: Changes the running average more slowly and averages over a longer window of updates. This can increase smoothness of the average, but it also makes the EMA weights react more slowly to recent improvements in the live generator.

Lower values adapt faster to recent weights, while higher values average over more steps. 0.9999 is not automatically better than 0.999, and there is no universal "best" decay for speech, singing, small datasets, or large datasets. If you are a beginner, starting at the default 0.999 and comparing real audio outputs before tuning is a practical baseline.

In deep learning literature (such as PyTorch's weight-averaging documentation and Morales-Brotons, Vogels, and Hendrikx, 2024), averaging weights along a training trajectory is studied because individual SGD/Adam updates can oscillate around good solutions.
Reduced step-to-step oscillation in exported weights.
Greater continuity between consecutive exports.
Attenuation of some update-level variability during training.
Potentially steadier exported model behavior, though actual audio improvement on your specific RVC dataset requires listening tests.
EMA does not replace a clean, well-prepared dataset.
EMA does not eliminate overfitting.
EMA does not prevent a broken or unstable training run from failing.
EMA does not guarantee higher voice similarity or better pronunciation.
EMA does not promise fewer training steps or epochs.
EMA is not an automatic "best checkpoint" selector.
EMA keeps an extra copy of the generator's weights in memory and adds a small per-step update cost.

In Redpanda-vc, four different things exist during a run. Do not mix them up:
Inference model (name_epoche_steps.pth)

logs/model_name/
Note: In the verified Redpanda-vc source (train.py), EMA is applied only to the generator (net_g), never to the discriminator (net_d).
Resuming training (and manual export)

What It Contains
What It Is Used For
Where It Lives
Epoch: One full pass over the prepared training dataset.
Batch: A small group of audio slices processed together in one forward/backward pass.
Step: One optimizer update after processing one batch. One step is not one audio file and not one second of audio.
Suppose your prepared dataset and Batch Size produce 100 steps per epoch:
100 steps ≈ 1 epoch
500 steps ≈ 5 epochs
1,000 steps ≈ 10 epochs
The actual steps-per-epoch ratio depends on your dataset length, slicing, Batch Size, and Max Audio per Batch (sec). Never assume 100 steps equals 1 epoch for every model.
Instead of waiting for an entire epoch to finish before saving, Redpanda-vc schedules saves by step count (tabs/train/rvc.py, lines 663-703; rvc/train/train.py, lines 917-921 and 1146-1195):
Default: 10000 (slider range 1 to 1000000, step 1).

Sets the overall target step count for the experiment, not "add 10,000 more steps." If your resumed model is already at step 10000, you must raise Total Steps (for example to 15000) to continue training.
Default: 1000 (slider range 1 to 100000, step 1).
Saves G and D checkpoints every X training steps (self.global_step % save_every_steps == 0).
Example: With Total Steps = 10000 and Save Every X Steps = 1000, Redpanda-vc saves at steps 1000, 2000, 3000, ..., 10000, regardless of whether those steps land mid-epoch.

Even if Total Steps is not a multiple of Save Every X Steps (for example, Total Steps = 2500 and Save Every X Steps = 1000), Redpanda-vc always saves both the G/D checkpoints and an inference .pth model when reaching the final step (final = self.global_step = self.args.total_steps).
Default: Enabled (True).
When enabled, Redpanda-vc exports an inference .pth model at every save interval and at the final step.
When disabled, G/D checkpoints still save every Save Every X Steps, but an automatic inference .pth is exported only at the final step.
Default: Enabled (True).
When enabled, G and D checkpoints overwrite fixed filenames (G_2333333.pth and D_2333333.pth, where 2333333 is LATEST_CHECKPOINT_SUFFIX) to save disk space.
When disabled, checkpoints include the step number (G_1000.pth, D_1000.pth, G_2000.pth, D_2000.pth).

Important: Save Only Latest only affects G/D training checkpoints, not exported inference .pth models (unless you disable Save Every Weights). Keep in mind that with Save Only Latest enabled, you cannot roll back training to an older intermediate G/D checkpoint if a run later degrades.

l: Your First RVC Training in Redpanda-vc

p: Install and launch Redpanda-vc (see Set up Redpanda-vc).
Open the Train tab and select RVC (if your build shows multiple model families).
Under Model Settings, enter a unique Model Name (your experiment name).
Choose a compatible Sample Rate (32k, 40k, or 48k), Version (v1 or v2), and Vocoder (HiFi-GAN, MRF HiFi-GAN, or RefineGAN depending on your pretraineds and target inference app).
Prepare a clean, dry dataset of authorized recordings in a dedicated folder.
Open the Preprocess accordion.
Enter or select your dataset folder path in Dataset Path (click Refresh if needed).
Click Preprocess Dataset and wait for it to finish slicing and normalizing the audio into logs/model_name/.
Open the Extract accordion.
Select your Pitch extraction algorithm (such as rmvpe) and Embedder Model (typically contentvec).
Click Extract Features. (This prepares pitch and content features for training; it does not train the .pth weights yet.)
Open the Training accordion.
Set Batch Size to a value your GPU VRAM can hold comfortably.
For a first illustrative test, you can leave the current defaults:
Total Steps: 10000
Save Every X Steps: 1000
Expand Advanced Settings to verify:
Save Only Latest: Enabled (True)
Save Every Weights: Enabled (True)
Generator EMA Decay: 0.999 (These defaults are illustrative starting values, not guaranteed optimal settings for every dataset.)
Click Start Training.
Monitor progress using the terminal/UI status, Pause Training / Resume Training / Stop Training, and TensorBoard logs (logs/model_name/eval/).
Once finished, click Generate Index if you want a matching .index file.
Inside logs/model_name/, you will find:
Resumable checkpoints: G_2333333.pth and D_2333333.pth (when Save Only Latest is enabled) or G_step.pth / D_step.pth (when disabled).
Inference models: model_name_epoche_steps.pth (for example, MyVoice_45e_1000s.pth). These are the files you load for voice conversion.
When you restart training on an existing experiment (rvc/train/train.py, lines 420-436, 528-538, 763-803, 844-853):
latest_checkpoint_pair() scans logs/model_name/ for the newest G_*.pth by modification time and pairs it with the matching D_*.pth suffix. Both G and D files must exist to resume.
restore() reloads epoch, start_batch (epoch_step), global_step (step), AMP scaler, RNG state, and both optimizers.

build_ema() restores GeneratorEMA from checkpoint[ema] when ema_decay 0. If ema state is missing or incompatible (for example, resuming from a non-EMA checkpoint), Redpanda-vc logs a notice and initializes EMA from the resumed generator weights instead of crashing.
Any steps completed after the last saved checkpoint before a crash or manual stop are lost and will be re-run from that saved step.

Reset Optimizer State: Keeps your model weights, global_step, and learning rate schedule, but clears the optimizer's momentum/moment buffers (state={}). Use only when intentionally resetting optimizer dynamics; normal resuming leaves this OFF.
Fresh Training (--cleanup): Deletes all previously generated G_* and D_* checkpoints, spec.pt files, and TensorBoard logs for that experiment. Leave this OFF whenever resuming.

Save Every X Steps vs. Checkpointing: Save Every X Steps controls how often checkpoints are written to disk. Checkpointing (in Advanced Settings) is activation checkpointing, which trades slower training speed for lower VRAM usage on GPUs with limited memory (it does not control disk saving).

Automatic exports during training (train.py, lines 1090-1091 & 1157-1163): Whenever save() triggers an inference export (Save Every Weights or the final step), export_state_dict() returns self.ema.weights if EMA is enabled (ema_decay 0), or the live generator's state_dict() if EMA is disabled (ema_decay = 0).

Manual exports (Export Model accordion -> rvc/train/process/checkpoint_exporter.py, lines 44-117): You can manually export any resumable G_*.pth checkpoint in fp16 or fp32. export_generator_checkpoint() checks if checkpoint[ema][weights] exists and automatically uses those EMA weights when present (reporting ... and the generator EMA in the status message).
There is no separate "Raw vs. EMA" toggle in the WebUI exporter; the exported .pth is for inference only, while G_*.pth + D_*.pth remain required to resume training.

There is no universal yes-or-no answer across all voices and datasets. Because the current WebUI does not export both Raw and EMA versions side-by-side from a single run, the cleanest way to test EMA is a controlled comparison:

Keep Batch Size, Total Steps, learning rate schedule, and pretrained weights identical.
Run one experiment with Generator EMA Decay = 0.999 and one with 0.
Compare inference .pth exports at the same step count (e.g., 5000s vs. 5000s) using held-out test clips not in the training set.
Listen for voice similarity, crispness of consonants, pitch stability, and artifacts rather than judging solely by TensorBoard loss curves.

What to Check
What does EMA mean? Exponential Moving Average: a running average of the generator's weights maintained during training.
Does EMA improve voice quality? It can smooth weight oscillations, but it is not a guarantee. Whether a specific voice sounds better depends on your dataset and requires listening tests.
Should beginners leave EMA at 0.999? Yes, 0.999 is the default in Redpanda-vc and is a reasonable starting point before experimenting with other values.
What happens if EMA Decay is 0? EMA is disabled (self.ema is not built) and inference models are exported from the live generator weights.
Is 0.9999 better than 0.999? Not automatically. 0.9999 averages over a longer history and reacts more slowly to recent updates.
Does EMA make training faster? No. EMA maintains an extra weight copy and performs an update step after each generator step.
Does EMA prevent overfitting? No. Overfitting still depends on dataset size, variety, and total training steps.
Is EMA applied to the discriminator? No. In Redpanda-vc (train.py), EMA is applied only to the generator (net_g).
What is the difference between an epoch and a step? An epoch is one full pass over the dataset; a step is one weight update after processing one batch.
Can Redpanda-vc save halfway through an epoch? Yes. Saves are triggered by Save Every X Steps, independent of epoch boundaries.
Will I lose progress if I stop training? You keep progress up to the last saved G/D checkpoint; steps run after that save are lost.

What is the difference between Save Only Latest and Save Every Weights? Save Only Latest overwrites G_2333333.pth / D_2333333.pth training checkpoints; Save Every Weights exports an inference .pth model at every save interval instead of only at the final step.
Is Checkpointing the same as saving checkpoints? No. Checkpointing in Advanced Settings is activation checkpointing to save VRAM, whereas Save Every X Steps controls disk checkpoint saving.
Can I resume training from an inference .pth? No. Resuming requires a matching G_*.pth and D_*.pth checkpoint pair in logs/model_name/.

l: Redpanda-vc vs Other RVC Versions - Complete Feature Comparison
p: Set up Redpanda-vc · Train RVC models (EMA & Steps) · Test live audio

This guide compares Redpanda-vc directly against RVC Mainline, Applio, and Ilaria RVC based on static source-code inspection of each project's main branch (without running live audio benchmarks or cross-OS hardware tests).
If you are new to AI voice conversion, it helps to know that these programs are not sequential versions of a single app. They are related projects with different goals:
RVC: A family of voice conversion architectures and models (Retrieval-based Voice Conversion).
RVC Mainline: The original reference implementation (RVC-Project/Retrieval-based-Voice-Conversion-WebUI).
Applio: A widely used RVC application that expands the WebUI, vocoders, TTS, and tooling around RVC.

Redpanda-vc: A fork of Applio (redpanda343/Redpanda-vc) that adds Generator EMA, step-based RVC checkpoint saving, Rectified Flow training/inference, Beatrice 2 training/realtime, and dedicated Vocoder training.

Ilaria RVC: A customized implementation built from RVC Mainline (TheStingerX/Ilaria-RVC) with its own inference pipeline, Training Target: Steps, RefineGAN/MRF HiFi-GAN support in the UI, Audio Analyzer, Voice Blender, and TTS tools.
A fork is not automatically better than the original in every area: each project trades simplicity, stability, model compatibility, and extra architectures differently.

(Quick terms for beginners: Inference means converting audio using an already-trained model; CLI means running commands in a terminal instead of clicking buttons in the WebUI; a vocoder turns acoustic features into an audible waveform; a decoder is the part of a program that knows how to read a specific model architecture.)

Inside a neural network, weights are the internal numbers that adjust after every training batch. Because each batch is only a small slice of your dataset, the live generator weights can wobble slightly from step to step.

EMA (Exponential Moving Average) keeps a separate running average of the generator's weights in memory (distinct from Adam's internal optimizer moments). In rvc/train/train.py, Redpanda-vc implements GeneratorEMA:
After every generator optimizer step (on rank 0), GeneratorEMA.update() blends the live generator weights into the running average (excluding enc_q, which is only used during training).
Generator EMA Decay (0 to 0.9999, default 0.999, step 0.0001) controls how slowly the average updates. Setting 0 disables EMA and exports the raw live generator weights.
Neither RVC Mainline, Applio, nor Ilaria RVC includes GeneratorEMA in their verified training scripts.

EMA can smooth step-to-step weight fluctuations, but it does not guarantee better audio quality, does not eliminate overfitting or training randomness, and does not make training faster. For full beginner explanations and math details, see Train RVC Models in Redpanda-vc - EMA & Step-Based Saving.

In RVC training, an epoch is one full pass over the prepared dataset, while a step is one weight update after processing a single batch. (Hypothetical example: if a dataset produces 100 steps per epoch, 1,000 steps is roughly 10 epochs, though the exact ratio depends on dataset length and batch size.)
The four programs handle step targets and checkpoint saving differently:

Redpanda-vc: Uses Total Steps (default 10000) and Save Every X Steps (default 1000). It saves resumable G/D checkpoints (and an inference .pth when Save Every Weights is on) at exact step intervals, even mid-epoch, plus a mandatory Final Save at Total Steps. Save Only Latest overwrites G_2333333.pth / D_2333333.pth to save disk space.
Applio & RVC Mainline: Both train by total epochs and save checkpoints on epoch intervals (save_every_epoch).

Ilaria RVC: Includes Training Target: Steps (ILARIA_RVC.py, train.py) so it can also stop at a target step count. However, Ilaria RVC's save frequency still counts epochs (save_every_epoch), and intermediate .pth weight exports only occur on completed epoch % save_every_epoch == 0 boundaries (not on a partial_epoch mid-epoch), whereas resumable training state saves on save_every_epoch, stop, or final_epoch.

l: Rectified Flow: A Different Voice Conversion Architecture
p: One of Redpanda-vc's biggest additions is Rectified Flow (tabs/train/rectified_flow.py, rectified_flow/). It is not a variant of RVC V2:
Acoustic model: Uses an architecture inspired by DiffSinger's acoustic model, taking ContentVec speech features in place of phonemes (README.md).
Output & vocoder: The flow model predicts mel-spectrogram representations, which a separate vocoder (such as PC-NSF-HiFiGAN, NSF-HiFiGAN, or Vocos) converts into an audio waveform.
Training presets: Includes standard, meanflow (MeanVC2-inspired), and smaller presets under rectified_flow/presets/.
Realtime support: Supported in Redpanda-vc's realtime GUI and WebUI realtime tab.

Compatibility warning: Even if an exported file uses .pth, a Rectified Flow model is not an RVC V2 model and will not load in standard RVC loaders unless a client explicitly implements that Rectified Flow decoder.
(No verified cross-architecture benchmarks exist in the repository proving Rectified Flow is universally faster, more natural, or higher quality than RVC.)
Beatrice is a separate, CPU-friendly voice conversion architecture (integrated from beatrice-trainer in tabs/train/beatrice.py, beatrice/, beatrice/realtime.py):
Separate from RVC: Beatrice uses its own model format (exported as a model folder, not an RVC .pth) and runs its realtime inference on the CPU (README.md).

Do not confuse with F0 pitch extraction: Some apps (such as Ilaria RVC) include beatrice as an F0 pitch extractor option during RVC inference. Redpanda-vc goes further by supporting full Beatrice 2 model training and Beatrice voice conversion in both its WebUI and run-realtime-gui.bat.
Models trained in Redpanda-vc's Beatrice tab work with Beatrice-compatible loaders (such as Beatrice VST / Beatrice clients), not as RVC V2 .pth files.
Redpanda-vc includes a dedicated Vocoder training tab (tabs/train/nsf_hifigan.py, nsf_hifigan/):
Supported vocoders: PC-NSF-HiFiGAN, NSF-HiFiGAN, and Vocos (24 kHz).
Modes: Train from scratch or fine-tune from a supported pretrained vocoder checkpoint (for example, PC-NSF-HiFiGAN 2025.02 or Vocos 24 kHz).
Acoustic model vs. vocoder: An acoustic model (like Rectified Flow) predicts spectral features (mel-spectrograms); a vocoder turns those features into audible sound waves.

Important limitation: This tab is tightly paired with Rectified Flow's mel configurations (check_registry_vocoder / mel_mismatch in tabs/train/rectified_flow.py). Selecting HiFi-GAN or RefineGAN inside the RVC training WebUI uses RVC's own integrated generator/vocoder architecture; you cannot arbitrarily plug a vocoder trained here into any standard RVC model.

l: Which RVC Version Should You Choose?
p: Choose RVC Mainline if you want the original reference codebase and classic realtime_gui.py workflow.
Choose Applio if you want a full-featured RVC workspace with epoch-based training and integrated TTS.

Choose Redpanda-vc if you specifically want Generator EMA, step-based checkpoint saving, Rectified Flow, Beatrice 2 training/realtime, custom vocoder training, or WebSocket/multi-stream realtime (note that Applio's tts tab is not present in Redpanda-vc).

Choose Ilaria RVC if you want an offline-focused RVC studio with Training Target: Steps, WebUI-selectable MRF HiFi-GAN / RefineGAN, integrated TTS (Kokoro, ElevenLabs, Windows), Audio Analyzer, Voice Blender, RMVPE High Register, and Proposed Pitch.

Can I use a Redpanda-vc model in another RVC program? Standard RVC V1 / V2 HiFi-GAN models exported from Redpanda-vc work in clients implementing those decoders; Rectified Flow, Beatrice, RefineGAN, and MRF HiFi-GAN require clients that explicitly support those decoders.
Can Redpanda-vc train normal RVC models? Yes, under the Train → RVC tab (HiFi-GAN and RefineGAN in the WebUI; MRF HiFi-GAN in code/CLI).
Does Ilaria RVC also support step-based training? Yes, via Training Target: Steps, though its Save frequency still counts epochs rather than arbitrary step intervals.
Does multi-GPU realtime make one voice conversion faster? No. Each stream stays on one GPU; extra GPUs allow multiple concurrent streams.
Does Redpanda-vc produce better RVC models? Not automatically. Voice quality depends primarily on your dataset, preprocessing, and settings; EMA and extra schedules are tools to test, not guarantees.
Does Redpanda-vc support realtime conversion? Yes, both via the WebUI Realtime tab and run-realtime-gui.bat.
Is Rectified Flow the same as RVC V2? No. They are completely different architectures and are not cross-compatible.

Is Redpanda-vc the same as Applio? No. Redpanda-vc is forked from Applio, so it shares Applio's base UI, but adds Generator EMA, step-based saving, Rectified Flow, Beatrice 2, and vocoder training, while omitting Applio's tts tab.

Should beginners choose RVC, Rectified Flow, or Beatrice? Start with RVC if you want the widest model and client compatibility; explore Rectified Flow or Beatrice only if you specifically want their workflows.
What does a vocoder do? It converts acoustic features (such as mel-spectrograms) into an audible audio waveform.
What is a fork of RVC? A separate project that copies an existing RVC codebase and modifies or adds features on top of it.
What is Beatrice? A separate, CPU-friendly voice conversion architecture (from beatrice-trainer), distinct from RVC and distinct from using Beatrice solely as an F0 pitch extractor.
What is EMA? Exponential Moving Average: a running average of the generator's weights maintained during training and used when exporting inference models.
What is Rectified Flow? A diffusion/flow-matching acoustic architecture inspired by DiffSinger that uses ContentVec features and a separate vocoder.

Which features are genuinely unique to Redpanda-vc among these four? Combining Generator EMA, step-interval RVC saving (Save Every X Steps), Rectified Flow, Beatrice 2 training/realtime, and dedicated nsf_hifigan vocoder training in one Applio-based fork.
Why does Redpanda-vc save by steps? Because step-based saving lets you save at exact update intervals (e.g., every 1000 steps) regardless of how small or large your dataset is.

RVC Blue is a Windows desktop voice changer based on RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC)'s real-time GUI.
GitHub · Hugging Face

RVC Blue (RVC-Realtime-GUI) is a Windows desktop client for low-latency, real-time RVC voice conversion. Based on RVC WebUI's real-time GUI, it adds upstream real-time inference optimizations, CUDA Graph warm-up (reducing steady-state GPU overhead), and input/output noise-reduction fixes.
Inference only: RVC Blue does not train models. Train your voice in Ilaria RVC (or another trainer) and import the exported inference .pth and .index files here.
Three input sources: live Microphone, Audio File (via bundled FFmpeg), and Windows Application Audio (per-process capture).
Included voice: comes with Sakura, a natural everyday voice model (commercial use permitted) so you can test right away.

Each Hugging Face package is self-contained and bundles its own Python runtime, PyTorch/CUDA stack, FFmpeg, HuBERT/RMVPE/FCPE assets, and the release model set. You do not need to install Python, CUDA Toolkit, or FFmpeg separately.

Native ASIO hardware: RVC Blue starts with your driver's preferred buffer size. You can also combine ASIO input/monitoring with WASAPI output, or use separate channel pairs on the same ASIO driver.

Important notes before you start
This tool is strictly a model merger: it does not convert audio, run live microphone conversion, or train new models. It only blends two or more existing RVC .pth models into a new .pth file.

YuneVoix is a real-time AI voice conversion application for Windows, powered by the YUNE engine.
Hugging Face (Download) · Ko-fi (Support & Premium)

YuneVoix is a real-time AI voice conversion application for Windows, powered by the YUNE engine. Just like RVC, it transforms your voice into someone else's - for both speech and singing, live or offline - but without training an individual voice model. Everything runs locally on your own graphics card: no cloud, no account, and your audio never leaves your PC.
Guide map: 1. Overview & Requirements · 2. Install & Update · 3. Voice Bank & Live Usage · 4. Settings & Audio Quality · 5. Song Cover & Karaoke · 6. Premium, Licensing & Help · 7. Changelog

Instead of spending hours training a model on a dataset, YUNE creates a Voice Bank profile from a short reference recording of the target voice (10–25 seconds). (Separate from that, the FlowEdit 3+1 LIVE method also uses a 5–20 second sample of your own plain voice as its starting point - for example, 15 seconds of your target voice in Voice Bank vs. 10 seconds of your own natural speech in Settings → Voice Timbre → Sample of your voice….)
According to the developer documentation, the YUNE pipeline splits your voice into what you say and how you say it:
Voice Bank & Speaker identity: Stores a vocal profile (.yvoice) from a 10–25 second target recording without training a separate neural network from scratch.
Content engine (Whisper or WavLM+): Captures your words, timing, and articulation.
Pitch tracking: Follows your melody and intonation.
Diffusion-based conversion: Rebuilds the audio in the target speaker's timbre using the Voice Bank reference.
Neural vocoder (PC-NSF): Outputs full-band 44.1 kHz audio.
Audio processing: Applies input cleaning, pitch/autotune tools, EQ/filters, and effects.
In LIVE mode, audio is processed in small blocks of about 160 ms, with roughly 0.7 seconds of total end-to-end delay at default settings (as reported by the developer).

Voice Bank: create a new .yvoice profile from 10–25 seconds of clear recordings. YuneVoix can automatically separate the voice from music/noise and remove reverb.
Three model methods (per developer documentation):
Classic: Earlier-version behavior with configurable Model steps, Solver, and guidance controls.
Learned 4 steps: Designed to achieve results similar to Classic 10 steps while using about 40% of the model's GPU time and less GPU memory.

FlowEdit 3+1: Starts from your own source voice (5–20 second own-voice sample in LIVE; the song's vocal in Song Cover) instead of noise and aims to preserve breaths, whispers, laughter, and articulation better (reported at about 60% of the model's GPU time).
Content engines: Whisper (default) and WavLM+ (on NVIDIA and AMD DirectML, aimed at clearer live speech and preserving laughter, whispers, and breaths).
Pitch tools: manual or automatic pitch shift, autotune with key detection, gentle pitch stabilizer, vibrato depth, and live harmony (thirds, fifths).
Voice character, EQ & effects: timbre strength, formant, warmth, softness, presence, de-esser, dynamic EQ, compressor, saturation, bitcrush, reverb, and peak limiter. See Settings & Audio Quality.
Song Cover & Karaoke (PREMIUM): re-sing full songs with automatic vocal separation or sing along to on-screen lyrics.
UI language selector: English, German, Italian, Spanish, Polish, and Portuguese.

Complete beginner tutorial for creating Voice Bank .yvoice profiles, routing YuneVoix into Discord, OBS, games, or VRChat, using built-in monitoring, and choosing Classic, Learned 4 steps, or FlowEdit 3+1.

Use this guide to create voices in the Voice Bank, route YuneVoix into Discord, OBS, games, or VRChat, use the built-in monitoring controls, and pick the right Model method for LIVE conversion. For a full breakdown of every slider, see Settings & Audio Quality.
Unlike traditional RVC, creating a Voice Bank profile in YuneVoix does not train a neural network from scratch - it builds a lightweight .yvoice speaker reference in seconds.
Open the Voice Bank tab.
Provide 10–25 seconds of clear recordings of the target voice:
What to use: One speaker only, clean and dry speech or singing without background music, heavy reverb, or overlapping voices.
Helpful variety: Including natural laughter, breaths, "mmm", and singing helps YUNE capture expressive tone.
What to avoid: Clips under 10 seconds, distorted/clipped audio, multiple people talking at once, or loud room echo (which can make the converted voice sound noisy or unstable).
Keep cleaning set to "Separate voice + remove reverb (recommended)" if the source clip has background noise or room echo.
Save the voice - it is stored as a .yvoice file inside models\yune\voices.
Click Play sample in Voice Bank to preview it (as of v0.7.0, Play sample plays through your Windows default output / headphones rather than the LIVE output).
To share or back up a voice, use Voice Bank → Open folder to find the .yvoice file, or load one via Import .yvoice….
Responsible use: Only use voices you have the right to use (your own, or someone's who agreed). Never use YuneVoix to impersonate real people, deceive, harass, or commit fraud.

l: 2. Set up live audio routing & monitoring
p: Always wear headphones for live use. With speakers (or loud, poorly isolated open-back headsets), the converted voice can leak back into your microphone and cause double audio, echo, or feedback loops.

l: Routing to Discord, OBS, games, or VRChat
p: With a virtual audio cable such as VB-CABLE (or VAC Line 1), remember that the cable has two sides: YuneVoix sends audio into the cable, and Discord / OBS / games receive audio from the cable:
Inside YuneVoix (LIVE tab):
Input (Microphone): Your physical microphone.
Output: CABLE Input (VB-CABLE) or Line 1 (VAC).
Inside Discord, OBS, VRChat, or your game:
Input Device (Microphone): CABLE Output (VB-CABLE) or Line 1 (VAC).
Output Device (Speakers/Headphones): Your headphones (never the virtual cable).
In Discord: Turn off Noise Suppression (Krisp) and automatic input sensitivity for this virtual mic - they cut off breaths and quiet words, and YuneVoix already handles input cleaning.
Do not use Windows "Listen to this device" on the virtual cable. YuneVoix provides built-in monitoring controls:
(Optional) To hear yourself: Use "Listen to input" (what the engine hears after input cleaning) or "Listen to output" (the converted voice) in the LIVE tab.
Choose your Monitor device (your headphones, never the LIVE virtual-cable output) and Monitor volume (default -6 dB) in Settings → General.
Direct monitoring note: Your headset's or audio interface's hardware direct monitoring has no delay at all, but it plays your original unprocessed voice, not the converted voice.

At default settings (Output buffer 200 ms), total end-to-end delay is about 0.7 seconds (as reported by the developer). This works well for voice chat, streaming, and recordings, though it is too high for singing strictly on-beat with a live track (for singing over music, see Song Cover & Karaoke).

l: 3. Model Method: Classic vs. Learned 4 Steps vs. FlowEdit 3+1
p: You can choose Model method in Settings → Voice Timbre (and separately in Settings → Song Cover for covers and karaoke). Changes apply at the next START.
Works as in earlier versions.
Model steps (10 default, or 8 / 6 / 4), Solver (Euler / DPM++ 2M), Guidance (CFG) only in the first half of the steps, and Timbre guidance apply only in Classic mode.
Tuned to sound like Classic 10 steps while the model needs about 40% of its GPU time and less GPU memory (per developer notes).
Best choice to try when gaming simultaneously or using slower graphics cards.

Starts from your own voice instead of noise and changes only the voice identity, aiming to preserve breaths, whispers, laughter, and articulation better (reported at about 60% of the model's GPU time).
LIVE requirement: Needs a 5–20 second sample of your own plain speech selected in Settings → Voice Timbre → Sample of your voice… (stored as my_voice.yvoice).

Automatic fallback: Without that sample, FlowEdit 3+1 automatically falls back to Learned 4 steps and the LIVE status line tells you so. With the experimental AMD MIGraphX engine, all model methods run as Classic (10 × Euler).
Room & mic tip: Because FlowEdit keeps more of your own timbre and room ambience, a quiet room or DF3 input cleaning helps keep the output clean.
Microphone level (Settings → General): Watch the meter and raise Windows mic gain so loud speech peaks near −6 dBFS. A quiet mic is the most common cause of robotic or "underwater" output.
Input cleaning (Settings → General): Keep DF3 on in noisy rooms (removes typing, clicks, and hiss; +30 ms). In quiet rooms, if laughs or breaths are clipped, keep Speech gate off and try Gentle.

Smooth out vocal fry (Settings → Voice Timbre, and Settings → Karaoke): If you speak or sing very low or with a creaky voice and the target sounds raspy, turn on Smooth out vocal fry (works live; breathiness is kept).

Pitch & Content engine: Set Pitch shift (Settings → Pitch Autotune) or an Automatic pitch mode, and compare Whisper (default) vs. WavLM+ (Settings → Voice Timbre, supported on NVIDIA and AMD DirectML) by ear.
If you notice stutters while gaming:
Limit the game's FPS.
Set Model method to Learned 4 steps.
Shorten Prompt length (e.g., below 20 s).
Turn off Harmony if you do not need it.
Check overall GPU load (reducing Model steps only applies to Classic mode).

Causal Voice Changer (CVC) is a 48 kHz real-time AI voice changer built to bridge the gap between ultra-low-latency systems (like Beatrice) and slower, high-fidelity systems (like RVC).
GitHub · Releases

Causal Voice Changer (CVC) is a 48 kHz real-time AI voice changer built to bridge the gap between ultra-low-latency systems (like Beatrice) and slower, high-fidelity systems (like RVC). Instead of trading away sound quality for speed - or speed for quality - CVC uses a distilled version of ContentVec and RMVPE in a causal architecture to deliver both clean audio and low delay.

l: How CVC differs from RVC (explained simply)
p: Traditional RVC was originally designed to convert complete audio files, not live streams:
RVC grabs a block of your voice, converts it, and stitches it onto the previous block using a crossfade.

When you lower the block size to reduce delay, RVC has less context - so quality and pitch accuracy drop. If you hold a note or draw out a word, you can often hear the seams between blocks as warbling or crackling.
Causal Voice Changer (CVC) works differently:
It is causal: it converts audio continuously as it arrives, looking mostly backward with only a 50 ms lookahead buffer on the 100 Hz v4 base (60 ms on legacy 50 Hz voices).
Because it streams continuously instead of stitching independent chunks, sustained sounds and held notes stay smooth without breaking or warbling.
You keep nearly all the quality of RVC at a much lower latency (for example, around 130 ms total end-to-end on Linux with JACK audio).
While CVC's source code is under the MIT license, the included pretrained base model was trained on EARS (CC BY-NC), VCTK, and LibriTTS-R.
Non-commercial use only: Because of the EARS dataset, you may not use the included pretrained base model - or any voice finetuned from it - for commercial purposes.

Important rule for first-time setup: Always run the training launcher (run-training.bat on Windows or run-training.sh on Linux) first, even if you only plan to use the real-time voice changer. The training launcher installs Python, PyTorch for your GPU, and the ~900 MB pretrained weights needed by both apps.
Choose one of the two options:

l: Option A: Pre-built Release (Recommended for beginners)
p: Go to the Causal Voice Changer Releases page.
Download the archive for your operating system:
Windows: Causal-Voice-Changer-version-windows-x64.zip
Linux: Causal-Voice-Changer-version-linux-x86_64.tar.gz (requires glibc 2.35+, such as Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, or newer)
Extract the archive into a writable folder (for example D:\CausalVC on Windows).
Note: The release already includes the compiled UI windows, so you do not need to install the .NET SDK or Rust manually.

If you clone the repository with git clone https://github.com/mojowozo/Causal-Voice-Changer.git, the UI windows are compiled automatically on first launch (and recompiled whenever source files change):
Windows: automatically installs the .NET 10 SDK into .dotnet if missing to build the WinUI 3 app.
Linux: builds the COSMIC Rust UI using cargo.
If a native UI cannot be built, a simpler Tk fallback window opens automatically with the core features.
Open the extracted CVC folder.
Run:
Windows: double-click run-training.bat
Because the app is not code-signed, Windows SmartScreen may warn "Windows protected your PC". Click More info → Run anyway.
Linux: open a terminal in the folder and run ./run-training.sh
Wait for the automatic installer:
It sets up a local Python environment (.venv-win on Windows, .venv on Linux) using uv.
It installs the matching PyTorch build for your graphics card.
It downloads the base model and RMVPE weights (about 900 MB) into the weights/ folder.

l: 3. Selecting your GPU on Windows (if needed)
p: On Windows, scripts/gpu-extra.ps1 automatically detects your GPU:
NVIDIA: installs CUDA PyTorch.
AMD RX 7000 / 9000, PRO W7000, Ryzen AI: installs ROCm PyTorch (rocm, requires AMD Software 26.2.2 or newer).
AMD RX 6000 / PRO W6000: installs AMD's newer nightly build (rocm-rdna2).
Older AMD Radeons: run on the CPU (when using real-time, set Chunk to 60 ms or higher).
If auto-detection picks the wrong backend, set the CAUSALVC_GPU environment variable before running the launcher:
CAUSALVC_GPU=cuda (NVIDIA GTX 16 / RTX 20-50 series, CUDA 13)
CAUSALVC_GPU=cuda-pascal (Older NVIDIA GTX 900/10, TITAN X/Xp/V, Quadro M/P, CUDA 12.6; or run run-realtime-gtx10.bat / run-training-gtx10.bat)

CAUSALVC_GPU=rocm-rdna2 (AMD Radeon RX 6000 / PRO W6000)
(If running uv commands manually on Windows, pass --extra cuda, --extra cuda-pascal, --extra rocm, or --extra rocm-rdna2.)

Starting in v0.3.1, CVC includes a built-in updater directly in the app. Automatic update checks run by default and can be turned off on the About page. Existing installs also upgrade weights/causalvc-base/ automatically on the next launch or voice build.
When updating manually or from source:
On Windows, if you run from source and the UI changed, run run-realtime.bat / run-training.bat with CAUSALVC_REBUILD=1 to rebuild the WinUI 3 interface.
On Linux, the Rust UI rebuilds automatically on the next launch after an update.

Live audio routing: Once installed, configure Input device = physical microphone and Output device = Line 1 (VAC) or CABLE Input (VB-CABLE) inside CausalVC, and Input Device = Line 1 or CABLE Output with Output Device = headphones inside Discord/OBS/games. See Using CausalVC Realtime.
Building a voice in Causal Voice Changer fine-tunes the base decoder on your target audio.

Building a voice in Causal Voice Changer fine-tunes the base decoder on your target audio. Unlike many older tools, you do not need to slice your audio files or manually cut out silences, and your recordings can be at any sample rate.
License reminder: Voices trained on the included pretrained base model cannot be used for commercial purposes.
Gather clean recordings of one speaker (no background music, heavy reverb, or overlapping voices).
You can point CVC to a single audio file or a folder containing multiple audio files.
No manual slicing or resampling is needed - CVC handles it automatically.

2. Inside Discord, Games, OBS, or Other Applications
Audio coming from Discord, your game, or other apps must play directly to your headphones (never back into the virtual cable).
Choose Microphone / audio device for live speech.
Correct Audio Routing
Input → Source:
Input Device: Line 1 (VAC, recommended) or CABLE Output (VB-CABLE).
Input device: select your physical microphone.
Input Device: Your physical microphone.
Monitor device (optional): select your headphones if you want to hear your own converted voice. Leave Disabled if you don't want to hear yourself.
Monitoring: Hearing your own converted voice in your headphones is a separate optional feature to enable only when needed. Avoid duplicate audio paths, echo, and loopback.
Output Device: Line 1 (VAC, recommended) or CABLE Input (VB-CABLE).
Output device: select where the converted voice should go.
Output Device: Your headphones (strongly recommended over speakers).

Speakers & Headset Bleed: Avoid using speakers; sound from speakers can leak into your microphone and cause double audio, echo, or other people's voices being converted too. This can also happen with headsets if the volume is too loud or the earcups are not closed and isolated enough.
To use CVC in Discord, OBS, VRChat, or games, install a virtual audio cable (such as VB-CABLE on Windows) and choose CABLE Input here, then pick CABLE Output as your microphone in Discord/OBS.

VAC vs. VB-CABLE: VAC (Line 1) is always recommended. If you have VB-CABLE installed as well (or instead), remember that the voice changer outputs to CABLE Input while Discord / games listen to CABLE Output.
c: Your Microphone → Voice Changer → Line 1 (VAC) or CABLE Input/Output (VB-CABLE) → Discord / Game / OBS

p: Pick your Model (and Checkpoint if the voice has multiple saved steps).
Pitch (semitones): shift your voice up or down to match the target voice (+12 = one octave up, -12 = one octave down).
Pitch match: don't guess! Drop clips of the model's voice into Pitch match to measure its median Hz, then talk while converting so CVC measures your voice and suggests the exact shift (Apply).
Advanced pitch (collapsed by default - most voices don't need it):
Pitch offset (Hz): adds a fixed Hz offset after the semitone shift. Positive values raise low notes more than high notes (narrowing range); negative values widen it.
Pitch ceiling (Hz) & Above the ceiling (%): pulls down squeaky high peaks above the ceiling while keeping notes below it in tune (great for singing; 0% stops strictly at the ceiling).
Formant: shifts vocal resonance (how "big" or "small" the speaker sounds) without changing pitch (0 = model's natural formant).
Index (%) (off by default): blends each 20 ms of speech toward the closest moments in the voice's training audio. Higher sounds closer to the target speaker, but too high can blur words.
Consonant protection (only applies when Index > 0): keeps breaths and consonants (s, t, k) closer to your own so words stay crisp.
Input gain: boosts or cuts your microphone before conversion.
Output gain: controls the volume sent to Discord/OBS/games.
Monitor gain: controls only what you hear in your headphones.
Noise gate: mutes your mic when you're quieter than the threshold (-60 dB = off).
Output level (LUFS): talk while converting to see your loudness and click Apply to auto-adjust Output gain toward Voice chat (-21 LUFS) or Streaming (-16 LUFS).
Click Start to begin live conversion, or Passthrough to send your raw mic straight through for quick volume checks.
Watch In / Out / Mon meters and the two timing readouts:
Latency: total delay from mic to output.
Inference: time your GPU takes to convert one chunk. Inference must stay well below your Chunk size (e.g., 10 ms for a 20 ms chunk), otherwise the audio will stutter.
You can record your sessions directly inside CausalVC Realtime (start conversion first):

Chunk (down to 10 ms / 20 ms): how much audio is converted at a time. Total delay is CVC's fixed 50 ms lookahead on the 100 Hz v4 base (60 ms on legacy 50 Hz voices) + 1 chunk + your sound card/virtual cable buffers.
Lower chunks = lower latency, but require a faster GPU.
If audio crackles or stutters (or if you are running on CPU on an older AMD card), raise Chunk to 40 ms or 60 ms+.
Extra inference buffer: how much recent speech the model looks back at for each chunk. More context gives steadier tone and pitch at a small GPU cost, with zero added delay.
Pitch detector:
RMVPE (recommended): most accurate.
FCPE: lighter on the GPU.
PM (fastest): fastest, but roughest.
Pitch smoothing (RMVPE only): tracks pitch as one continuous line so held notes don't wobble or flip octaves (no added delay).
Volume envelope: 0 matches your microphone's loudness moment-to-moment; 1 keeps the model's own loudness.

Fast GPU replay (on by default): records the GPU's work once and replays it for every chunk - roughly 2× faster and much steadier (for example, an RTX 5050 converts a 20 ms chunk in 4.4 ms instead of 9.7 ms). Turn it off only if your GPU converts wrongly or fails to start with it.
Audio seam & quality helpers:
Soften sudden treble: smooths brief clicks when treble switches on mid-word (adds 5 ms delay).
Match level across seams: keeps high-frequency levels steady between chunks (no added delay).
Hold context during silence: remembers your last words during pauses so the first word after silence isn't slurred.
Silence detection: Loudness (-50 dBFS) is best for quiet rooms; Voice detection (experimental) uses RNNoise so fans/hum don't count as speech.
Input noise reduction: removes keyboard, fan, or room noise before conversion:
Hushwire (Amazon Voice Focus) (default): strongest cleanup and most natural voice; adds about 55 ms delay. Its model is downloaded once from Amazon's servers only after you accept the prompt.
RNNoise: lighter cleanup with lower delay (20 ms).
Output noise reduction: cleans hiss from the converted voice using spectral gating. Leave off unless you hear hiss, as it can make the voice slightly duller.
You can record your sessions directly inside CausalVC Realtime (start conversion first):
Separate files: saves raw input and converted output as two separate files.
Mix: saves input + output mixed together.
Split L/R: raw input on the Left channel, converted output on the Right channel.
Library page: search and sort your voices, Rename, Move to Trash, Open folder, Add/Replace .index, or Export any voice as a .cvc file with its settings.
Offline whole-file conversion: to convert full audio files from the command line without using the live window, use the causalvc.infer module:
Log page: if something goes wrong, open the Log page and click Save log to export diagnostic logs for troubleshooting.
Complete Causal Voice Changer (CVC) release history and changelog from v0.1.0 through v0.3.3.1, covering older NVIDIA GPU support, 100 Hz v4 base, and realtime fixes.
GitHub Releases

Older NVIDIA GPU support: Added support for older NVIDIA cards dropped by CUDA 13 (GeForce GTX 900/10 series, TITAN X/Xp/V, Quadro M/P) using the CUDA 12.6 PyTorch build (cuda-pascal / run-realtime-gtx10.bat / run-training-gtx10.bat).
Realtime stability: Improved realtime performance so a glottal period cannot exceed the 10 ms causal period and cause audio degradation (requires no model rebuilds).
Windows & updater fixes: Fixed window transparency on Windows and fixed a bug where the app could try to use the old engine after an update.
Minor release improving overall sound quality in both training and real-time inference.
Added a built-in updater directly in the app. Automatic update checks run by default and can be toggled off in the About page.
Fixed a Windows bug where GPUs could fail to be detected.
Improved real-time handling for lower-pitched voices to improve output quality.
Upgrades the default 100 Hz base model to v4 (causalvc-base-v4-100hz) while keeping the same 50 ms model latency and full CUDA Graph support.
Improved laughter, sighs & whispers: Replaced binary voiced/unvoiced switching with continuous periodicity confidence (0..1), smoothly blending harmonic pulse and breath turbulence.
CUDA-Graph spectral tone conditioning & L2-SP anchoring: Voices trained on calm speech datasets retain natural laughter and whisper behavior.
Wider pitch range (32 Hz - 1400 Hz): Expanded pitch tracking and continuous log-F0 register conditioning from deep vocal fry up to soprano notes so large upward shifts lighten naturally.
Dead-air silence & click rejection: Added a dedicated silence floor loss cutting unvoiced mic-click and snap bleed by ~33-40 dB even when Ignore background sounds is off.
Seamless compatibility: Existing installs automatically upgrade weights/causalvc-base/ on next launch/build, and earlier 50 Hz and 100 Hz .cvc voices continue to run unchanged.
Switches the default base model and streaming front-end from 50 Hz (20 ms frames) to 100 Hz (10 ms frames).
Lower latency (50 ms): Built on causalvc-base-v3-100hz, reducing algorithmic model delay from 60 ms to 50 ms while doubling temporal resolution on fast consonants and breaths.

Eliminated harmonic aliasing & frame-rate buzz: Smooth raised-cosine Nyquist roll-off (exc=bandlimit) and continuous fractional pitch interpolation (smooth_in=p) reduce aliasing spurs and smooth glissandos/vibrato.
High-note pitch tracking (350-1000+ Hz): Re-distilled pitch tracker (-3 to +14 semitones) and extended encoder distillation (EARS + VCTK + LibriTTS-R) prevent dropouts and octave flips on high notes.

Training & .cvc fixes: Fixed single-file --perturb + self-index bug, added automatic bandwidth detection (detect_fmax) for 16/24 kHz source datasets, added a Random microphone colour toggle, and auto-bundled custom encoders/pitch trackers in .cvc exports (~46 MB standard).
CUDA Graph streaming: Full CUDA Graph support for 100 Hz streaming down to 10 ms / 20 ms blocks.
Pre-built app windows in releases: Windows (.zip) and Linux (.tar.gz) archives now include built app windows so .NET 10 SDK or Rust are no longer required on first launch.
AMD Radeon RX 6000 fix on Windows: Fixed library load order before PyTorch so AMD ROCm builds start properly (eliminating The engine is not available / Windows error 1114).
Launcher & environment fixes: Ensures the voice changer uses the launcher-installed Python environment, prints Python/PyTorch details on startup errors, and honors CAUSALVC_GPU.
Initial public release of Causal Voice Changer:
48 kHz streaming voice changer with 60 ms look-ahead (lower latency than chunk-stitching RVC).
Training app (run-training.bat / run-training.sh) with bfloat16 training, queued builds, and no manual slicing needed.

Realtime app (run-realtime.bat / run-realtime.sh - WinUI 3 on Windows, COSMIC on Linux) with per-voice pitch/Index controls, Hushwire/RNNoise denoising, Soften sudden treble, CUDA Graphs, recording, file input, and ASIO on Windows.
Single-file .cvc voice format and NVIDIA CUDA + AMD ROCm GPU support.
Licence note: Base model trained on EARS, VCTK, and LibriTTS-R (non-commercial due to EARS).

UVR5 (Ultimate Vocal Remover v5 GUI) is a free, open-source desktop application for AI audio source separation. It runs locally on your PC and lets you split songs or dialogue into clean vocals, instrumentals, backing vocals, individual stems (drums, bass, other), and remove reverb, echo, and background noise - making it one of the most popular tools for preparing RVC datasets and covers.
VR Architecture (v4, v5, v5.1): fast, reliable models great for vocals, karaoke (lead vs. backing), de-echo, de-reverb, and denoising.
MDX-Net (v2, MDX23C, plus BS-Roformer, Mel-Roformer, SCNet, and Bandit in beta Roformer patches): state-of-the-art architectures grouped under the MDX-Net menu in UVR5.
Demucs (v1–v4, such as htdemucs and htdemucs_ft): Meta's multi-stem models (4 stems: vocals, drums, bass, other; or 6 stems) ideal for isolating instruments or building ensembles.
Built-in Audio Tools: Manual Ensemble (combine outputs from multiple models via Min/Max Spec or Average), Ensemble Mode, Vocal Splitter, Demudder (Windows patch #14+), and Apollo audio upscaler.

Requirements & Acceleration Notes
Windows 10/11 (64-bit)
Must be installed on the C:\ drive (secondary drives can cause instability). Intel Pentium and Celeron CPUs are not guaranteed to work.

Maxwell (GTX 900 series, compute 5.0) or newer. GTX 600 / GT 700 and older are unsupported for CUDA. 6 GB+ VRAM (e.g. RTX 3050 6–8 GB or better) is recommended for Roformers; 2–4 GB works with smaller chunk_size / dim_t values. RTX 5000 series requires the dedicated CUDA 12.8 patch.

Uses DirectML (labeled OpenCL in older v5.6.0 builds). Tested on AMD RX 4 GB+ (RX 6600 XT / 7600+ recommended for Roformers) and Intel Arc / Xe iGPUs. 16 GB VRAM is recommended if using default Roformer chunk_size (otherwise lower chunk_size). Note: Apollo, Bandit, and SCNet fall back to CPU on DirectML.
macOS
macOS Big Sur or newer (Catalina or lower not guaranteed). Apple Silicon (MPS) acceleration works for Demucs, MDX-Net, and Roformers. Place UVR directly inside root /Applications.

Native v5.6.0_roformer_add+directml branch, or run the Windows installer inside Bottles (WINE gaming profile in drive_c) for newer Roformer patches with GPU acceleration.

Select Input / Output: choose your audio file(s) and output folder. Use WAV for RVC dataset preparation (Additional Settings also lets you enable 64-bit float output).
GPU Conversion: keep this checked whenever you have a supported NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, or Apple Silicon GPU.
Note: if you get silent output on a GTX 10XX GPU, leave Inference Mode off under Settings → Advanced MDX-Net Options → Multi-Network. Newer RTX / GTX 16 GPUs can enable it for extra speed.
Vocals Only / Instrumental Only: check one if you only need one stem (for example, check Instrumental Only if you only want the instrumental or the de-echoed/dereverbed track depending on the model).
Segment Size (MDX-Net tab, e.g. 256): controls chunk memory usage for standard MDX-Net models.
Note for Roformers: when Segment Default is enabled in Advanced MDX-Net Options, UVR5 reads chunk_size directly from the model's .yaml file instead of the main window's Segment Size dropdown.

Overlap (for Roformers): 4 offers the best balance of speed and SDR quality; 8 can give slightly smoother consistency, while 16–32 is much slower for very little gain. The GUI Overlap value overrides the .yaml.
VR Architecture settings:
Window Size: 512 (more accurate) or 320 (faster / popular in metal & ensembles).
Aggression Setting: usually 5–10 for vocals/karaoke; 3.0–5.0 for UVR-DeEcho-DeReverb; and negative values (-10 to -25) for UVR-DeNoise on vocals to avoid hollowing out the voice.
TTA (Test-Time Augmentation): improves separation quality at ~2× processing time.

Open Choose MDX-Net Model → Edit Model Config (or edit the model's .yaml in models\MDX_Net_Models\model_data\mdx_c_configs\) and lower chunk_size (ensure Segment Default is checked in Advanced MDX Options):
352800 (8s) - default for most models; max for ~8 GB AMD/Intel GPUs.
220500 (5s) or 200655 (4.5s) - safe for 4–6 GB VRAM cards.
112455 (2.55s) - minimum safe starting point if crashes persist.

Roformer missing from Ensemble / Vocal Splitter: open its .yaml and rename stem labels from other / vocals / Karaoke to case-sensitive Instrumental and Vocals.
PC freezes during separation: set UVR's priority to Idle in Windows Task Manager.

Audio Restoration: DeReverb Stereo, DeReverb Room, DeNoise (by aufr33 & gabox), and DeEffect.
Multi-stem & specialized models: 4/6/10-stem DrumSep, bass, guitars, piano, strings, synth percussion, and audio upscaling.

Go to mvsep.com and register a free account.
Why register?
Lossless audio: unregistered users only get lossy MP3 files. Registered accounts unlock WAV 16-bit and FLAC 16-bit output.
No CAPTCHA and faster queue priority.
124-band Polar & BS-Roformer models are accessible to free users (BS variants allow up to 5 separations/day per model).
Output format: always choose WAV (or FLAC) before starting separation if you plan to train an RVC model or chain multiple cleanup steps.
Post-processing / chaining: log in and go to Advanced settings → Home Screen, then enable "Show post-processing algorithm" if you want to chain a cleanup model right after separation.
Slow upload/download? MVSep provides regional mirrors - if the main site is slow for file transfers, switch to the mirror option.
If you process long files (up to 100 minutes / 1 GB), want WAV 32-bit float / FLAC 24-bit, or want to avoid peak-hour queues:
Credit packs never expire (starting around $3 for 60 credits, $5 for 200 credits, $10 for 600 credits).
Standard models cost 1 credit per minute of audio; heavy ensembles use multipliers (2×–6×).
API access: logged-in users can generate an API token in their account to automate batch separations from Python scripts via https://mvsep.com/api.

A high-precision Band-Split Roformer variant using Polar Positional Embeddings (PoPE) for long-context separation.
When to use: your primary first-pass choice for clean vocals and minimal instrumental bleed.
MVSep DnR v3 - Open preset on MVSep
A cinematic multi-stem (Divide and Remaster) model designed to split audio into speech, music, and SFX.
When to use: game dialogue, movies, videos, or clips with heavy sound effects.
Recommendation: BS Polarformer is generally stronger on its own, but running both (passing the output through the second) eliminates almost any chance of leftover background music or SFX.
MVSep Karaoke - Open preset on MVSep
Isolates lead vocals from backing vocals / harmonies.

Note: this model can be a little finicky and may occasionally confuse backing vocals with lead vocals depending on how the track is mixed - listen to both stems before deleting anything. Even with that quirk, it remains very useful.
Run these on your isolated vocal stem to turn "wet" studio/room vocals into dry recordings.
DeReverb Stereo - Open preset on MVSep
Targets stereo vocal reverb and reflections.
DeReverb Room - Open preset on MVSep
Targets room acoustics and natural room echo.
Recommendation: it is best to use both to eliminate any remaining reverb. Whichever one you run first depends on your specific audio - test both orders on a short clip if the reverb is heavy.
DeNoise by aufr33 and gabox - Open preset on MVSep
A specialized community Mel-Roformer denoising model designed to clean hiss, static, and residual artifacts without dulling high frequencies.
Recommendation: use this as your final step to polish the audio and ensure it is clean. (Keep in mind it can occasionally miss certain types of noise, so always verify the final WAV by ear.)
DeEffect - Open preset on MVSep
Removes heavy vocal modulation effects and reverb, and can even act as a fallback instead of a dedicated lead/reverb pass or remove some background noise.
Warning: do not rely on DeEffect for anything other than removing voice effects and reverb - use the dedicated models above for vocal/SFX splitting and final denoising.
Extract Vocals / Speech: run BS Polarformer (and optionally MVSep DnR v3 if SFX remain).
Isolate Lead Vocal (songs with harmonies only): run MVSep Karaoke.
Remove Reverb: run DeReverb Stereo and DeReverb Room (plus DeEffect only if heavy vocal effects/reverb persist).
Final Clean: finish with DeNoise by aufr33 and gabox and download the WAV result.

l: Convert a recording with Ilaria RVC
p: Download Ilaria RVC 2.4.7 for Windows (ZIP)

Voice conversion starts with a performance. The output usually follows the source words, timing, articulation, and pitch contour while changing the sound of the voice. Decisions about delivery still start with the original recording. For a sung cover, plan to convert an isolated lead vocal and mix the converted vocal with the instrumental afterward.

Open Ilaria RVC and import the inference model you want to use. An optional index belongs with the checkpoint it was built for. If an imported voice is absent from the selector, see RVC models and files.
Open Single Inference, choose the voice, and drag in a short recording you can recognize by ear. A phrase with a pause, several consonants, and a longer vowel makes a useful reference.

Set Pitch to zero and Index Ratio to zero. Match the content embedder to the one used in training when the model author provides it. Start with the app's default pitch extractor and leave optional audio processing off.
Convert the file and check the output. Use the waveform player to revisit the same phrase, then save a WAV or FLAC copy as your baseline.
Compare the original and the converted clip at similar playback levels. Note the first audible problem and use Pitch and audio quality to decide what to change.

Current Ilaria RVC releases automatically look for a matching index when you select a voice. Selecting an index and giving it influence are separate actions. A loaded index contributes only when Index Ratio is above zero. Older builds may show a different layout or ask you to select the index manually.

Workflow

Open Batch Inference after a single file produces a usable result. Group files that need the same model, pitch, and processing profile. Run one representative file from each group and save to a separate output location so you can compare results safely.

For a long song, audition a section with exposed high or low notes before converting the whole file. Split Audio can help with long recordings or memory limitations. Listen across segment joins and pauses after the run. If a version of the app exposes a console or conversion log, use it to identify any failed items and retry those files separately.

In a release with the TTS workspace, supply text or a UTF-8 text file. Current Ilaria RVC releases offer Microsoft Edge online voices and installed Windows voices for offline TTS. Pick a source voice in the language of the script, listen for pronunciation and pauses, and then apply the RVC model to that generated recording. If the first stage reads a name incorrectly, fix the text or change the TTS voice first. RVC will generally carry those source pronunciation choices through.
When privacy or an unreliable connection matters, select an installed Windows voice and check that it works with your text before starting a long job. The Edge option requires a network connection.

l: Save the conversion and your settings
p: Keep an unprocessed WAV or FLAC master before adding compression, reverb, or limiting.
For music, align the converted vocal against the original, check its timing at consonants, and listen to both solo and in the mix before exporting.

Save your settings alongside the result. Include the source file, model and index versions, speaker ID if applicable, embedder, pitch extractor, pitch shift, index ratio, processing, and output format.
When a model is missing or inference fails before producing audio, start with Troubleshooting. For microphone conversion, see Real-time voice conversion.

l: Convert a recording in RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC)

p: On Windows, use a RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) package compatible with your hardware. Extract the entire archive to a local directory before running its launcher. Windows packages that include go-web.bat use it to start the local WebUI. Leave the console open while converting. If the browser does not open automatically, use the local address printed in the console.

Place the inference checkpoint in assets/weights and its matching retrieval index, if supplied, under logs. Open Model Inference and refresh the voice and index lists. Choose the checkpoint and matching index. Set the retrieval ratio to zero for models without an index.

Give the WebUI the full path to a short local WAV file. If the path fails, copy the test file to a simple location such as C:\RVC\input\test.wav. Keep transposition at zero for the first pass and select RMVPE if your build offers it. Click Convert, then listen in the output player and save the result using its download control. If generation fails, read the console message before changing settings. A model that does not appear in the list usually needs to be moved to the weights directory or rediscovered using refresh.

In Desktop, wait until the engine is ready, add the inference model to the library, and open Convert Audio in single-file mode. In Gradio, open the browser interface and select Convert Audio or Inference, depending on the release. Refresh the model list after adding a checkpoint if it is missing.

Select the voice and its paired index, then confirm the content embedder expected by that model. Load a short recording and choose WAV or FLAC for the test. Check for settings carried over from a previous run, especially pitch, retrieval and effects. A useful baseline starts at zero semitones with effects off. Start the job once, wait for the output, and compare the same phrase in both recordings.

What to try

The converted voice retains the source timbre

Generic HuBERT embedders can retain speaker information. Verify the encoder matches the model and test several clean clips with retrieval off. If the voice was trained with an encoder that leaks source timbre, retrain with a compatible voice-conversion encoder such as ContentVec and rebuild the index.
