Code-verified guide to improving RVC inference audio quality in Ilaria RVC: diagnostic baseline, pitch, F0 methods, Index Ratio, Protect, Formant Shifting, Volume Envelope, and Post-Process.
Download Ilaria RVC 2.4.7 for Windows (ZIP)

In RVC voice conversion, audio quality depends on two halves working together: the source recording you feed in and the model + inference settings you apply. In pitch-guided RVC models, conversion synthesizes the target voice's timbre using the F0 contour extracted from your source recording; the target voice does not automatically impose its own pitch range (results still depend on the model's training data and range limits). RVC cannot repair clipping, heavy background music, room echo, or slurred diction already present in the input file.

l: Start with a concrete diagnostic baseline
p: Before changing advanced sliders, run one diagnostic conversion in Ilaria RVC. This helps you assess the selected model without FAISS feature retrieval or optional audio effects; the default Volume Envelope handling still applies.
Open the Inference tab.
Select your target voice in Voice Model (click Refresh if you just added it).
Stay on the Single Inference sub-tab.
Load your recording in Audio to convert. (A short excerpt can help isolate a specific timestamp faster, but short clips are never a requirement.)
Set Pitch to 0.
Under Inference Settings, select RMVPE in Pitch Extraction.
Set Index Ratio to 0 (disables FAISS feature retrieval so you hear the .pth generator without index blending).
Leave all optional Audio Processing checkboxes (Split Audio, Autotune, Proposed Pitch, Clean Audio, Formant Shifting, Post-Process) and RMVPE High Register turned OFF.
Click Convert.

Listen to Output Audio and read Output Log for conversion status, timing information, and available index or embedder details. These messages do not necessarily confirm that FAISS retrieval completed successfully (an index can be selected and reported as enabled in settings while FAISS loading fails or is skipped, and Embedder may not be printed explicitly when Auto (model default) is selected). Check the console diagnostics if index loading fails or the result is unexpected.

Diagnostic baseline only: This setup disables FAISS retrieval and optional audio effects, but it does not bypass the normal RVC processing pipeline or its default Volume Envelope value (0.25). It is not a guarantee of optimal final quality. If you need to compare the generator output without source-RMS envelope matching, set Volume Envelope to 1 as a separate test. Change one control at a time and compare at similar listening levels.

Source audio & isolated vocals: RVC expects a single, dry, clean vocal. Tools such as UVR5 or MVSep can help separate vocals from backing tracks, and specialized models target tasks like denoising, dereverberation, de-essing, or audio restoration depending on the model used (no single tool removes every type of noise or reverb).

Speech vs. singing: Speech often tolerates small Pitch adjustments, whereas singing over an instrumental track usually keeps Pitch at 0 to stay in key with the backing track (a non-octave transposition may be appropriate if the accompaniment's key is also changed).

Model & embedder compatibility: Leave Embedder Model on Auto (model default) unless you intentionally trained or downloaded a model requiring a specific encoder (contentvec, spin-v2, klm-vocal-contentvec, etc.). Using an incompatible embedder can cause an error or degrade conversion quality and break index matching.
Non-pitch-guided (if_f0 == 0) vs. pitch-guided (if_f0 == 1) models:

Non-pitch-guided models (if_f0 == 0): Skip F0 extraction (pitch and pitchf are not passed to the .pth generator). Because there is no F0 conditioning, Pitch, Pitch Extraction, RMVPE High Register, Autotune, Proposed Pitch, and Protect (hidden in the UI when if_f0 == 0) do not apply. Embedder, Index Ratio, Formant Shifting, Volume Envelope, Clean Audio, and Post-Process (including Post-Process → Pitch Shift) still run normally.

Pitch-guided models (if_f0 == 1): Extract an F0 contour from the 16 kHz input and pass it to the .pth generator alongside the content features. Pitch Extraction, Pitch, RMVPE High Register, Autotune, Proposed Pitch, and Protect (when Index Ratio 0 and protect 0.5) are all active, making these models suitable for singing and pitch-controlled speech.

Optional index & lossless export: Keep Index Ratio at 0 for your baseline, then test your matching added_*.index if desired. Use wav or flac for lossless exports; flac reduces file size without lossy audio compression. mp3, ogg, and m4a use lossy encoding in the current Ilaria RVC exporter, and the export format never adds detail that the model did not produce.

l: B. Fixing Pitch and Singing Problems
p: Pitch (Semitones): Pitch changes the extracted F0 contour by semitones (-24 to +24; 12 semitones = 1 octave). At 0, pitch-guided conversion follows the source pitch without an additional transposition. Choose a different value only when needed for the target performance or musical arrangement (for singing, a non-octave transposition may be appropriate if the accompaniment's key is also changed). There is no universal pitch shift for converting between different voice types. Requires a pitch-guided model (if_f0 == 1).
Pitch Extraction (F0) in Ilaria RVC: Estimates fundamental frequency (F0) from the 16 kHz input before synthesis (separate from Pitch shifting).

Single & Batch Inference (standard, non-DirectML backend): rmvpe (default), swift, beatrice, fcpe, parselmouth, harvest, crepe. These options do not all run on CUDA: for example, swift uses ONNX Runtime on the CPU in the current implementation. (On DirectML builds: pm, harvest, rmvpe, fcpe.)
Training feature extraction only: Includes rmvpe_gpu (and dio); rmvpe_gpu is not a separate button in Inference.

Median filter (Harvest only): filter_radius values 0–2 disable the optional median filter. Values 3–7 all enable the same three-sample median filter; increasing from 3 to 7 does not increase its strength. The UI default is 3.
Note: If rmvpe produces an octave jump on a specific note, test fcpe, swift, beatrice, or crepe on that same passage rather than assuming one method is universally "best" or fastest for every voice.
RMVPE High Register (visible only when rmvpe is selected):
Enable high register: Enables secondary octave-error correction for very high singing notes. Do not leave it enabled by default for normal speech or mid-range singing.
Mode (true_pitch / fold): true_pitch keeps corrected F0 up to Maximum F0 (Hz) (1000–2000, default 1250); fold keeps corrected notes an octave lower.
Advanced (Activation threshold 800–1500 Hz default 1040, Sensitivity, Minimum note duration 0–300 ms default 60): Tunes when high-register correction triggers.

Preview original and corrected F0: Plots the first 30 seconds of estimated vs. corrected F0 without running full voice conversion. A cleaner plot helps diagnose octave flips, but does not automatically guarantee better sounding audio.

Autotune & Autotune Strength (0–1, default 1.0): Snaps voiced F0 frames toward the nearest equal-tempered chromatic note (G1–C6), scaled by Autotune Strength. Because it pulls toward every chromatic semitone (there is no musical key/scale selector in Ilaria RVC), high strength can flatten natural vibrato or expressive pitch slides.

Proposed Pitch & Target Pitch (Hz) (50–1200, default 155): Computes the median of interpolated voiced F0 frames across the source audio and adds an automatic semitone offset (-12 to +12) toward Target Pitch (Hz) on top of your Pitch slider. Useful as a quick transposition test, though the mathematically centered pitch is not always the best musical or vocal fit. Both Autotune and Proposed Pitch require a pitch-guided (if_f0 == 1) model.

l: C. Fixing Voice Identity and Timbre
p: Content Embedder vs. Voice Generator (.pth): The trained .pth generator produces the target voice, while the content embedder (default Auto (model default), typically contentvec) extracts speech features from the source recording. The embedder is intended to reduce source speaker-identity information, though it is not necessarily completely speaker-independent, and it does not define the target voice identity. Use the embedder expected by the model to preserve compatibility and avoid conversion artifacts. Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Portuguese HuBERT Base embedders require an RVC v2 model.

How Index Ratio (0–1, default 0) actually works: A .pth generator is always used regardless of Index Ratio. When an added_*.index FAISS database is loaded and Index Ratio 0, RVC searches the 8 nearest feature vectors in the index and blends them with your input's extracted features before the .pth generator: features = retrieved_features * index_rate + original_features * (1 - index_rate)
Index Ratio = 0 disables FAISS feature retrieval (original_features only) while the .pth generator remains active, providing a useful diagnostic baseline without FAISS feature retrieval.

Index Selected vs. Retrieval Applied: If Index Ratio 0 but the selected index file is missing, Output Log reports Voice index: off (no index file found). If the file exists but FAISS cannot load it, the backend catches the loading error and proceeds without retrieval, although Output Log can still say Voice index setting: enabled. Check the console traceback when a seemingly enabled index produces unexpected results.

Increasing Index Ratio pulls features closer to the index's stored feature vectors. A matching index can improve some conversions, but it can also worsen results (for example, muffled diction or dataset artifacts) depending on the audio and model. No single value guarantees better pronunciation.

Formant Shifting (apply_formant_shift, 0.7–1.4, default 1.0): Uses Praat/Parselmouth (Change gender) before RVC synthesis on the 16 kHz input to shift vocal tract resonances. 1.0 is neutral; values below 1.0 aim to darken/deepen vowel resonance, while values above 1.0 aim to brighten it. The algorithm aims to preserve pitch and duration, though artifacts can still appear, especially at extreme values. Formant Shifting is not equivalent to changing Pitch or Post-Process → Pitch Shift (which shifts output pitch post-RVC).
How Protect clear consonants and breathing sounds (0–0.5, default 0.33) works:
In the inference pipeline (vc()), when protect 0.5 and the model uses pitch guidance (if_f0 == 1), RVC saves a copy of the original un-blended features (feats0) before FAISS index retrieval.

After retrieval, unvoiced frames (frames with no detected F0, pitchf 1) are blended back toward feats0: lower values move those frames closer to feats0, while 0.5 disables protection. This is not a general adjustment for low-pitched voiced speech.

Critical limitation: Because Protect blends back to feats0 (the pre-retrieval features), when Index Ratio = 0, feats and feats0 are identical, so changing Protect produces little to no difference. Furthermore, Protect is not an audio denoiser or restoration filter and cannot fix clipped or distorted consonants already present in the source audio or model.

l: E. Fixing Volume, Noise and Distortion
p: Volume Envelope (0=Input source volume, 1=Normalized Output, default 0.25): Uses change_rms() to blend the RMS amplitude envelope of the input audio (1 - rate) with the RVC output's RMS envelope (rate).
0 makes the converted audio follow the source audio's RMS envelope closely.
1 keeps the RVC generator's own output RMS envelope.

Note: Despite the UI label, 1 does not normalize to a fixed LUFS loudness target and is not a compressor or limiter. Changing Volume Envelope adjusts dynamic level matching, which can help when silent gaps or level differences cause pumping.

Clean Audio & Clean Strength (0–1, default 0.5): Runs noisereduce after RVC conversion on the converted audio, with Clean Strength controlling reduction intensity. Depending on the recording and noise present, overly aggressive reduction can alter consonants, breaths, and vocal details; there is no universally correct threshold. Clean Audio is post-processing noise reduction, not audio restoration: it cannot repair clipping or fix a poorly trained model.
Post-Process Effects (applied after conversion via FFmpeg/librosa; leave OFF for baseline testing):
Pitch Shift (-12..+12): Post-RVC librosa pitch shift (alters the finished audio rather than the RVC F0 contour).

Limiter (-24..0 dBFS, default -6) & Gain (-24..+24 dB): In the current FFmpeg filter chain (ilaria_inference_effects.py), Limiter runs before Gain when both are enabled. Because Gain is applied after Limiter, positive Gain can push peaks back into clipping; Limiter does not guarantee clipping-free final output when positive Gain follows it.
Creative/utility effects: Reverb, Distortion, Chorus, Bitcrush, Clipping, Compressor, Delay.

Resampling (0–48000, 0=none) & Export Format: Leave 0 to keep the model's native sample rate (32k/40k/48k). In this backend, resampling occurs only when the requested rate is at least 16000 Hz and different from the model's output sample rate; selecting a nonzero value below 16000 does not trigger resampling. Set 44100 or 48000 only if your DAW/project requires that output rate (resampling changes sample rate, not underlying synthesis quality). Use wav or flac for lossless exports during quality checks.

l: F. Long Recordings and Batch Inference
p: Split Audio: Calls silence_split_points() to insert frame-aligned cut points inside quiet pauses while retaining RVC's normal long-audio cuts (opt_ts). This changes the segment sizes passed to synthesis and can alter behavior at join boundaries. It does not necessarily avoid loading the full audio into memory, does not eliminate all causes of excessive memory usage, and is not a fix for volume, distortion, or voice quality.

Single vs. Batch Inference: Both tabs expose the same core settings (Pitch, Pitch Extraction, Index Ratio, Resampling, Volume Envelope, Protect, Export Format, Audio Processing, Embedder Settings, and RMVPE High Register). Use Single Inference to dial in settings on one file with immediate playback; use Batch Inference (InferOutput/ or chosen folder) once settings are verified to convert multiple files in one pass.

Connect a microphone and headphones. In the converter, select your physical microphone as the input and your headphones as the output.
Load a known compatible inference model and its matching index if you use retrieval. A successful short file conversion is a useful reference before you test the live path.
Start the stream and speak at a normal level. Check the input meter or make a dry recording. Reduce input gain if peaks clip before conversion.
Verify that the headphone signal changes when conversion is toggled. If you hear the original at the same time, check for direct hardware monitoring or a second route through the operating system.
Test for longer than a single word. Include quiet speech, a loud phrase and a short pause. Listen for cutoffs, drift or glitches under the same workload you plan to use live.
Avoid listening through speakers near an active microphone. Headphones help you identify a routing issue without feeding the output back into the input.

Appears under Windows Recording (e.g. Line 1 in VAC Lite or CABLE Output in VB-CABLE). Select this as the Microphone in Discord, OBS, or games.

Before wiring any app, know what each endpoint does:
Correct Audio Routing
Input Device
Input Device: Line 1 (VAC, recommended) or CABLE Output (VB-CABLE).
Input Device: Your physical microphone.
Monitor Device
Monitoring: Hearing your own converted voice in your headphones is a separate optional feature to enable only when needed. Avoid duplicate audio paths, echo, and loopback.
Optional second output so you can hear your own converted voice in headphones while Output Device feeds a virtual cable.
Output Device
Output Device: Line 1 (VAC, recommended) or CABLE Input (VB-CABLE).
Output Device: Your headphones (strongly recommended over speakers).

Speakers & Headset Bleed: Avoid using speakers; sound from speakers can leak into your microphone and cause double audio, echo, or other people's voices being converted too. This can also happen with headsets if the volume is too loud or the earcups are not closed and isolated enough.

VAC vs. VB-CABLE: VAC (Line 1) is always recommended. If you have VB-CABLE installed as well (or instead), remember that the voice changer outputs to CABLE Input while Discord / games listen to CABLE Output.

Virtual Cable Output (Recording side)

l: USB microphones, audio interfaces, and backends
p: USB microphones: Plug directly into a rear motherboard USB port (avoid unpowered hubs), set Windows format to 48000 Hz, and disable USB selective suspend if the mic drops out.
Audio interfaces (XLR): Use ASIO when supported by your voice changer (such as RVC Blue or w-okada) for lower driver buffer latency, or WASAPI when routing to standard Windows virtual cables.

WASAPI Shared vs. WASAPI Exclusive: WASAPI Shared is the safest starting point because Windows and virtual cables can share 48000 Hz streams cleanly. WASAPI Exclusive bypasses the Windows mixer for lower driver latency when supported, but locks the device so other apps cannot share it.

l: App-specific setup (Discord, OBS, games, calls, recording)
p: Discord / calling apps: Set Input Device to your virtual cable recording endpoint (Line 1 / CABLE Output), set Output Device to your headphones, and turn OFF Krisp, Echo Cancellation, and automatic input sensitivity if Discord clips breaths or word endings.

OBS Studio & local recording: Add an Audio Input Capture source pointing to the virtual cable recording endpoint, mute any separate raw microphone source, and record a local test clip to check sync and levels.

Games: Select the virtual cable recording endpoint as your in-game mic (or set it as Windows Default Communication Recording Device). Always cap in-game FPS or leave GPU headroom so the game does not starve the voice changer.

l: Send converted audio to another app
p: A virtual audio device provides a playback endpoint for the converter and a corresponding recording endpoint for the receiving app. Endpoint names depend on the driver. For example, a virtual cable may call its playback endpoint “Input” and its recording endpoint “Output” because the instructions use the cable's perspective.

Select the matching recording endpoint as the microphone in the receiving app and make a short test recording there. If your local monitor sounds correct but the recording does not, verify the destination input and remove any duplicate microphone source. If you monitor the converted audio, use a separate headphone output. Avoid routing your entire desktop mix or the receiving app's audio back into the converter.

Check the device and virtual-cable sample rates if you hear unusual speed or crackle. Start with compatible settings across the chain.
Control
Crossfade
Device rate
Extra context
If a setting produces unstable timing, compare available predictors using the same phrases. Select the one that handles your pitch range with enough processing margin.
Increase cautiously if you hear rough joins between blocks. It changes how neighboring blocks overlap.
Increase it if speech breaks up under load. Once stable, try a smaller setting and keep it only if normal speech stays clean. Smaller blocks leave less time to finish processing.
Lower a threshold that cuts off soft syllables. Evaluate this during pauses and quiet speech, not just a sustained loud input.
Pitch predictor
Practical adjustment

Processing latency vs. total end-to-end latency: The GPU Delay / inference time shown inside your voice changer is only how long the GPU takes to convert one chunk. Total end-to-end latency adds microphone input buffering, Block Size / Chunk Size, crossfade/context overhead, virtual cable buffering, and Discord/OBS/game audio buffers. Do not confuse a low GPU Delay (e.g. 15 ms) with total round-trip latency.
Silence detection or input threshold

Try less context if the converter falls behind. It can help the model follow transitions, at the cost of more processing.

A stem is an isolated part of a mix, such as the vocal or instrumental. RVC is easiest to control with a clean vocal on its own.

A stem is an isolated part of a mix, such as the vocal or instrumental. RVC is easiest to control with a clean vocal on its own. If you have the original microphone recording or an official isolated vocal, use it as your source.
Start with a recording you have permission to process. Keep the original file and work on a copy.
When the only source is a mix, try a stem separator such as Ultimate Vocal Remover.
Listen to the entire vocal stem. Check for percussion bleed, missing syllables, backing vocals and long reverb tails. Compare separators on the hardest ten seconds before processing a whole track.
If harmonies or doubled vocals bleed heavily into the lead stem, convert a cleaner take. When separate tracks are available, process each part individually.
Convert a short verse or chorus and compare it with the isolated source at a similar listening level.
Export a lossless result and align it with the instrumental in your audio editor. Keep the instrumental on its own track so balance and timing can be adjusted independently.
Apply EQ, level changes and placement in the mix after conversion. Keep a dry copy so you can return to it.
Listen on headphones and speakers. Check quiet syllables, the switch between verse and chorus and the ending. Avoid clipping at export.

Noise, reverb and other performers in the stem can affect pitch tracking and intelligibility. Heavy cleanup can also damage a useful take. Save alternatives and compare by ear before committing to a whole song. For one-clip experiments, see Voice conversion.

Every clip teaches the model something about its target voice. Before training, decide which parts of that voice you want the model to handle, then keep recordings that demonstrate those parts clearly. Start with material you have permission to use for training, and keep a separate copy of the original files.
Goal
What to collect
Conversational speech
Questions, statements, longer sentences, and short responses with varied consonants and vowels.
Expressive speech
The intended delivery styles at both quiet and emphatic levels. Record variations across several phrases.
Singing
Sustained vowels, note changes, and examples near the comfortable high and low ends of the intended range.
More than one language
Clear examples of the sounds and phrasing that differ across languages, recorded by the same speaker.

ContentVec can be a bottleneck in multilingual models. A dataset containing the target language cannot guarantee that the encoder preserves its phonetic distinctions. Set aside recordings for each language, including difficult sound contrasts, and compare pronunciation after a short training run. If the same errors recur on clean test clips, document the limitation for that language. Changing the encoder or training configuration does not reliably resolve it.

A clean, varied set of recordings is a better starting point than a larger collection of repeated phrases or damaged audio. There is no duration that guarantees a good result. Audit what the recordings cover before deciding whether you need more material.
10 minutes
20 minutes

A recording can be free of noise and still cover very little of a voice. Build the session around the performance you expect to convert. For narration, record clear reading with intentional phrasing. For conversation, include spontaneous replies and changes in pace. For singing, collect dry a cappella takes across the intended register, with sustained vowels and transitions between notes. Spoken lines alone give the model little exposure to those singing sounds.
Collect unscripted speech with questions, short reactions, and longer answers.
Conversation
Example allocation
Expressive narration
Performance range
Phonetic coverage
Read a passage with shifts in emphasis, emotion, and pace.

Record the delivery the model needs, from soft speech to projection. Try varied tempos, emotions, and clear chuckles or sighs where relevant. For a multilingual model, include intentional coverage of the target languages.

Record yourself, or agree on the intended model and its use with the performer before recording. For a remote conversation, have the speaker capture their own microphone locally and use only that track.
Session block

That 50-minute plan is an example for expressive speech. A focused ten-minute set can be more useful than a larger set of repetitive or damaged recordings. Add material to fill an audible gap in coverage. Dataset duration alone does not determine overfitting.
Use material such as Harvard Sentences, the Rainbow Passage, or Comma Gets a Cure to exercise vowels, diphthongs, stops like P/B/T/K, and sibilants like S/Z/SH.
What to capture

Capture a single microphone on a mono track. Use a pop filter or windscreen, keep the mic distance consistent, and set gain while testing the loudest planned line. A quiet room with soft furnishings reduces reflections at the source. Prefer a dry original over a heavily cleaned recording with audible reverb or separation artifacts. If converting existing stereo recordings to mono, listen to both channels and the fold-down. Use a clean channel if the combined signal sounds hollow or loses detail.

Sample rate: Keep the originals at their recorded rate. Choose a training rate supported by the architecture and pretrained weights. The preprocessing stage can resample when needed. Upsampling adds no detail to the original recording.

Levels: Compare session levels and fix large gain differences caused by mic placement or recording settings. Preserve intentional changes in delivery. Check what the training frontend already normalizes before applying a separate loudness pass.
Breaths and reactions: Keep natural breaths and clean expressive cues where they serve the intended use. Trim clipped laughs, harsh gasps, and plosive bursts. Audition uncertain edits in headphones.

Pauses: Keep natural pauses and remove long empty spans. If you want to test a standalone silence clip, run a comparison with the same settings and listen to held-out pauses. Some preprocessing pipelines already handle silence.
Use one speaker for a first model. Exclude overlapping voices, crowd responses, and dialogue where the speaker changes mid-clip.
Listen for fan noise, echoes, music, and digital distortion. A clip that sounds acceptable in a loud mix can still contain problems that are obvious when the voice is isolated.
If you are recording a new session, use a consistent mic position and leave peak headroom. Test the loudest phrase before recording the full session.
When combining sessions, listen to them side by side. Keep useful variation in the voice and discard abrupt differences caused by heavy effects, room sound, or an unreliable microphone.
Remove duplicate takes if they add little variety. Put different sessions or passages aside for evaluation before editing adjacent cuts into the training folder.

Isolate the target voice. If the source includes an accompaniment, try separation and audition the resulting vocal stem. Reject sections with instrument bleed, backing vocals, or obvious separation artifacts.
Make cuts at natural boundaries. Trim long dead air and remove unusable sections. Listen across each cut for lost consonants, abrupt changes, or a second speaker entering.

Apply only the cleanup the recording needs. Compare any denoising pass against the original. If the cleaned version swallows consonants, blurs syllables, or introduces a pulsing sound, reduce the processing or replace the take.

Check levels across files. Keep enough headroom for loud passages and balance major recording-level differences. Lowering the volume of an already clipped file leaves the damaged peaks in the recording.
Export in a lossless format your build can read. WAV is a practical working format. Re-encoding a compressed file as WAV preserves the result of that decode and cannot restore lost detail.

The training engine may divide files into its own segments and resample them to the selected model configuration. Keep usable words and phrases intact during manual editing and let the training preprocessing stage handle its own segmentation.

l: Organize the dataset and listening tests
p: Keep comparison inputs, discarded recordings, and converted output outside the training folder. This example uses separate folders for originals, training, and evaluation.

Point preprocessing at training-audio/. Keep evaluation/ separate. A useful comparison set might include an unfamiliar spoken phrase with sharp consonants, a quiet passage, and a short expressive phrase. For a singing model, include a held note and a phrase crossing registers. Hold back whole passages or sessions when you can, so the test audio does not duplicate nearby training clips.

If you train with an interface that supports more than one speaker, follow its speaker-folder and ID rules. A single-speaker folder with audio files directly inside it is easier to audit for a first run.

l: Review the dataset in Ilaria RVC
p: Recent Ilaria RVC builds let you drag audio or a dataset ZIP into the training interface and manage imported datasets there. Select the intended dataset and run the Dataset Checker. Use its short previews to inspect files flagged for silence, clipping, inconsistent levels, or decoding problems. The Audio Analyzer can help compare suspect files using waveforms, pitch, and level measurements. Confirm the diagnosis by listening before removing otherwise useful material. Availability and control labels follow your installed release.
What you notice
What to do before training
File will not decode
Check that it plays in an editor. Re-export from the original if possible and verify the copy opens.
Sections of near-silence
Audition the flagged range and trim empty spans. Keep natural pauses that help preserve phrase boundaries.
Distorted or flattened peaks
Compare with the original recording. Replace an audibly clipped take when you have a clean alternative.
Background sounds follow the vocal
Listen to the isolated stem in headphones and exclude the affected parts when separation sounds unstable.
One session is much quieter
Check whether the speaker's performance is intentionally quiet. Adjust recording gain differences while retaining useful natural dynamics.
Before continuing, play a few clips from each session, confirm you selected the prepared folder, and record the folder version in your notes. Then run a training experiment.

Training learns a target voice from a prepared collection of audio. Use this guide when you want to build a model from your own or authorized recordings. If you already have an inference model, see RVC models and files to start using it.

Prepare the audio with the dataset guide, then select it in Training. Give the experiment a unique name and choose one short recording outside the training set for listening tests. Start with a modest run that can complete all stages and produce a usable export. This gives you a baseline for changes to data or settings.

Record the application version, dataset revision, model format and sample rate, embedder, pitch method, pretrained pair, batch size, and planned save interval. Add the name of the held-out test clip. If a later run sounds different, these notes help you identify what changed.
Setting
What to check
Model format, vocoder, and sample rate
Select a combination supported by the app and intended playback client. A fork-specific architecture can limit where your model loads.
Pitch guidance and extraction
Pitch guidance is useful for modelling pitch-dependent material, especially singing. Pick an extractor available for training in your build.
Embedder
This defines the representation extracted from audio. Record the choice so you can use the matching representation in supported inference clients.
Pretrained generator and discriminator
Use a matched pair compatible with the selected architecture, rate, and pitch configuration. Generator and discriminator files serve different roles in training.
Batch size
Controls how much data is processed per update. Begin with a setting your GPU can fit and lower it if training runs out of memory.
Target and checkpoint interval
An epoch is approximately one pass through the prepared dataset. Steps are individual training updates. Save periodically so you can compare exports and recover after an interruption.

Use the pretraining choices shown as compatible by your installed build. In Ilaria RVC 2.1.0, for example, the project documents RefineGAN training at 32 kHz with RVC V2 and pitch guidance. The same release also documents a downloader for compatible pretrained pairs.

Epochs: Try a first comparison run with a target around 200 epochs and listen to several earlier saves. This is a starting point for auditioning, since the strongest checkpoint can come earlier or later. A 1,000-epoch run offers no quality guarantee.

Batch and precision: Start with a moderate batch, for example 8, and treat 16 as a conservative upper starting point. Reduce it if memory runs out. FP16 mixed precision can reduce VRAM use and speed up training on supported hardware. Check whether your build already enables it, and try FP32 if mixed precision produces non-finite losses.
TensorBoard: Use metrics to track progress and spot stalled or unstable runs. Loss curves alone cannot tell which checkpoint sounds best. Compare conversions of the same held-out clips.

Normalization: In Applio builds with these controls, Pre adjusts levels before slicing and Post adjusts them after slicing. Use None if the original levels are already suitable. In Ilaria RVC, Process Data applies level adjustment automatically to each slice. The public implementation has no separate Post toggle.

Noise filtering: Start with optional noise reduction off for clean recordings. If the frontend also exposes a high-pass filter, use it for audible low-frequency rumble and compare the result by ear. High-pass filtering and noise reduction are separate operations.
GPU dataset cache: Leave it off for a baseline. It consumes extra VRAM. Measure time per epoch before enabling it for a longer run.

Pretrained weights: Match the G/D pair to the architecture, vocoder, sample rate and pitch configuration, and use the embedder specified by the pretraining author. For standard RVC pretrainings built with ContentVec, select ContentVec for feature extraction and inference.

l: Choose a rate using the source bandwidth
p: Check the sample rate in the file metadata and inspect several representative clips in a spectrogram viewer such as Spek. Look for useful vocal detail rather than isolated noise or a sharp cutoff left by compression. Half the training sample rate is the highest frequency that rate can represent. A 32 kHz model can represent frequencies up to 16 kHz, a 40 kHz model up to 20 kHz, and a 48 kHz model up to 24 kHz. For usable detail above 20 kHz, choose 48 kHz if the architecture and pretraining support it. Use the lower compatible rate when it already covers the source bandwidth. Preprocessing can resample recordings, but cannot restore missing detail.

Feature extraction

Retrieval index
Stage
The index belongs to this experiment and matches the exported voice. If you skipped it, test the model independently.
The log names the intended folder and reports successful processing for usable files. Check skipped files before continuing.
Training steps advance and expected files are saved. Read the first error if progress stops.

Use the automatic workflow where available, or finish and verify each stage before starting the next. A changed dataset or sample rate can invalidate prepared audio and extracted features. A changed embedder requires new feature extraction. When testing an incompatible configuration, start a separate experiment so existing caches and checkpoints stay available.
What it produces
What to check
Use Training Dashboard to check step count, time per epoch, and loss curves. A curve can help explain a stalled run, while listening tests tell you how the output sounds.
Configure training previews with a constant test clip so the app can generate comparable conversions as checkpoints are saved.
If you use the Training Queue, set a distinct experiment name and dataset for each job. Before resuming or retrying, confirm which stages the job completed and where it will save output.
When your release exposes Stop and save, use it when you need to interrupt and continue later. Wait for the checkpoint to finish writing before closing the app.
Ilaria RVC 2.1.0 supports epoch and total-step targets, including resuming partway through an epoch for step targets. Other frontends can expose different controls and resume behavior.

An epoch is one pass through the prepared dataset. A training step is one batch update. Divide the number of clips after preprocessing by the effective batch size to estimate steps per epoch. For example, 10,000 clips at a batch size of 8 gives 1,250 batches per epoch in a single-worker run. Dropped partial batches, multiple GPUs, or gradient accumulation can change how the trainer counts updates. Use the count reported by your run when comparing experiments.

Choose a save interval that gives you several checkpoints to audition. Saving about every 40 epochs is one possible starting point for a run measured in hundreds of epochs. Use the same held-out clips and inference settings for each comparison. Listen for intelligibility, stable pitch, natural pauses, and consonants that stay clear. If later exports sound harsher or work well on only a few phrases, compare with an earlier checkpoint and inspect the dataset for repeated takes or artifacts. Pick the checkpoint that works best across your intended inputs.

Open inference with an exported .pth. Use the same short held-out recordings and the same conversion settings to compare models from different checkpoints. If you make an index comparison, hold the checkpoint steady and compare the same clip with retrieval disabled and enabled.
Compare these four qualities across exports.
Timbre. Does the converted recording resemble the intended vocal character across the whole phrase?
Intelligibility. Are consonants and word endings still easy to understand?
Pitch stability. Do notes or syllables jump, warble, or lose their intended inflection?
Artifacts. Does the output add buzzing, embedded room noise, harsh tails, or odd transitions?

Keep the best sounding export and its test outputs. More epochs can be worth trying when results improve across several examples. If later exports only improve one clip or begin reproducing flaws from the dataset, return to the best baseline and review the recordings.
Use in inference. Select the exported model .pth. Keep its corresponding .index alongside it when you want retrieval. Record any required embedder, supported client, and sample-rate information.

Resume training. Back up the experiment and keep the matching generator and discriminator training checkpoints, commonly named G_*.pth and D_*.pth. Resume with the same experiment and compatible configuration, then inspect the log for the checkpoint and step or epoch you expected. An inference export alone lacks the full training state.
Share a model. Share only files you have permission to distribute. Include listening examples, compatibility notes, the matching index if useful, and any usage terms the recipient needs.

In Ilaria RVC, recent releases use the model library for inference exports and associated indexes. Export paths and naming can differ across frontends. Save the experiment logs separately if you want to recreate the model later.
Symptom
Check first
Preprocessing found no audio
Verify the selected dataset folder and play an input clip. Check whether your build reads nested folders.
Extraction fails or reports a missing model
Check the selected embedder and pitch model assets, and read the first message in the extraction log.
GPU memory runs out
Reduce batch size, stop competing GPU jobs, and disable GPU dataset caching if your build offers that control. Retry the failing stage.
Training restarts at the beginning
Check that the experiment points to compatible training checkpoints and that any fresh-start option is off.
A .pth will not load for conversion
Check whether you selected a training checkpoint instead of an inference export, and verify architecture and embedder compatibility with the client.
A usable model has no index
Check whether index generation was skipped or failed. Export and test the checkpoint independently, then build its index from the matching experiment if needed.
Keep the first failing message and the configuration associated with the run. For more checks, see Troubleshooting.

l: Indicative Training Profiles (Adapt to Your Data & Hardware)
p: These three presets are indicative starting points, not universal rules. Always adjust Batch Size to fit your VRAM and judge checkpoints by listening to the same held-out test clips.
Best for: First voice model, 5–15 minutes of clean single-speaker audio, 6–8 GB VRAM GPUs.

Settings: RVC v2 · 40 kHz (or 32 kHz for RefineGAN) · Pitch Guidance ON (rmvpe) · Embedder contentvec · Stock/verified HiFi-GAN pretrain · Batch Size 4–8 · Epochs 200 (save every 25–50 epochs) · Precision FP32 (or BF16 on RTX 30/40/50) · GPU Caching OFF · Workers 2 · Fused AdamW OFF.
Why: Prioritizes stability and avoids out-of-memory errors or early overfitting while producing multiple checkpoints to compare.
Best for: 15–30 minutes of cleaned speech/singing, 8–12 GB VRAM GPUs.

Settings: RVC v2 · 40 kHz or 48 kHz (if source bandwidth reaches >20 kHz) · rmvpe · contentvec or klm-vocal-contentvec / spin-v2 (matched to pretrain) · Batch Size 8–12 · Epochs 250–350 (or equivalent Total Steps) · Save every 25–50 epochs · Precision BF16 (RTX 30/40/50) or FP16 (T4/RTX 20) · Workers 4, Prefetch 4–8 · Build FAISS Auto index after choosing the best checkpoint.
Why: Uses faster mixed precision and larger batches while keeping regular checkpoints and held-out listening previews.
Best for: Large or curated multi-emotion/singing datasets, 12–24 GB+ VRAM, custom pretrains.

Settings: RVC v2 · Matched rate (32/40/48 kHz) & vocoder (HiFi-GAN, MRF HiFi-GAN, or RefineGAN at 32 kHz in Ilaria RVC) · Custom/matched G/D pretrain & embedder · Batch Size 12–16+ · Total Steps target (for consistent gradient updates regardless of dataset size) · GPU Caching ON (only if VRAM comfortably fits the dataset; benchmark epoch time first) · Fused AdamW ON (test in a fresh run) · Training Queue for overnight A/B runs · TensorBoard monitoring + Audio Analyzer comparison.

Learning rate: Most RVC WebUIs (including Ilaria RVC) use the standard RVC v2 optimizer schedule (1e-4 base); only change learning rate in frontends that expose it if you understand how it scales with batch size.

l: How to Spot Underfitting vs. Overfitting by Ear
p: Underfitting (too early): The output still sounds mostly like the input speaker, misses target timbre on sustained vowels, or loses character on high/low notes. Fix: Continue training from the latest G_*.pth/D_*.pth checkpoint.

Overfitting (too late): The voice sounds robotic/metallic on unfamiliar words, reproduces dataset room noise or breath artifacts, or sounds great only on phrases similar to the training set. Fix: Roll back to an earlier checkpoint (50–100 epochs earlier) and inspect the dataset in Audio Analyzer.
If you are training with Redpanda-vc (which adds Generator EMA and step-based checkpoint saving), see Train RVC Models in Redpanda-vc.
